texto: Adelaide was born in Burgundy (France) and very young married Lothair, King of Italy. He was murdered, leaving her a widow with a daughter at 19. The usurper Berengar wanted to marry her to his son to consolidate his power. She refused and was imprisoned, but accepted everything as coming from God. Her jailers said: “How much heroism this queen has! She doesn’t shout, she doesn’t despair, she doesn’t insult. She only prays and smiles through her tears!”

Her chaplain helped her escape, and she turned to the German king Otto I to defeat Berengar. They married in 951, and the Pope crowned them in Rome as emperors of the renewed Holy Roman Empire. She was kind and generous to her subjects, winning their affection. She devoted herself to relieving the poor and helping missionaries and religious. She founded several monasteries and cared for the evangelization of those who did not yet know the Catholic faith.

Widowed in 973, she was mistreated by her stepson Otto II and his wife, who forced her to abdicate. Despite her suffering, she always responded with kindness and meekness. After both died, she was regent for her grandson Otto III until he came of age. She retired to a monastery and spent her days in prayer until 999. Pope Urban II canonized her in 1097.
They came from Rome around the year 50 and, being tentmakers like Saint Paul, began to accompany him in his apostolate in Ephesus and Corinth.
They welcomed the local Christians to hear the Word and celebrate the Eucharist; this is how the Church took shape in believers’ homes.
They trained the young Apollos, who became a great preacher.
Saint Paul mentioned them in his letters as “a unit” and tells with great gratitude how they “risked their necks” for him. They are believed to have been martyred later in Rome.
They embody the era of Christian resistance for religious freedom against the Moors in Spain.
At first they hid their faith, and some pretended to be Muslims, but later they resolved to bear witness to their Christian faith, whatever the consequences.
The enthusiasm of Aurelius and Natalia inspired their friends Felix and Liliosa to give public witness, even knowing they were risking their lives.

Forewarned by two angels, the friends, together with the monk George, took up a regime of discipline and prayer to prepare for martyrdom, which finally came when they publicly professed their faith in a town square.

Of noble lineage, her father governed the main Swedish province. At barely 6 years old she had her first apparition of the Blessed Virgin, who invited her to lead a holy life. Heavenly apparitions would be frequent throughout her life, especially of Jesus Crucified.
As a couple they fed the poor from their palace. She was summoned to court, where she tried to cultivate the virtues and relationships of the royals, but was disappointed by its vices and frivolity.
She asked her husband Ulf to go on pilgrimage together to Santiago de Compostela. On the way back he fell gravely ill, but she prayed for his healing and was heard.

Once widowed, she founded the Order of the Most Holy Savior, which her daughter Saint Catherine of Sweden would carry on. She lived 14 years in Rome to meet with authorities and the Pope, giving counsel; she traveled to the Holy Land.
Her revelations were so highly valued that they used to be read at Mass.
They married in 996, and in 1000 Pope Sylvester II crowned him king; together they pioneered the evangelization of Hungary, both human and cultural, founding schools, hospices and monasteries.

He personally attended to everyone with great kindness, gave an extraordinary amount of alms and, it is said, went out at night disguised as a bricklayer to help; he wrote for his son a book of very wise reflections and counsels for life.

They prayed together, had an enormous devotion to the Virgin and invoked her in difficult moments; they were a shining example of family life: with their son Saint Emeric, the people call them “the Hungarian Holy Family.”

In their last years they suffered great trials: the death of their son and heir in a hunting accident, and the exile of the widowed Gisela at the hands of relatives who wanted her away from the throne; she died as an abbess.

Gianna was born in Magenta (Milan) in 1922. From childhood she embraced the faith and a Christian upbringing. In high school and university she was active in Catholic Action and the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, devoting herself to young people and the needy. She qualified as a surgeon in 1949 and then specialized in pediatrics. She considered her work a mission, but it did not keep her from devoting herself even more to the apostolate with young women.

In 1955 she married the engineer Pietro. She harmonized with joy and balance her duties as mother, wife and doctor. In 1961, during her fourth pregnancy, she was diagnosed with a uterine tumor. Before surgery she begged the surgeon to save the life in her womb at all costs, and entrusted herself in prayer to Providence.

On April 21, 1962, Gianna Emanuela was born. A week later, saying “Jesus, I love you; Jesus, I love you,” she died a holy death at 39. She was beatified by John Paul II in 1994, the International Year of the Family. Her daughter today gives pro-life talks and testimonies around the world.

Louis’s mother, Blessed Queen Blanche of Castile, gave him a very Christian upbringing. As a couple they enjoyed each other’s company and were an example to their kingdom. He said he never undertook anything important without agreeing on it with his wife.

Louis founded libraries and a hospital for the blind, and was famous for imposing absolutely impartial justice. He invited the poor to eat and had food distributed to them. Amid his duties as monarch, he prayed the Liturgy of the Hours daily and read the Scriptures and the Church Fathers assiduously.
He organized two of the Crusades, feeling called by God to free Christian lands; on the first he traveled with his wife.
His friend and biographer Joinville said: “We do not know what to admire most in him: the knight, the religious man, the patriarch, the king or the man.”

They married in Alençon (France) on July 12, 1858, only three months after they first met. They taught their daughters to see worldly things as pure vanity. They bore the death of 3 young children with fortitude.
In their last years, until Zélie died of a tumor, they kept exchanging letters when apart, tenderly expressing how much they loved and missed each other.

Grounded in a solid family spiritual formation, all five daughters embraced religious vocations. Louis joyfully supported each one’s decision. In his last years he suffered in silence an illness that left him bedridden.
In 2015 they became the first married couple canonized together.
“God gave me parents more worthy of heaven than of this earth” (their youngest daughter, Saint Thérèse of Lisieux)

Margaret descended from the English nobility but was born in Hungary, where her family was in exile. Her family failed to regain the English throne, and while trying to flee, a storm landed them in Scotland, where they sought asylum at the court of King Malcolm.

Although he was a widower 20 years her senior, they married in 1050. He was illiterate but would spend hours listening to his wife read the Scriptures. She gradually transformed him until he became a great Christian sovereign; she instructed her husband and children in the faith and doctrine. Among their children were 2 saints and 3 kings.
They lived in strict austerity, with penitential practices such as serving the poor and orphans. She encouraged her subjects to read the lives of the saints.

Little by little she managed to root out the pagan practices of the druids and establish Christian customs. Father Turgot, her confessor, wrote: “The queen joined to the sweetness of her character a strict sense of duty, and even in her severity she was so gentle that everyone instinctively came to love her.” Her health weakened and she died at only 47. She is patroness of mothers and of education.

They had a very difficult marriage because of her husband’s infidelity and mistreatment for almost all his life. Monica persevered and prayed in silence for some 30 years until he fell ill and, moved by her example, repented and converted shortly before his death, dying in peace.

Monica traveled to Rome and then to Milan, sleepless over the worldliness of her son Augustine. There she drew close to Saint Ambrose, the influential bishop who was standing up to the Roman emperors and their Arian heresy. He would be the main influence on Augustine’s conversion and baptism.

With everything she had prayed for in her life fulfilled, she set out with Augustine to return to Africa. But after moments of mystical ecstasy and rich shared conversations at the port of Ostia, she died. In time he would be recognized as the great Saint Augustine of Hippo, bishop and Doctor of the Church.

He was the son of a chief who converted with the first generation of Catholics in the region. He prayed fervently, visited the Blessed Sacrament on his way to work and received Communion daily with deep devotion.

He became the youngest catechist in the area, and his peers soon recognized his undisputed leadership. He fell in love with and married his student Paula; they were very happy, though they had their difficulties.

In 1945 the Japanese took it out on the population, pressing for a return to pre-Christian customs, especially polygamy. Taking the risk, Peter kept baptizing, marrying, caring for the sick and helping the poor, until he was arrested for serving as a catechist of “forbidden Christianity.” At 33 he was martyred by lethal injection. He was canonized on 10/19/25 by Pope Leo XIV.

The Mores led a truly happy and devout family life. Thomas used to lead everyone in his house (family and friends) in night prayer in his chapel; his son-in-law said in his biography that he “never remembers seeing him in a bad mood.”
He taught his wife or his daughter Latin and Greek for 1 or 2 hours every night. He was a writer and poet, and his most famous work is “Utopia,” on the social problems of humanity.
He acted as a lawyer for the needy and the weakest. He was well off but had no interest in accumulating money.
Although he had been an upright and exemplary chancellor, he bravely accepted the martyrdom imposed by Henry VIII for defending the true faith and the indissolubility of marriage.

Anna Maria was a model wife and mother, carefully raising her children in Christian principles; she made her house a home of prayer, order and serenity. She kept peace in the home and did everything from the heart: “The best penance is patience.”
From her sewing work she set aside some money for the poor and the sick; she became a Trinitarian tertiary together with her friend, Blessed Elizabeth Canori Mora.

Although she was practically illiterate, God gave her incredible insights and revelations about the dangers threatening the Church; she was consulted by everyone from cardinals and society ladies to workers and professionals.

Domenico was a hardworking but coarse and bad-tempered man; little by little she transformed him into a good Christian. At 91 he testified for his wife’s beatification: “Anna Maria was the happiness of the family, always kind and smiling.”

Born in 1862, she became engaged at 13, out of love: “the engagement did not make me any less God’s; it was so easy for me to join both things!” For the wedding “I asked Jesus a great deal to help me make my companion happy” and “I asked my husband to let me receive Communion daily.” She offered God a son and a daughter, who would become a priest and a nun.

She had powerful mystical experiences during her busy life as a mother, and kept a personal diary for 40 years, 66 volumes of revelations from Jesus for laypeople, married people and religious. A panel of theologians concluded that she was inspired by God.

In her last conversation with Pancho, gravely ill, she asked: “What is your last wish for me?” and he answered: “That you be all God’s and all our children’s.” Widowed at 39, God consoled her with the news that Pancho had been freed from Purgatory, and that He would now take her as His spiritual spouse. She later lost 4 children.
During the Cristero revolution she bravely hid priests and bishops. She founded the Works of the Cross, which include laypeople, missionaries, nuns and priests.

Born in Milan in 1813, he was a professor of law in Lyon and of literature at the Sorbonne. He married Amélie, the rector’s daughter, and she accompanied him in all his undertakings. In 1833, a time of upheaval in society and in the Church, with 7 friends and only 20 years old, he took action by founding the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, devoted to home visits to the most afflicted.
He was also one of the forerunners of Christian Democracy, making an in-depth study of democracy and Christianity, out of concern over Catholics’ indifference to joining political life.

Frédéric was a witness of charity in his family, professional and civic life, and a faithful defender of the poor. Gifted with a rare sensitivity, he deeply impressed those who knew him. Although he died at 40, he greatly influenced lay charity in 19th- and 20th-century Europe: his work spread around the world and today has some 750,000 lay members in 30 countries.
Born in Austria to a Jewish family, she converted one Easter after a miraculous healing of her kidneys and seeing the witness of service of the hospital nuns.

She studied philosophy and earned a doctorate in economics. She was elected to parliament for the Christian Social party and, as the only woman, the bishop of Vienna nicknamed her “the conscience of Parliament.”
She was advised to have an abortion because of her fragile health, but said it “would be murder.” Despite the risks, her daughter Lisa was born healthy.

A tireless social worker, she founded works for Christian women working at home, an association of Christian women workers and the charitable congregation “Sisters of Caritas Socialis.” She was about to be appointed Minister of Social Affairs when she died, at only 50. In 2012 she became the first politician to be beatified.

Luigi was a brilliant Sicilian lawyer who rose to deputy attorney general of the state and knew the great politicians of the postwar era. Maria was a teacher and writer on education, committed to several associations (Catholic Action, Scouts, etc.). She did not hesitate to serve as a volunteer nurse in the Ethiopian war and World War II. They married on November 25, 1905.

They lived ordinary life in an extraordinary way. They reached a deep interior life: life as a vocation, the family as a domestic church, work as an evangelical mission, and talking over their needs with God. At the center, daily Eucharist and filial devotion to the Virgin with their rosary every evening.

3 of their children became priests or religious. She said: “We raised them in the faith, so that they would know God and love Him.” While expecting their last daughter, a complication was diagnosed and doctors advised abortion given a 5% chance of survival, but they chose to take the risk; Enrichetta later thanked her parents for “the act of Christian heroism.” In 2001 their 3 surviving children witnessed their parents’ beatification alongside Pope John Paul II.

Born in Carpi in 1907. A fervent Catholic, he was formed in Catholic Action and at 19 was already secretary of the diocesan youth federation; he founded the Catholic Scouts, becoming their leader in his diocese and a reference in Italy. At 27 he was president of Catholic Action in Italy, when the Fascists were competing to win over young people.
He married Maria, from Catholic Action, in 1930 and went from selling insurance to becoming, in 1937, managing director of the newspaper Avvenire, which wrote fiery criticism of Fascism.

In 1943, together with Fr. Dante Sala, he organized a network that smuggled more than a hundred Jews into Switzerland. He obtained the documents and arranged the funding. He was told, “You’re exposing yourself too much, are you thinking of your children?” He replied: “If you had seen in prison, as I have, what the Jews suffer, you would regret not saving more.”

In 1944 he was arrested by the Nazis in a hospital while caring for a sick Jew. He was sent to the Hersbruck camp to do inhuman labor. He died on December 27, 1944, at 37, of an untreated wound. The Jewish community awarded him a gold medal, and he is one of the few non-Jews named Righteous Among the Nations.

Carlo was born in Italy to a family of French nobles; he was admitted to Napoleon’s court, where he met Giulia; they married, and in 1810 he became a count. They settled in Turin, where as mayor and city councilor he developed infrastructure and education and set up a shelter for the children of poor workers.

Shaken by the conditions of women prisoners, she created a project for their social rehabilitation: she taught them to read and write, gave them clothes and blankets, and introduced choral singing to steer them away from alcoholism.

As they could not have children, they decided to adopt poor children from the town. In 1834 they founded the Sisters of Saint Anne to educate young people and 2 Catholic schools, and in 1835 they housed and cared for cholera victims in their own home.

Giulia was widowed in 1838 and became a teacher and a Franciscan tertiary. She founded a hospital for the disabled (with Don Bosco as chaplain), vocational schools and shelters for women and girls, known today as the Barolo Social District.
Dorotea was born in Santiago in 1816 into a wealthy Catholic family with 18 children! When she was 3, as Chile became independent, her royalist family fled to Barcelona.

At 16, against her family, who wanted to take her to Uruguay, she married José María, a businessman and banker who had also emigrated from Chile (later Chilean consul and co-founder of the Bank of Barcelona). They were happily married for half a century; she accompanied him on his travels. José said: “our love grew daily.”

Dorotea was energetic, lively, enterprising and very devout: daily Mass, the rosary and a confessor she kept for 50 years. After a mass burning of monasteries, they undertook a great transformation: 32 works including kindergartens, schools, hospitals (the first children’s hospital in Spain) and workshops. She was called “God’s almoner.”

She was received with great deference by Leo XIII. When she was widowed she was among the richest people in the city; she donated her half of the inheritance to the works. In 1882 she asked Don Bosco to found a work for young workers. She became a Salesian Cooperator. In 1886 they met: he called her “our mother of Barcelona.” Finally she gave the savings of her old age to found another school and died poor in 1891.

Born in 1921. Sailing with the Naval School, he bore witness to his faith through committed apostolic work. In the history of the Argentine Navy he is the youngest officer ever to graduate. A book on the responsibilities of a Christian changed his life; he felt God calling him to the mission of humanely leading the lives of workers.
As a married couple, they radiated a climate of family joy that they generously shared. They led a sober life and took part in the aid to postwar Europe that the bishops promoted in 1946.
As a company director, Enrique lived his work as an apostolate, with constant concern for his employees. When he fell ill with cancer, 260 of them donated “workers’ blood,” as he himself put it.
In 1952 he co-founded the Christian Association of Business Leaders (ACDE) and was its first president. He was declared venerable in 2021.
Jérôme was born in 1926, and in 1952 he married the Dane Birthe, who converted to Catholicism; he would write to her every single day they were apart.

After qualifying as a pediatrician, he joined the National Center for Scientific Research, the largest in France. In 1958, examining the chromosomes of a child with Down syndrome with a photomicroscope of his own invention, he discovered the anomaly in chromosome 21 that causes it. He became a world authority, the “father of modern genetics.”

He treated more than 9,000 patients with intellectual disabilities and was a candidate for the Nobel Prize, but it never came, since he campaigned in defense of life even in parliament, with Christian and scientific conviction. He lost his funding and became a professional outcast.

On the day in 1981 when John Paul II was shot, he had had breakfast with Lejeune and his wife. They became close friends, and in 1994 the Pope named him first president of the newly created Pontifical Academy for Life, but he died days later. Birthe took up his crusade, with which she fully identified. She died in 2020. In January 2021 Pope Francis declared him venerable.
In 1947 he took part in the blessing of the cornerstone of the Schoenstatt Shrine in Santa Maria (Brazil), where he met Fr. Joseph Kentenich. He was 50, and it marked him forever.

In 1950 he was entrusted with the beginnings of what would become the Rosary Campaign, now in 100 countries. While caring for his home (“my family is my first mission”), he walked 140,000 km across Brazil carrying the Schoenstatt “Mater,” doing true family ministry and calling himself “Mary’s little donkey.”

Around 1955 he founded the “Noble Village of Charity,” building by hand houses for poor families who lived on the street. In 1985, after 40 years of daily apostolate, he offered his life for the growth of the Campaign, and days later he was run over on his way to his usual morning Mass at the shrine.
In June 2025 Leo XIV declared him venerable.

Born Marcello Loewy, son of a wealthy Hungarian-Jewish banker and a mother from Trieste (Italy). He married Elsa in 1912 in a Jewish ceremony, and World War I took them to Slovenia, where in 1914 they were baptized in fulfillment of a vow to the Virgin.

He earned a reputation as the doctor of the poor in Pula (Croatia) and did passionate research to treat tuberculosis. From 1929 the couple rediscovered the faith, with their apostolate in Catholic Action and the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul.

Elsa endured an ordeal of illness that ended in the amputation of a leg. She prophesied that, once widowed, he would become a priest. So it happened at 48: with his children grown and his possessions given away, he was ordained a priest in 1940.

He had to go into exile for being Jewish, and later, at the end of the war, the Communists arrested him for 4 months because of his preaching. He would later be monsignor and rector of the seminary and then pastor of the Cathedral of San Giusto in Trieste. In 1954 he suffered a heart attack, which he himself diagnosed as terminal. He has been Venerable since 2015.

Pierre Toussaint grew up as a slave on a plantation in Haiti, with the rare fortune of being allowed to study. At 21 he moved with his owners to New York, where they let him train as a hairdresser. He quickly became so well off that he was soon helping financially the lady of the house, who had been widowed.
When she died he became a free man at 45 and managed to buy the freedom of Juliette, also a Haitian slave, 20 years younger, who was in another city with her owners. They married in 1811.

The Toussaints went to daily Mass and undertook a series of charitable works: the first school for Black children, an agency to help people find jobs, microloans for the needy, donations to an orphanage, and they even took in homeless people in their own home.
Pierre personally cared for cholera victims during an epidemic and raised substantial funds for the construction of Saint Patrick’s Cathedral.

Sergio was born in 1882 and received a good moral and religious education. At 25 he married Emilia Romani, but he immediately lost his first child, soon afterward his parents and his brother, then his second child, his wife and his youngest daughter. He was left alone with many debts to pay. He worked as a bricklayer with his uncles and went with companions to a mine in America, hoping to pay off his debts.

Back in Modena, his parish priest asked him to become a priest, but he preferred to think of marrying and met Domenica. They formed a solid couple grounded in prayer, the daily rosary and Sunday Mass, even though the church was several kilometers away.

Their children took part in the Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament and in the Office of the Franciscan Tertiaries; 6 became nuns (5 Paulines and one Ursuline) and 2 Capuchin friars (one became bishop of Smyrna, Turkey). An adopted son of Sergio would also become a bishop in his country, Nigeria.

Through the illness and painful crisis of hope that Sergio suffered in his last two years, his wife was always close to him. They lived with simplicity and authenticity, as credible witnesses of the Church. Pope Francis declared them venerable.

In 1976 their only biological son was born; a month later Vittorio suffered severe ulcerative colitis that nearly cost him his life and left serious after-effects, though only his wife and colleagues knew.
They then adopted 7 children, some with disabilities.
He studied the Scriptures and enjoyed collaborating with Jews at the Ecumenical Center of Perugia, where they nicknamed him “our rabbi.”
With his wife and some friends he founded an association to welcome women and children facing social exclusion.
Because of his commitment to the sick and his closeness to those who suffered, his colleagues called him “the saint of the operating room”; he died at 54.
The humble son of a policeman, he studied in Vienna and was a deputy for the Italian People’s Party; in 1927 he was imprisoned for denouncing the Fascist dictatorship.
After the war he founded a Catholic-inspired party to stop the rise of communism: Christian Democracy; he led the government for 8 terms (1945–53), promoting the establishment of the republic in ’46.
He was a Franciscan tertiary and took a family member on every state trip; he described himself as “first a Christian, then a European, then an Italian.”

He sowed the seeds of today’s European Union together with Konrad Adenauer and the now Venerable Robert Schuman. He died in 1954 without much property and without seeing all the fruits of his efforts, but with a reputation for holiness. His coffin was greeted in every city by grieving crowds, and today he is considered one of the fathers of the Italian Republic and the European Union.

A lawyer, he took part in Catholic Youth and the Workers’ Circle. Adela was Colombian and studied in Europe. Her concern for social problems led her to Caracas, to the Catholic School of Social Work, where they met.
They married in 1949 and chose the humble standard of living he could offer at the time, turning down the house her parents wanted to give them.

Teaching was his constant vocation. He acted as an independent politician but identified with the Church’s social doctrine. He founded the institute (IFEDEC) that bears his name and presided over the Christian Democratic Organization of America. He was a deputy, senator and Minister of Foreign Affairs, and took part in drafting the 1961 Constitution. He advocated democratic solutions to the civil wars in Central America.

In 1986, in a plane crash in Guatemala, the couple and two of their daughters lost their lives. Christian Democracy awards the Arístides Calvani Prize every year for peace, democracy and human development.
Well-off Brazilians, they loved books and the arts, spoke several languages and were raised in solid Catholic principles.

After they married, Jerônimo became a Franciscan tertiary and Zélia taught catechism and literacy, founded a school for children and parents, and in the afternoons was teacher and catechist to her children, her employees and their families.

On their estate they were always attentive to the needs of their servants and slaves; when the slaves were freed by law, they did not leave, because they admired their masters: “they are a holy couple!”
Their nine surviving children embraced the priesthood or religious life: 2 Good Shepherd Sisters, 4 Dorotheans, 1 Lazarist, 1 Jesuit and 1 Franciscan.
Widowed, Zélia took the religious habit in the last year and a half of her life.

She grew up in an aristocratic Orthodox Christian family in pre-revolutionary Russia in 1896. In World War I, serving as a nurse, she was decorated for bravery. But she was captured, and promised God to consecrate her life to Him if He saved her. Later, escaping death under the Bolsheviks, she went into exile.
She converted to Catholicism and in 1921 arrived in Canada in extreme poverty. She worked as a domestic servant, and her marriage to her adulterous cousin was soon annulled.
She prospered financially thanks to her talent as a lecturer, until in 1939 she felt that keeping her promise required giving everything to God and the poor.

She founded a Friendship House in Toronto to help those affected by the Great Depression, and later another in Harlem. There the Irish journalist Eddie interviewed her, was amazed by the work, and they married in 1943. They returned to Canada and founded the Catholic newspaper Restoration and a lay formation center, Madonna House, which they consecrated to the Virgin, focused on holiness in daily life. He became a Greek Catholic priest, and she wrote several spiritual books read worldwide.
They met on a pilgrimage to Medjugorje in 2002.
They refused to abort their first 2 children, who had malformations; the babies lived only half an hour, but they were able to baptize them. They gave many pro-life talks about their experience.
In 2011 they had a healthy pregnancy, but a carcinoma appeared; once again she refused abortion and delayed her treatment: “I don’t want to die for Francesco, I want to give my life to Francesco.”

After the metastases, she entrusted her son to God in Assisi, left him letters, and in May they met Benedict XVI; on June 16, 2012, a thousand people packed the parish to bid her farewell with guitars, bongos, violins and a huge choir.

Born in Rwanda. Cyprien was sent to the seminary; without much spiritual motivation, he lost his faith under the influence of existentialism. As a government official he promoted traditional art and became a renowned poet, composer and choreographer.

His fiancée was murdered and, to honor the family, he married her cousin Daphrose, a woman deeply devoted to prayer. For 17 years they went through great conflicts and separated for a time. They reconciled even though he had been unfaithful. His arrogance and atheism caused her great suffering, but she believed in the holiness of marriage and prayed patiently.

In 1982 Cyprien fell gravely ill. Fearing for his life, he wrote a song about his death; suddenly he was filled with the Holy Spirit, came to believe in God and underwent a radical conversion. He asked Daphrose’s forgiveness for her sufferings, their marriage was restored and renewed, and he became a humble and faithful husband, open to all.
So in 1990 they founded the Emmanuel Community to help street children, open to all ethnic groups. Today it is the second-largest Emmanuel community in the world.

Their multi-ethnic commitment put them on a list of undesirables, and on April 7, 1994, the first day of the genocide of 800,000, they were murdered with 6 of their children after praying before the Blessed Sacrament. The song of theirs he had rehearsed with his choir that day was “I Will Enter Heaven Dancing.”

Elisabeth discovered that her future husband was an atheist but, deeply in love, agreed to marry him if he promised not to stand in the way of her faith. After 7 years it was she who stopped going to church and seeing Catholics. Then Félix gave her an anti-Christian book to draw her toward his atheism... and achieved exactly the opposite.

Elisabeth built her own personal Catholic library and acquired a solid, fervent faith. He mocked her faith, but even amid their bitter differences they truly loved each other. In 1914 she died of cancer in Félix’s arms. Then his sister-in-law gave him his wife’s private diary to read for the first time, and so he learned of the cares and sacrifices she had made for his conversion. He set off for Lourdes in a resentful mood, but there the Virgin granted him conversion and the forgiveness of his sins.

He received a peace and serenity his soul had never known. He wrote: “I had been conquered! Light had been made.” In 1917 he published Elisabeth’s Diary, which sold 100,000 copies. He felt called to total self-giving: he entered the Dominican novitiate, was ordained at 62, and was given as his apostolate spreading the story of Elisabeth’s life.

In 1971 a tragic road accident and Saint Louis de Montfort’s Consecration transformed them; the Conikers sold their successful systems company and left with their 8 children for Fatima to rethink their lives.

They felt called to transform families spiritually and returned to lead the Militia of the Immaculata (founded by Saint Maximilian Kolbe). In 1975 they founded the Apostolate for Family Consecration in the U.S., restored a seminary to promote “family retreats,” and for many years produced television for EWTN with Jerry as narrator.

Strongly pro-life, Gwen was advised to have an abortion for health reasons but refused, and so their 11th child was born healthy; she had two more. They became very close to Mother Teresa and John Paul II. Their work spread to 8 countries; they published a Family Catechism approved by the bishops.
Gwen died in 2002; Jerry in 2018, having first managed to open her cause.

Both born in Canada; she considered becoming a nun, but when World War I broke out she secretly enrolled in a nursing course and went to work in a military hospital. In 1921 she married the war hero Georges Vanier and, posted abroad, worked for dozens of social causes. In postwar Paris in 1945, while he was ambassador, she helped the flood of refugees through the Red Cross with workshops and housing. France awarded her the Legion of Honor for her heroic efforts.

Georges became Governor General of Canada in 1959, and she became a memorable First Lady, visiting hospitals, schools, factories and prisons. They convened the first Conference on the Family, which gave rise to the Vanier Institute of the Family, still active today.

After Georges’s death in 1967, Pauline became chancellor of the University of Ottawa. But she still felt an emptiness in her life, and at 73 she went to France, where her son had founded the L’Arche community for adults with disabilities. She offered them formation and spiritual support, living there 19 fulfilling years until she was 93.
Both French, they met at 15 and married at 22. At 17 he had published the Book of Love, which sold 10 million copies.

Raoul was a journalist, and in 1935, when the Argentine newspaper La Nación sent him to Africa to research the story of the now Saint Charles de Foucauld, he discovered that there were still millions of lepers in the world, which changed their lives forever. They would travel the world embracing these sick people.

He created a foundation to fight leprosy and got the UN to formalize the annual worldwide celebration of World Leprosy Day. He promoted crusades: “The Hour of the Poor,” youth service for peace, “Give Me 2 Bombers for Leprosy” and the “1st World Day of Peace.” Raoul gave up his soul in 1977 and Madeleine in 1991.
Takashi was a radiology student from a Shinto family, lodging in the Moriyama home. Christians by Jesuit heritage, they gradually converted him by their example.

He went to the war in Manchuria, and in 1934 he married Midori. He became a prestigious radiologist and researcher. But during World War II he was diagnosed with leukemia from accumulated exposure to radiation; Midori prayed for him every day.

In 1945 the atomic bomb fell on Nagasaki, destroying everything. Takashi survived, and from the hospital he cared for everyone for 2 days with a deep wound in his temple. Then he found Midori’s charred body in their home, praying with her rosary in her hand. He grew worse for weeks until he was given up for dead and received the last rites. But an inner voice told him, “Ask Maximilian Kolbe for your life,” whom he had known. So he made a miraculous recovery and lived 6 more years with his children.

He went on to study the effects of the explosion, publishing 12 books with his experience as a scientist and survivor and calling for peace. He kept providing heroic medical service despite his leukemia until he was bedridden in a small wooden hut. His fortitude lifted the spirits of all the people of Nagasaki. Thousands honored him at his death.

Tomás and Paquita met in Barcelona and it was love at first sight, but 13 years passed before they could marry in 1939. He became a professor, educator and school principal. They took great care to live humility with their children and always raised them in an atmosphere of freedom.
Tomás met Saint Josemaría Escrivá and during the Civil War crossed the Pyrenees with him to rejoin his family. He asked to be admitted to Opus Dei in 1947, and Paquita 5 years later.

For many years they kept one afternoon a week to go out together to the theater, the movies or for a walk. Their children said that “from the way their parents looked at each other, all the children wanted to imitate them.” He said: “When we are at home we need nothing else. I love her more every day. Much, much more than when we were engaged.”

Abraham lived in a tiny room in a poor neighborhood of Caracas (Venezuela). In 1940 he was 23 when his young neighbor Patricia took him to meet the Virgin, the Divine Shepherdess. They married in the Jesuit church, and Abraham soon joined the Legion of Mary. Later he would be one of the first 8 married deacons in the country.

When they already had 6 children, a firework fell on their shack one Christmas and burned it down. He was a bricklayer and saw it as a sign to build something roomier with the future in mind. They came to have 13 children, plus 6 others they raised, children of neighbors who had to work or were in prison. Patricia carried water 3 km every day.

With the Jesuit Fr. Vélaz they evangelized boys who had nowhere to study, among other basic needs. Abraham immediately offered his house to gather and teach them. Thus took shape the work “Fe y Alegría” (Faith and Joy), today in 17 Latin American countries and in Spain and Italy, serving migrants and offering many other training and development programs for Latin Americans in Italy. Abraham died in 1988 and Patricia on 2/15/2006. Their cause was opened in 2022.
Acahilda was born into the German nobility and was the sister of Saint Cunigunde. Her name means “God keeps fighting.”
She married Thietmar and was the mother of quintuplets. When she was pregnant, in the middle of winter she longed for cherries, and a tree in her garden suddenly produced a full crop of them.
Later she and her husband, drawn to religious life, took vows of celibacy.
She stood out for her charity toward the poor and as a wonderworker.

She died in 970 of natural causes and is buried in the church in Wendelstein, Germany, which she had founded. Her tomb was found in 1147, and the stone bore an inscription calling her “holy woman” and “founder of the parish church.” After the discovery many miraculous healings took place, especially on behalf of children, and as a result many offerings were made.
Regina came from an important family and became a countess by marrying Adalbert II, Count of Ostrevent; ten children were born of their happy marriage.

In 764 they founded a Benedictine convent in Denain, near Valenciennes (France); widowed while still young in 790, the countess took the religious veil there, seeking holiness through prayer and work.
Her eldest daughter Renfrida also entered and soon became her spiritual mother, taking on the role of abbess of the convent (of which only ruins remain today).
Such was Regina’s voluntary submission to her abbess daughter that both would later be venerated as saints.

Adrian was born in Constantinople (c. 278) and, like many young nobles, served in the guard of Emperor Galerius. Before his conversion he had persecuted Christians, until, in the line of duty, he witnessed a trial of 22 Christians. They were finally sentenced to be tortured and executed, but the serenity, peace and courage with which they faced pain and death made a tremendous impression on the soldier’s heart. After that experience young Adrian decided to become a Christian.

He soon fell in love with a young Christian woman named Natalia, whom he married. A path marked by the practice of charity followed, until later he was denounced for his faith and subjected to terrible torments after being arrested with companions with whom he was going to Caesarea to proclaim Christ.

The governor of Palestine had him scourged with hooks and then thrown to the beasts for refusing the offer of freedom if he renounced his faith. His wife Natalia stood by him in his hour of trial, encouraging and comforting him. He was executed around the year 309. He is patron of soldiers and intercessor against plagues.
Albertina taught combining gentleness with authority, using an integral education that sought the spiritual growth of the person. She was a mother, while remaining above all an educator.

In 1945 she became the first president of the Italian Women’s Center, where she opened training courses and summer camps for children and helped many young people to study. She moved with her husband and son to a school in Modena for poor pupils and often invited them to lunch.

She met Chiara Lubich, became a Focolarina and widened her family commitment by taking responsibility for many: women, young people and even a child with cancer whom she cared for in her home until he died.
The 2007 congress “The Courage of Education” in Florence was based entirely on Teacher Albertina’s educational method.

Born in Logroño in 1888, he was a farmer. Father of a large family and an ordinary Catholic in the first years of family life, at 31 he had a conversion experience, turning to a passionate love for God and an active, self-sacrificing love for the poor, the sick and vagrants, with his modest means.
At 40 he built a small house next to the family farmhouse, where he personally cared for the sick, those who needed lodging, and the abandoned. His charity was esteemed by the whole town.

His devotion to the Eucharist became very intense. He was a regular member of the Association of Adorers of the Blessed Sacrament, and later its president. Alberto took one hour a week and chose the hardest hours in the middle of the night for 15 years.
He died in 1965, and in 1998 the Holy Father signed the decree of his heroic virtues. One of his daughters is a Dominican sister in Peru.

He was simply a farmer from the Bergamo area, where he was born in the early 13th century. From childhood he walked in God’s path, putting into practice the precept of charity. On his family’s advice he married, but found neither affection nor understanding in his wife; yet his patience never wavered. His wife did not at first object to his generous example and devotion to the poor, but after her father-in-law’s death she began to criticize his work. Then, in a sudden conversion, she began to follow his example; she died shortly after 1240. They had no children.
When some powerful people disputed his ownership of his land, for the sake of peace he left his town and went to Cremona, living from the work of his hands.

Joining the Dominican Third Order, he devoted himself tirelessly to works of mercy, holding that it is always time to do good if there is the will to do it. He preached eloquently with deeds, giving a shining example of a charity little understood and even less practiced by so many Christians.

On May 7, 1279, he died peacefully. Many people came to venerate his body, drawn, according to popular tradition, by the miracle of the bells that rang without being touched. Pope Benedict XIV approved his cult in 1748 “from time immemorial.”
Alda was born in Siena in 1245 to the nobleman Francesco Ponzio and Agnese Bulgarini. From a very young age she felt the radical change the Gospel proposes to those who want to do God’s will.

After a good education, she was given in marriage to her fellow citizen Bindo, a man “virtutibus ornatissimus” (adorned with virtues), with whom she had no children. She was an exemplary wife at home and, above all, during her husband’s long illness.

After her husband’s early death, she took the habit of the Third Order of the Humiliati, who were very important throughout the Middle Ages. She gave herself to a life of penance in the solitude of her small property.

She spent her last years at the hospital of Sant’Andrea serving the poor, the sick and pilgrims. Alda was a soul devoted to the spiritual, and she distributed her property in Siena among the poor. She died on April 26, 1309, and her cult spread thanks to the Order of the Humiliati.

Aldo was born in 1916. He married Eleonora in 1945 and as a young man took part in drafting the new Constitution; he was undersecretary to De Gasperi and held several ministries. In 1963 he was elected head of government for the first time, a post he would hold for 4 more terms until 1976.

Moro was kidnapped in March 1978, on the day Andreotti’s new government was being presented. To capture him, the Red Brigades, left-wing extremists, killed his 5 bodyguards. A phase of communiqués and blackmail followed, during which Moro showed an unshakable faith over 55 days of captivity in the “people’s prison.” Pope Paul VI, his personal friend, asked the terrorists to free him unconditionally. But the government stood firm, and on May 9, 1978, his body was found in a car in the center of Rome. He was 61.
His daughter affirms that he is worthy of beatification for the way he lived and died. In 2017 the Vicariate of Rome accepted the process for his heroic virtues.
Alessandro was born in Verona in 1943 and graduated in medicine in the ’70s.

He married Luisa in 1971, and in 1978 they went to Brazil to work as a doctor in the missions of the Amazon region of Rondônia. He cared for sick children and lepers, until they had to return to Verona in 1982 after one of their daughters contracted malaria.

In August 1986, with his savings, inheritance and donations, he established the Regina Pacis Community in the hills near Verona, bringing together laypeople and consecrated persons. Thirty-four days later he died of a sudden heart attack. Twenty-eight priests concelebrated his funeral. The community would grow to 7 communities in the Veneto, Brazil and Budapest. His wife still lives in Italy.
In 2017 Pope Francis promulgated Alessandro’s heroic virtues. In 2021 the Community lost its papal approval after an apostolic visitation.

Diban was born around 1875 in southern Upper Volta (today Burkina Faso, Africa). At 17 he and his brother were captured and sold separately as slaves in Mali. He would never see him again. He tried to escape but was recaptured and suffered ever more inhuman treatment from his master. In 1899 he managed to flee, helped by a “young woman full of light” whom he did not know but later recognized in a convent: it was the Virgin Mary.

In 1901 he became the first Catholic of Upper Volta, with the name Alfred Simon. He married Louise in 1904. Once he learned to read and write, he began teaching catechism to his countrymen. He helped found missions, churches and a convent. Widowed, he married Folo Ki in 1914, who was baptized thanks to the catechism he taught her, taking the name Thérèse. They had many children, including the historian and politician Joseph Ki-Zerbo. A tireless catechist, in 1975 he went on pilgrimage to Rome with the cardinal and they saw Pope Paul VI, who, to honor him, offered him the papal throne.

In 1980 John Paul II, traveling in Africa, sent him his blessing, and Alfred, in the hospital, listened on the radio to the Mass in Ouagadougou on May 10. He gave up his soul at the very moment of the final blessing, at 105. Thousands from all over the country came to his funeral. Almost 80 years after his conversion, more than 500,000 of his countrymen professed the faith!

His family ruled this ancient region of western Britain. In 855 his father, King Æthelwulf, went on pilgrimage to Rome, taking Alfred with him. When he came to the throne, he made Wessex a rallying point for all the Saxons and, after fighting off repeated invasions, freed the country from the Danes. Without realizing it, he unified England and paved the way for his successors.

Alfred codified and promulgated laws, and insisted that justice be dispensed without fear or favor. He is often credited with establishing trial by jury. He devoted his energies to restoring what the long wars had destroyed, rebuilding and founding monasteries.

He brought scholars from other lands, encouraged intellectuals and himself focused on learning, translating into Anglo-Saxon several philosophical treatises and the “Dialogues” of Saint Gregory the Great.
The people named him “the Great,” and for many centuries he has been admired as one of the first virtuous monarchs who evangelized their kingdom.

Aleth was born in Montbard to nobles descended from the Dukes of Burgundy. At 15 she married Tescelin, a man of great virtue. They formed a marriage of deep Christian life. As an exemplary wife and mother she formed her children in the faith.

Her son Bernard (Doctor of the Church) had a close relationship with his mother from childhood; while pregnant, she had had a vision of her son’s life as a saint. He said his parents were “illustrious for their rank and high lineage, but more illustrious for their virtues.”
Tescelin forgave a knight who challenged him to a duel and wounded him with his lance. He instilled in his older sons the importance of mercy.

Aleth showed great charity toward the poor, going from house to house to help them generously; she did the same with the sick. She died praying the rosary, and the abbot had the images of 6 of her sons engraved on her tomb in the monastery of Clairvaux.

She was born in a small town in Lazio in 1914. At the age of 4 she fell into a cauldron of boiling water and died, but recovered miraculously after a vision of a smiling monk: Saint Anthony the Abbot.
She began her teaching career and in 1940 married a railway engineer. They went to live in Foggia, and she began a constant wandering through Italy following her husband.

What is extraordinary about Alma’s life lies in her daily life, dotted with singular religious experiences: the “silent” apparition of the Virgin in 1981 and her “Communications” with God the Father from 1984, almost daily, for more than 10 years. She had to transcribe these “Suggestions” from God exactly as they were dictated, and they have been collected and published in 3 volumes of more than 500 pages each, titled “Work of Gold: Colloquy with the Father.” The dominant theme is the love of the Merciful God the Father for all humankind.

Her life was a continuous dialogue with God, for whom she felt a sincere filial love that became an inner strength enabling her to face and overcome many difficulties. She retired from teaching in 1975 and died in Rome in 2000.

His father died when he was 14 and studying with the Jesuits, so he had to take over the family business. He married and the family began to grow. But they lost all their children and, shortly after, María died too. Alone and unhappy, he went to live with 2 sisters who encouraged him to make friends with God.

Once he managed to surrender himself to God, in 1571 the Jesuits accepted him as a lay brother. He served as doorkeeper of the College of Montesión in Palma de Mallorca for... almost 40 years! There he went through trials of dryness and scruples and suffered violent temptations. He bore these torments heroically, always faithful to his work and using his working hours to pray.
At 70 and very ill, he was ordered to go to the Indies, and even so he obediently headed out the door. A superior had to step in to stop him from leaving.

When someone knocked, Alonso would say “Coming, Lord,” and always opened with joy, even when the visitor did not return the kindness: “Jesus, who disguises himself as our neighbor, can never be treated harshly or rudely” (Saint Alphonsus Rodríguez)

He was born in eastern France, near Geneva. His family’s religious tradition led him toward the good, and his works won him admirers and followers. He often suffered from epilepsy, which he considered a providential brake on the passions (today he is invoked against this illness). From the throne he knew how to discover Christ in his brothers and sisters, ruling justly but for only 7 years, troubled by frequent feudal struggles.

Very young he married Yolande, daughter of the King of France. It was a happy and fruitful union; each tried to make the other’s needs and tastes their own: they made love the motto of their relationship with each other and with God. One daughter was Blessed Louise of Savoy.

In a large courtyard he had a procession of servants attending to and feeding more than 500 poor people. He said: “These are distractions with which I try to gain the kingdom of Heaven. (...) That is what I have learned from Jesus Christ. My soldiers defend me from men, but the poor defend me before God.” And to his wife, moments before dying: “I strongly commend the poor to you (...) Do justice to all without favoritism; apply all your efforts (...) so that God may be served.”

Born in 1911, the eldest of 9 siblings, he studied at the University of San Agustín. As a teenager he set up an improvised movie theater where he gathered people to watch films on the lives of saints and apparitions of the Virgin. He married Ángeles and settled in Jaro.

A great Marian devotee, from childhood he always helped people understand the importance of praying the Rosary and devotion to Her. He started a daily “Dawn Rosary” on the radio from 4 to 5 a.m., getting up at 2:30 to prepare it. He encouraged people to go to Mass and distributed material to remote areas: prayer books, novenas and rosaries. He used his ventriloquist skills, imitating animals and birds, to catch attention and invite people to catechism.

During World War II, Amador asked the Virgin that if his family survived, he would devote himself to serving God and Her. Faithful to his promise, he deepened his apostolic work. When he learned that the Blessed Mother had said in the Lipa (Philippines) apparition that her message was similar to Fatima’s, he decided to be more bold and passionate in spreading the messages of Fatima.
He died in 1977 at 65 of heart failure. In 2014, during the Philippine Year of the Laity, the archbishop formally opened his cause for beatification.

She was born in Valencia in 1925. In 1943 she received the medal of a Daughter of Mary and chose the motto “Mother, take from me whatever takes me from You,” to which she was faithful all her life. With her husband she joined the Christian Family Movement, actively collaborating on its leadership team and spreading it in parishes, schools and institutions in various cities. She took part in TV programs on raising children.

One of her most remarkable traits was how she saw positive values in people, turning a deaf ear to gossip and not judging: “Every person, as a child of God, has dignity and a good side,” she said. She never had personal enemies; she tried to act always in good faith. The elderly and the disabled truly loved her: she always took an interest in them, visited them and cared for them.

In 1994 she was diagnosed with lung cancer; she accepted it naturally as God’s will, offering it for her children. Her right lung was removed, and she required daily treatments for 556 days, until she died in 1996 with fortitude, joy and gratitude. Since then, reports have come in of favors attributed to Amparo’s intercession.

She was born in Genoa into a well-off family and received a cultural and religious education. In 1852 she married her cousin Girolamo, and they moved to Marseille. A financial crisis plunged them into poverty and they had to return. Their daughter was left deaf and mute by an illness, and her husband died after 6 years of marriage, leaving her with two children, since the third had died. All this brought about a radical change, her “conversion.”

She privately took perpetual vows on becoming a Franciscan tertiary. From 1855 she obtained permission to receive Communion every day, and in the Eucharist she found comfort and missionary zeal. In 1862 she received the gift of hidden stigmata, felt most intensely on Fridays. She devoted herself to visiting the sick and the poor.

She was entrusted with the presidency of the new Ursulines, and in 1866 she received the inspiration to found the Daughters of Saint Anne to serve the poor, the sick, the abandoned, the elderly and young people at risk. She encouraged them “to evangelize above all with their lives.”
It spread throughout the world with schools, centers and a foundation for the deaf. At her death she left 368 houses with 3,500 sisters. She was beatified by John Paul II in 2000.
He was born in Tepatitlán, Jalisco, in 1888, in extreme poverty. When he understood that his vocation was not the priesthood, he entered law school.

A remarkable educator, orator, catechist and Christian social leader, he became the lay champion of the Catholics of Guadalajara. He wrote books full of Christian spirit and hundreds of newspaper articles. In 1922 he married Conchita, who did not share his love for the apostolate; even so, he was a model husband and responsible father.

As the high point of his life, he founded the Popular Union, which came to have tens of thousands of members. In 1926, with all legal and civic means exhausted and the active Catholic resistance being organized, he supported with his whole person the projects of the League for the Defense of Religious Freedom.

On April 1, 1927, he was arrested and subjected to very cruel torture to make him reveal the archbishop’s whereabouts. His executioners dislocated his limbs and flayed the soles of his feet. Before dying, he said to his executioner: “I forgive you with all my heart; very soon we will see each other before the divine tribunal, (...) and then you will have in me an intercessor with God” (Anacleto González Flores)

Andronicus was an Alexandrian who settled in Antioch as a blacksmith and lived very happily with his wife and their two children, John and Mary, and his business prospered. But after 12 years of marriage both children died suddenly on the same day. From then on, Athanasia spent most of her time weeping and praying in the nearby church.

One day Saint Julian the Martyr appeared to her and assured her that her children enjoyed the happiness of heaven. Joyfully she told her husband that it was time for them to leave the world, and Andronicus agreed. So together they went to their native Egypt, to the desert of Scetis, in search of Saint Daniel the Wonderworker. They spent the following years as anchorites, each in solitude.

After twelve years they made a journey to the Holy Land, according to tradition without recognizing each other, only as new friends, and returned to the desert. They were buried together; the Coptic, Ethiopian and Byzantine Churches commemorate them, as does the Roman Martyrology.

Born in 1248 in Foligno, Italy. In her early years she was proud, vain, worldly and not very devout. She married very young, had riches, castles, luxuries and estates, and nothing made her happy. But at 35 her mother, her husband and her children died one after another.

In the midst of immense grief, Angela heard the Franciscan Fr. Arnaldo preach and realized how wrongly she had lived. She went on pilgrimage to Assisi, where Saint Francis told her in a vision to sell everything she had for the poor and devote herself to meditating on the Passion. Only then was she able to make a general confession of her whole life, and she became a Franciscan tertiary.

She sold everything except one castle, until Christ crucified said to her: “And for love of your Redeemer will you not be able to sacrifice your favorite palace too?” She sold it as well and devoted herself to a life of contemplation and meditation on the life, Passion and Death of the Lord. Looking at an image of the suffering Jesus was enough to leave her as if in ecstasy. At Mass she often saw Jesus Christ in the Sacred Host.
She wrote several books about her mystical experience and died in 1309. Numerous miracles took place at her tomb. In 2013 Pope Francis decreed her equivalent canonization.

She was born around 1569 in Dunmow (Essex) into a wealthy Calvinist family. Her original name is thought to have been Alice Heigham, and on converting with her brother as a teenager she took the name Anne. Her parents opposed them, disowned them and forced them to leave. The government persecuted the Catholic Church, imposing the death penalty on priests and anyone who helped them. Anne was one of the many housewives who hosted secret gatherings to celebrate Mass and administer other sacraments.

In 1583 she married the fervent Catholic Roger Line. Under pressure to conform to the Protestant church, he suffered great financial losses. He said: “If I must give up either the world or God, I will give up the world to hold fast to God.” He was arrested with Anne’s brother for attending Mass and banished to Flanders, where he died around 1594.

Now a widow, she kept offering her house to shelter priests; she ran it, cleaned it and kept hosting Masses. Until the house was searched and the altar found; she was condemned in London in 1601. Bravely proclaiming her faith, she recited prayers, kissed the gallows and attained martyrdom together with 2 priests, one of them her confessor, Fr. Filcock. Paul VI canonized her in 1970 among the “Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.”

Born in León, he wanted to study for the priesthood, but as the eldest of 9 siblings, his parents’ finances made it impossible. After marrying he moved to Barcelona to earn a living for his family and found work on the railway.

There they came to know the Dominican fathers, and both professed in the Dominican Third Order. He had a great love for the Eucharist and the Rosary, which they prayed as a family. He joined Nocturnal Adoration and practiced works of solidarity with the sick.
Later one of their daughters became a Discalced Carmelite, and a son was a Dominican missionary in Latin America.

During the Civil War, in 1936, militiamen took him at nightfall from the station where he worked and stabbed him to death under a bridge out of hatred for his faith. His body was found with the hammer and sickle carved into his bald head.

Born in 1874, he attended the Salesian school in Catania, where he stood out for his piety and his studies. Very young he took part in the Work of the Congresses, which paved the way for Catholic Action and the Catholics’ Popular Party.

He married at 22 and received his 9 children “as a sacred trust,” he said. At 25 he became a Secular Franciscan and refined his spirit by detaching himself further from the riches he had inherited, turning them into an instrument of good for the poor. He learned to deepen the humility, modesty and smiling gentleness that marked his face.

He co-founded the Saint Vincent de Paul Conferences in Palermo with a group he inspired with his spontaneous, captivating naturalness. A model “visitor” of the poor, he gave incalculable material help with his intelligence and practical sense joined to his spirituality. A comfort to lost souls, the sick and the dying, he was called “the priest in a jacket.” Knowing the importance of the press, he supported at great sacrifice the major Catholic daily “Corriere di Sicilia.”
He loved the Virgin with filial tenderness and generously forgave those who had made him suffer. He died in 1935 kissing the Crucifix, like someone setting off on a long-awaited journey.

Antonio was born in 1896 on the island of Brač (Croatia), and at 3 his family settled in Antofagasta. He qualified as a surgeon in 1922 and that year married Amy, from Copiapó, of British descent in Chile. They had no children.

He was known as “the doctor of the poor” for treating free of charge those with few resources in Antofagasta. He was director of the Chilean Red Cross and of the 3rd Fire Company of Antofagasta. He was a member of the Chilean Academy of Medicine.
He excelled in poetry under the pen name Ivo Serge, publishing some 40 works that made him known in America and Europe; he wrote the Anthem of Antofagasta.

In 1963 Paul VI made him a Commander of the Order of Saint Sylvester for his medical and personal merits. He died in 1993 at 96. At least 3 high schools bear his name, as does the avenue where the Family Health Center (CESFAM) where he worked is located, renamed Dr. Antonio Rendic.

Argentino del Valle was born in San Miguel de Tucumán (Argentina) in 1932. The youngest of 8 siblings, he entered the Military College, where he began an exemplary career as a technician, comrade and respected leader.
In 1955 he married Marisú de San Martín and lived his faith in everyday life, as husband, father, soldier and educator. He was a professor at the Catholic University of Argentina.

In 1969 he was appointed deputy director of the Military Gunpowder and Explosives Factory in Villa María, Córdoba. There he was kidnapped by the ERP (People’s Revolutionary Army) in August 1974, under a democratic government.

The terrorists demanded that, as a weapons and explosives specialist, he agree to work as an adviser for their factories, and he would be freed. He bravely replied: “Not at this price… weapons are not for Argentines to kill one another.” In his cell, which he called “the kennel,” he could be heard singing the national anthem and praying, offering forgiveness. After a year of hunger, cold and mistreatment, but firm in his faith, he was murdered on August 19, 1975. In his diary was found: “I want to die standing, invoking God in my family, the homeland in my army, my people uncontaminated by ideas steeped in division and blood. I ask God in His mercy to grant me this grace.”

Aristea was born in Ancona in 1883, the first girl after 11 boys. From a wealthy family, her father was cultured but violent, a drinker and a gambler. She was not sent to school, and when she made her First Communion no one even went with her.

Gino was chosen as her husband; he turned out to be a womanizer and a blasphemer who often insulted her. They lived with his parents, shopkeepers very hostile to religion and Christian morals, who saw her more as another servant than as a daughter-in-law.

Aristea lost the sight of one eye shortly after marrying and spent much time ill in hospitals; later she devoted herself to caring for the sick and the poor. Into old age she still drew people of every age and condition who asked her for advice, prayer, intercession, light, help and spiritual comfort.

Her infinite patience with her bad husband bore fruit in 1948, after 47 years of marriage, when he turned to God and to respecting his wife. He died in 1964, reconciled with God. In her diary she wrote: “I would repeat it to every bride: adorn your soul inwardly as best you can for Jesus, and outwardly for your husband. If you draw him to you, you draw him to God himself.” (Maria Aristea Ceccarelli)
In the year 302 Artemius was the keeper of the Roman prison where the two future martyrs Peter and Marcellinus were then held.

Artemius and Candida had a daughter named Paulina who was possessed by the devil. Peter promised him his daughter’s deliverance if he became a Christian, but Artemius refused, considering the saint a madman. But after a miracle he changed his mind and converted together with his wife Candida and his daughter, who was thus healed.

Denounced as a Christian before the court of Judge Serenus, Artemius was sentenced to death along with his family, and they were led along the Via Aurelia. Candida and Paulina (venerated as a holy martyr) were thrown into a pit and buried under a mass of stones; Artemius was put to the sword.

Attilio was born in Milan in 1913. As a child he discovered Don Bosco and the Salesian oratory, which he would always love dearly. There he received his first formation and committed himself as a diligent catechist and a brilliant, simple and serene Salesian youth leader.
During his military service he showed an apostolic vocation among his comrades. He found work at Pirelli in Milan, where he also spread joy and good humor.

After the war he married Noemi. Every day they were faithful to meditation, the Eucharist and the Rosary. To give hope back to children troubled by the war, he started the “Crusade of Goodness,” which would spread throughout Italy.

In his family he was a present husband, rich in great faith and serenity, in deliberate austerity and evangelical poverty for the benefit of those most in need. Their children went to Brazil as missionary volunteers, and they decided to follow them to fully share their parenthood and their children’s vocation to volunteer work. There he continued as a catechist and youth leader. In 1972, while speaking enthusiastically and ardently about the duty to give one’s life for others, he suddenly felt faint. He barely had time to tell his son, “Pier Giorgio, now you carry on...” and died of a heart attack.

He was educated as a boarder with the Piarist Fathers and graduated in law in Naples. But he got caught up in the anti-Christian fashions of the time, politics and superstition; he was absorbed by books and amusements, and so God gradually disappeared. Philosophical rationalism won him over and he preached against the Church. He renounced his faith, becoming a “medium” and a spiritualist priest.

A professor and the Dominican Fr. Radente were key to his return to the faith. He felt chosen by the Virgin to build in Pompeii (Italy) a shrine where other sinners could find peace. There he worked with the widowed Countess De Fusco on charities and on spreading the Holy Rosary. In 1885 they entered a Josephite marriage, with papal permission.

When he died at 85 he left the Shrine of Our Lady of Pompeii, a great Marian city visited by millions of pilgrims, charitable institutes and homes for thousands of children. He was canonized on 10/19/2025.
Begga was the daughter of Pepin of Landen, mayor of the palace of Austrasia (a region in present-day Belgium), and his wife Itta of Nivelles.
She married Ansegisel, son of Saint Arnulf of Metz, with whom she had three children, one of whom, Pepin of Herstal, was the founder of the Carolingian dynasty.
In 691, at her husband’s death, she took the veil and built seven churches representing the seven churches of Rome.
She founded a convent at Andenne on the Meuse river, Andenne-sur-Meuse, where she spent the rest of her days as abbess.

He was born in 1946 into the Lemba tribe, a community with Jewish traditions. As a child he herded livestock, as was the custom in his tribe. His father died, and so he went to work with an uncle in Johannesburg, where he had his first contact with Catholics. He was baptized at 16, taking the name Benedict and the motto “ora et labora.”

He became a teacher and worked with young people as a mentor, using sport as his main tool. He was appointed principal of the primary school, from which he carried out many works to help his community, and he was recognized as a leader and an influential person, supporting the construction of the first Catholic church.
He fed people from his crops, and those who could not afford school fees he invited to work in his vegetable garden as a form of payment.

In 1990, after storms battered the village, the council of elders decided to consult a witch doctor because they believed it was witchcraft. Daswa refused to pay toward the services so as not to go against his faith. Days later he was ambushed and chose to give himself up. He commended himself to God as he was killed with stabbing, clubbing and boiling water. In 2015 Pope Francis beatified him before 30,000 people, with traditional dances and songs.
He was born near Lyon, France, around 778. He joined the army and, after seven years of married life, decided to renounce the world.

He founded the Benedictine monastery of Ambronay, where he became a monk in 803 and, four years later, abbot. He was elected Archbishop of Vienne in 810 and played an important role in the synodal movement that sought to restore peace and order in both Church and State. He was a leading figure of the Frankish episcopate in the Carolingian reform.
He enjoyed the favor of Louis the Pious for a time; but when he sided with his son Lothair against him, he was forced to flee to Italy after the emperor’s victory.

He was able to return to his see and founded the monastery of Saint-Séverin, Exupère and Félicien, where he retired to spend his last days and where he was buried when he died on January 22, 842. His cult was reconfirmed in 1903.
She was the daughter of Duke Lorenzo, a German prince of the Rhine region. She was married to the pagan prince Robold during the reign of Charlemagne.

A practicing Christian, she tried to convert her husband without success, as he died still young, in battle. Bertha faced widowhood with courage and devoted herself zealously to the Christian upbringing of her 3-year-old son, Rupert, on her estate at Bingen.

Rupert grew up faithful to his mother’s teachings and, with the counsel of his tutor and spiritual director, devoted himself to devotional practices and works of charity. When he was 12, his mother involved him in founding a monastery in Bingen and a hospice for the poor: their works of mercy toward the weakest continued in fruitful collaboration between mother and son. But they were cut short by Rupert’s early death at 19. Bertha felt great sorrow, which was consoled by seeing the veneration the people showed him.

Bertha lived some 25 more years in prayer and penance, donating her property and riches to support the monks. She was buried next to her son’s tomb and became the object of pilgrimages and veneration.
Moved by her deep religious spirit, Bertha felt it was necessary to found monasteries for the religious perfection of women, and especially of her daughters.
After her husband’s death, in 678 she founded the monastery of Blangy in Normandy, which King Theuderic later placed under his direct protection.
She built three churches in honor of the saints of her devotion.
After several years of governing, Bertha resigned as abbess in favor of her daughter Deotila and spent her last days enclosed in a small cell with a window onto the church and the altar.

Born in Palencia in 1188 to Alfonso VIII of Castile, she had 16 siblings. In 1200 she married Louis VIII, who would be King of France from 1223. From the start she showed a lucid intelligence in a country beset by difficult problems and by the spreading Cathar heresy. She took part in affairs of state, including the victorious campaigns against the English, while giving birth to one child after another and seeing to their education, though her greatest care went to the instruction of her firstborn, the future Saint Louis IX.

In 1226 she was widowed and ruled as regent until Louis came of age, in a complex kingdom where the nobles did not accept a foreign queen and England was a threat. Far from being intimidated, she took command of her army and put down the seditious factions, while also subduing the Cathar heresy.

When Louis was king, he was captured on crusade and the queen mother had to return to government, ruling with a good measure of wisdom and justice. She later went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land and died in 1252 in a monastery she had founded. Her contemporaries called her “the good and just queen”; the French still regard her as an example of a capable queen in the years when France was being built into a great power.
Boutros was born and lived in Cairo, Egypt. He held a university degree and a doctorate. He was a family man.

He worked courageously and zealously in several Church organizations, but especially in the Catholic Youth Association, which he led for decades. He served young people in many ways and guided them spiritually. He said: “Working for the Youth Association is my whole life.”

He also worked in other institutions of the Melkite Greek Catholic Church and directed the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul for the care of the poor. He was, according to many, the most influential person in the Egyptian Church.

He died in Cairo on March 24, 1986, with a reputation for holiness. The beatification process opened in 2015, and many fellow believers testified, but also Muslims who had come away from their encounters with him deeply moved spiritually. Patriarch Gregory III said at the opening of his process: “He was the Apostle of Upper Egypt and the Apostle of Youth, a committed layman living entirely by Gospel values.”

He was born in Rome in 1913 into a poor family; his father was an alcoholic who spent time in prison. As a young man he drifted from the faith and joined the Communist Party. A German Protestant turned him against the Virgin and the Eucharist and filled him with a deep hatred of the Church, to the point of planning to kill the Pope.

In 1947 his children were playing among bushes near an abbey. Looking for the ball, he saw one of them kneeling with hands joined; he had a vision of a lady in intense light who told him: “I am the Virgin of Revelation. You have persecuted me; enough! (…) Obey the authority of the Holy Father.” Bruno was reconciled with the Catholic Church, abandoned his violent plans and received messages for priests about prayer and obedience to the Magisterium. He devoted his next 54 years to giving more than 7,000 talks around the world. The apparitions have not been formally approved, but they received the blessing of Pius XII, who also blessed the statue carried in procession with 500,000 faithful.
He died on June 22, 2001. In 2017 his beatification process was opened.
Canute inherited a kingdom still stumbling over paganism and strove to restore good customs.
Devout and compassionate toward the weak, he enacted humane and wise laws, built hospitals, supported the Church’s mission with churches and monasteries, and his treasury was for the poor.
Among his religious traits his love and veneration for the Eucharist stand out; he was capable of laying his sword, his crown and the royal insignia at the feet of Christ crucified, and he did!
With Adela he was the father of Blessed Charles of Flanders, “the Good.”
In the end he was betrayed by his brother Olaf while attending Mass: after he had confessed and received Communion, the rebels surrounded the church, and he died there at 42, forgiving his enemies.

She was the daughter of a count; beautiful, of fine stature, very modest and retiring; despising all vanity and worldly things, very devoted to Saint Francis of Assisi and wholly given to the service of God and the good of her neighbor.

Castora married very young the jurist Santuccio (or Gualtiero) Sansoneri, Count of San Martino and Bassinario. It was a difficult marriage, as her husband treated her harshly; yet she bore everything for the love of God, with admirable patience.

She was a woman of rare piety and deep charity. At her husband’s death, with the consent of her son Odo, she distributed her goods among the poor.
