She took the habit of the Franciscan Third Order and spent the rest of her life in penance and prayer until her death in 1391. Still today, in the Franciscan church of Sant’Angelo, she is venerated as patroness of difficult marriages.

Charles was the son of Saint Canute IV, King of Denmark, and on coming of age he was proclaimed Count of Flanders and Amiens. His wise and beneficent rule, as well as his personal holiness, earned him the title “Bonus,” that is, “the Good.”

During a long, cold winter food was scarce. Charles took measures so that the poor would not go hungry, preventing grain from being hoarded to be sold at excessive prices. He made friends among the humble and enemies among speculators such as the Erembald clan, who plotted his death.

In 1127, as he prayed barefoot as usual before the altar of Our Lady in the church of Saint Donatian in Bruges (Belgium), he was warned that a plot against his life was afoot. Charles calmly replied: “We always live in the midst of danger, but we are in God’s hands; if such is His will, there is no nobler cause than truth and justice to give one’s life for.” The conspirators appeared and beheaded him. He was immediately regarded as a saint and martyr. Leo XIII confirmed his cult in 1883, and his remains rest in Bruges Cathedral.

To his physical and intellectual gifts he joined deep Christian virtues: piety, humility and a spirit of sacrifice. He entered the Franciscan Third Order, striving all his life to follow its rule and spirituality.

In 1337 he was married to Joan of Penthièvre, niece of the Duke of Brittany and his presumed heir. After the death of John III of Brittany, Charles had to take up arms to defend his wife’s rights against John of Montfort, the late duke’s half-brother, who claimed the duchy. In this war of succession Charles, a loyal knight, took upon himself the duty to fight, though he would have preferred a life of contemplation and prayer.

In 1347 he was taken prisoner and endured a long, painful captivity in London until 1356. There he wrote the life of his favorite saint, Saint Ivo of Brittany, who had recently been canonized. There were a few years of peace, but in 1363 war returned and Charles fell in battle. He was buried in a Franciscan church in the habit of the order, and the people venerated him as a saint. Seven years later Joan began the process for his canonization.

Charles received a Catholic upbringing and was surrounded with prayer, since a stigmatized nun had prophesied great sufferings for him. He developed a great love for the Eucharist and based his decisions on prayer.

In 1911 he married the Italian princess Zita, promising “to help each other get to heaven”; they began a happy and exemplary married life. In 1916 he became emperor; he also saw his duty as a way to follow Christ: in love for the peoples entrusted to him and the gift of his life. He supported Benedict XV’s peace efforts during World War I. He undertook broad and exemplary social legislation, inspired by Christian social teaching.

With communism in Hungary, they were exiled to Switzerland and then to the island of Madeira (Portugal), sinking into poverty. There he accepted his terminal pneumonia as a sacrifice for the peace and unity of his peoples. On his deathbed at 38, Charles told Zita: “I love you endlessly!” She would wear black until she died at 96. John Paul II set October 21, their wedding date, as the Blessed’s feast day.

Carmela was born in La Palma del Condado (Huelva) in 1933. From a Christian family, she soon became involved in parish activities. In 1958 she married Salvador, with whom she raised their children in the faith. One is a nun of the Company of the Sisters of the Cross and another is principal of the local Salesian school.
She lived her Christian life at home through her work as a housewife, with self-denial and generous service, strengthening the family.

She was a catechist and had a great love for the poor and the sick, toward whom she practiced charity rooted in a deep experience of the Christian faith. She belonged to the group “Experiences of Faith,” a school of the Gospel and prayer. She took an active part in the Association of Mary Help of Christians (ADMA).
She died on March 24, 2007, and her reputation for holiness has kept growing.

Born near Florence in 1895 into a poor, religious family of sharecroppers. She studied up to 3rd grade and then worked in the fields to help her parents. From childhood she prayed, carried the rosary and often sang hymns of praise.

She married Olinto in 1919 and they went to live in Florence in a damp basement, in poverty. They both found jobs but, with the 1929 crisis, she offered to be laid off to make sure her husband kept his position.
She became a Franciscan tertiary in 1921 and was very zealous for the Divine Office of the Third Order and in works of charity.

Many young people did not receive First Communion because their families could not afford to organize the ceremony. She launched the Work of First Communions to promote the sacrament, into which, having no children, she poured all her maternal vocation. Later came her work “Assistance to Cloistered Monasteries,” which would reach some 275 monasteries in Italy and Yugoslavia.
She died in 1986 at 91. Her beatification process was opened in 2001.

Born in England, in 1830 she married Archibald, an officer of the East India Company, and took up his Catholic faith. In Madras (India) she saw that girls growing up with their families in barracks picked up the soldiers’ bad behavior. In 1834 she founded the Female School of Industry for soldiers’ daughters: reading, religion, cooking and nursing. The soldiers asked that their wives be allowed to attend too.

In 1838, now in Sydney, she founded a home for destitute immigrant girls, for whom she found work. Her report “Female Immigration” (1842) was the most important publication by an Australian resident up to that time. In 7 years there, she found homes and jobs for 11,000 people. From 1846 she raised funds in England for emigrant families, helping more than 3,000. She returned to Australia to give lectures and inspect living conditions in the goldfields.

Her pioneering social work was always acclaimed, and she has appeared on Australian stamps and banknotes. A Canberra suburb and educational institutions in both countries bear her name. Pius IX awarded her a papal medal. Both spouses died in 1877.
Born in 1829 in Metz, France. By 16 she had finished her studies and showed an unusual seriousness of character. She went to daily Mass and tried to influence her friends.

At 20, following her parents’ wishes, she married her cousin, Captain Paul Carré. As he did not fulfill his religious duties, she had to make many sacrifices to win his soul. He treated her as uneducated and narrow-minded and reproached her in front of others. Caroline kept the peace, prayed and showed him only love and affection. And so in the end she won the heart of the rough soldier, who in 1852 attended Easter services in Metz.
Madame Carré was a truly Christian mother to her children. She had to bear the sorrow of seeing all of them die in childhood, except one, who reached 29.

With the help of Abbé Chaumont, in 1872 she founded in Paris a religious league of devout women living in the world: the Daughters of Saint Francis de Sales. It aimed to lead women to perfection in their station in the world according to the principles set out by Francis de Sales in his “Philothea.” It received canonical approval in 1901; by 1906 it had 8,000 members, and today it is present in many countries. Caroline died in 1891, and in 2014 Pope Francis recognized her heroic virtues.

During the reign of Diocletian, Pope Saint Caius was deeply worried about the safety of the Christians of Rome. Castulus, a zealous Christian who was a chamberlain of the emperor, offered to arrange for religious to stay in the imperial palace itself; what is more, he sheltered Christians in his own house next to the palace and provided them a place for their meetings.
He and his friend Tiburtius went around Rome converting men and women to Christianity and bringing them to the Pope to be baptized.

He was later betrayed by an apostate named Torquatus. Brought before Fabian, prefect of the city, he was cruelly tortured and then thrown into a pit covered with sand. Legend says he was buried in the cemetery that bears his name in the catacombs on the Via Labicana in Rome.
The Acts of Saint Sebastian mention that Castulus’s widow, Irene, was the one who nursed the saint back to health when he was wounded by arrows.
Castulus has been honored since antiquity as patron of farmers and shepherds.

Catherine was born in Genoa in 1447 into a noble family. Very young she was married to Giuliano, mostly for political convenience. The first years were sad and desolate because of his difficult character, totally opposite to hers, worldly and without compassion or scruples. After enduring many infidelities, after five years she felt desolate, even toward God.

On the advice of friends, she threw herself into frivolity, going from party to party, trying to find meaning. But in 1473 she fell into ecstasy and saw Christ shedding blood, who showed her her life. She could see her betrayal of Love, but at the same time His great mercy. From then on she began to reject sin.

Her example and sacrifices eventually brought about her husband’s conversion. In 1478, when she was 30, they joined the Franciscan Third Order and moved from the palace to a small house next to a hospital, caring for the sick and the dying. From her experience of purification would come her brilliant “Treatise on Purgatory,” and her influence on the Church life of her time was decisive.
Cecilia was born in 15th-century Italy.
She married a very devout young man, with whom she devoted herself to the Church and to spiritual growth.

After eight years together, each entered religious life: he became a Dominican and she entered the monastery of Saint Catherine Martyr in Ferrara, where she spent thirty years of ascetic life as a Dominican.
She was known for her personal piety, her ascetic life and her devotion to Dominican life, and was elected prioress three times.
She died at the end of December 1511, shortly after a heavenly vision. Miracles were reported at her tomb.
Her feast is December 19, but some calendars celebrate it on February 25, January 25, May 4 and March 7.

Ceferino was a Roma (gypsy) man from a humble family, a livestock dealer, a typical Roma trade. As a child he led a wandering life, traveling the mountain roads of the Huesca region and Catalonia (Spain).

He joined with Teresa according to Roma custom, and in 1912 sealed their union in a Catholic marriage. He went to church regularly until he became a model Christian. They had no children but adopted a niece named Pepita.

He was known as a good Roma man, honest in his dealings and very religious: daily Mass and rosary. Because of his prudence, both Roma and non-Roma sought him out to settle conflicts. He gathered the neighborhood children for catechism. He became a Franciscan tertiary and a nocturnal adorer.

At the start of the Civil War he was arrested for defending a priest who was being dragged through the street. He was offered freedom if he stopped praying the rosary he always carried. On August 2, 1936, he was shot, rosary in hand, shouting “Long live Christ the King!”

Born in 1844 into a noble family, at 17 she married the Marquis Fernández de Córdoba, 11 years her senior. She asked him to distribute a thousand loaves of bread to the poor on their wedding day. Widowed without children at 30, she sought to change the course of her life. Two months later she met Father Marcelo Spínola, and together they began a spiritual search.

They set up a school for girls in which she and her 4 sisters became improvised teachers. Then in 1885 they founded the Handmaids of the Divine Heart, dedicated to the education of women, for whom there was little schooling, and opened the first school in Málaga.

Celia was always firm in her dedication, gentle with others and joyful in doing God’s will. Under the religious name Maria Teresa of the Heart of Jesus, she died in Seville in 1908. Pope Francis recognized her as venerable in 2020.

Born in Poland (in what is now Belarus) in 1833, she felt called to religious life, but following her parents’ wishes and the advice of her confessor, a bishop, she married in 1853. She was an exemplary wife and mother of four. She always sought to discover and carry out God’s will, regarding the risen Christ as the center of her life.

In 1863 she was arrested for helping insurgents against the tsarist regime. Later, in Vienna, she devoted herself to caring for her paralyzed husband and raising her daughters. In 1875, already widowed, she moved to Rome and came to know Resurrectionist spirituality, confirming her religious vocation together with her daughter Jadwiga.

In 1891 they made their profession, the official founding of the Congregation of the Resurrection of Our Lord, with the mission of educating young Christian women and the religious and moral renewal of women. After her daughter’s death in 1906 she made long journeys to visit the houses in Europe and America. She wrote “Memoirs for My Daughters” and died in Kraków in 1913. In 2006 Benedict XVI beatified her. The congregation has 53 houses with 500 members in 9 countries.

Celina and her husband belonged to the nobility. A monk named Montanus foretold that Celina would give birth to a son who would become a man of the greatest merit. She was puzzled, since both she and her husband were already advanced in years. But Montanus, who was blind, repeated his prophecy and added: “When you have borne the child whose birth I announce, you will rub my eyes with a few drops of your milk and so I will recover my sight.”

Remigius himself, a few days after birth, placed his little hand wet with milk on Montanus’s eyes, and the monk received the grace of seeing again. He was named Remigius because he was destined to “steer” (regir) the ship of his Church through stormy waves and to be the “remedy” (another meaning) against the ferocity of the pagans.

After brief studies in which he excelled greatly, Remigius wished to imitate the monk Montanus, withdrew to the monastery and parted from Celina forever. She was famous because of her sons: Saint Remigius (or Remi), Bishop of Reims, and the less renowned but also saintly Principius, Bishop of Soissons.

Claude Toussaint Marot de La Garaye was born in Rennes (France) in 1675. He was a parliamentary councilor, a musketeer of the king and a keen hunter. Holding the title of count, he led a rather lavish life in the family château. In 1701 he married Marguerite Piquet de La Motte.

But in 1703 Marguerite miscarried after falling from a horse and could no longer have children. Seven years later, the death of a brother-in-law brought about a radical conversion in the couple. With the spiritual guidance of Fr. Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort, they turned their stables into a 60-bed hospital serving the sick and the poor. To fund it they sold horses, tableware, jewels and weapons. They often welcomed 300 people to their table.

In 1714 they decided to train in medicine in Paris. They set up a laboratory to make medicines in their château and opened a salt works and factories to provide jobs. She specialized in ophthalmology and first aid. After 45 years serving those in need, they died in 1755 and 1757. Only in 2024 was a joint beatification process begun.

Clotilde, daughter of King Chilperic of the Burgundians, was probably born in Lyon around 474. As wife of the pagan king Clovis, she soon gained great influence over him. For a long time her efforts bore no fruit, although he did allow their first children to be baptized.

But when the Germanic tribes invaded, Clovis cried out in despair: “God of my wife, if you grant me victory, I promise to convert”; against all expectations, the Franks drove out the barbarians. At Christmas 496, after years of Clotilde’s prayer, Saint Remigius baptized the entire court. Together they were thus the instrument for the conversion of “the eldest daughter of the Church.”

As queen she was admired for her generous almsgiving, the purity of her life and her fervent prayer. She suffered as her 2 surviving sons fought over the throne; she prostrated herself at the tomb of Saint Martin begging that fratricide be avoided, and a terrible storm arose that scattered the armies.
After 34 years as a widow, in which she lived more as a nun than as a queen, she died in Tours on June 3, 545. Her feast is also celebrated on December 22.

Colette was born in June 1923 in Lévis, Quebec, and became local president of the Young Christian Students movement. In 1974 she began visiting prisoners at what is now the Quebec Detention Center. Her heart was moved by these outcasts, and many began calling her “Mom.”

In 1978, newly widowed, she rolled up her sleeves and opened the doors of a modest apartment to the poorest: thus was born Maison Revivre, a shelter for homeless people. They receive a compassionate ear, hot meals and a clean bed, the foundations for recovering their dignity. Since Colette’s death, Maison Revivre continues to shelter, feed and clothe people in difficulty who knock at its door, without any government subsidy, living solely on donations.

She was named “Personality of the Year” in 1980 by the Quebec Regional Chamber of Commerce, “Honorary President” of Prisoners’ Week in 1984 and Knight of the National Order of Quebec in 1987. A street there bears her name.

Consilio was born in 1937 into a large farming family. From childhood he faced the hard work of the fields to help his family, taking his father’s place. In 1962 he started work as a welder at a truck company.
Bruna was born in Martorano in 1945 into a family of artisans, and her mother died when she was 20 months old. She graduated in accounting with brilliant grades.

In 1965 they married in Martorano and immediately joined parish life, living their spiritual life intensely, with regular participation in the sacraments and Christian witness at work. In the ’70s she was treated for a long time for a tumor with cobalt therapy; she was left permanently weakened and unable to have children.

They lived a family life of wonderful harmony, with daily Eucharist and spiritual reading, often shared. They showed great dedication to the poor and needy and a marked gift for discernment in counseling people.

Later they took charge of equipping a “Bethany House” to take in women in emergency situations. With the Pope John XXIII Community they devoted themselves to caring for children without families. In 1996 Consilio was ordained a deacon in the cathedral. Both died of cancer, in 2010 and 2012. Their beatification process was opened in 2020.

Born in 1904, Cora rejected the Mormon faith in 1924 after experiencing the secret rituals of Mormon marriage, and began a 10-year search for the true religion. Listening to Catholic radio when she was too sick to change the station, she saw that it was nothing like what she had been taught about Catholicism, and she was eventually baptized in 1935. Her two children and her husband converted soon after, as did many Mormon relatives and friends.

She moved near Monterey, California, and began to have visions of Jesus and the saints. In a vision on December 24, 1946, Jesus entrusted her with the mission to “promulgate the mystical humanity of Christ (the divine indwelling) within souls.”

Cora kept a great affection for Mormons, wanting them to know who Jesus was and to have the Eucharist; she prayed much for them. She died on March 30, 1957, the anniversary of her baptism. The Diocese of Monterey opened her cause.
Csaba was a Hungarian goldsmith who made metal reliefs: chalices, crucifixes, reliquaries, church doors. He said that working a face of Christ into the metal was a very special mystical feeling.

Benedict XVI’s writings meant a great deal to him and his art. In 2009 he managed to speak with the Pope and give him his unity cross, carved like the one on his family altar. Three months later, at a gathering of the Schoenstatt Movement’s Families Federation, he, his wife Imri and 10 couples from their group made a vow offering their lives for the spiritual renewal of Hungary. Then, during the meal, Csaba lost consciousness and his heart stopped.

Fr. Beller told Imri: “It is no coincidence that it happened right after this event. Here, Heaven and Earth meet.” He was buried on July 25, the day he would have turned 46. His community later set up a memorial at the site and promotes his beatification.

World War II was raging, and the South African Daniel wanted to enlist with the Allies. After escaping from a prison camp he took refuge in northern Italy, where he found hospitality with Domitilla’s family. She already carried in her heart the desire to be a missionary in Africa.
The war ended, and Daniel returned home to finish his studies; in 1947 he went back to Italy to marry his Domitilla.

In Johannesburg they raised their family of 6 children, and then in 1967 they opened “Little Eden,” where they took in children with severe mental disabilities. They would welcome more than 300 over the years, including a Black girl in 1971, defying the racial policy of the time.

Today there are two residences with chapels and 6 Indian nuns. They received several awards for their work, including a papal medal. In 2002 Nelson Mandela called Domitilla a “heroine of South Africa.”

Daniela was born in 1966 and at 18 devoted herself, through youth ministry, to serving disabled people and other works of charity. She married, became a mother and joined, with Patrizio, the diocesan couples’ group “Cana.” They took part in retreats and marriage preparation courses, supported couples in difficulty and took people in need into their home.

One night, at 26, Daniela woke up in extreme pain. It was the metastasis of a tumor so advanced that there was no hope of survival. Patrizio took her to Lourdes, her favorite place, to tell her the truth about her illness: Daniela listened calmly and suddenly seemed to understand many things. She revealed to him that she had prayed to the Lord to be able to offer a serious illness for an intention very close to her heart. She took it as a gift and felt fully responsible for it.

She drew strength from her constant relationship with God, daily Eucharist and the daily rosary, prayed with those who came to her room every day, drawn by her serenity and faith. Her room became a little church. With Patrizio she chose the first reading and psalm for her funeral. She wished to be dressed in her wedding gown for her beloved Bridegroom.
Darerca, also called Monenna, was the youngest sister of Saint Patrick. She could work miracles and had the gift of prophecy, with which she contributed greatly to the evangelization of Ireland.
She was married twice, having been widowed, and had children by both husbands; some credit her with as many as 17 children.
Her fame endures not only as a great saint but as the mother of many saints. Almost all her sons became bishops or deacons. And one of her sons later became the king of Brittany, Gradlon the Great.

Born in Edinburgh, the youngest son of Saint Margaret of Scotland and King Malcolm III. When his parents died in 1093, he went to England with his siblings to be educated in a monastery and later at court, when his sister married King Henry I.

David married Matilda, quite a bit older than him, thus becoming an English baron. When his brother died in 1124 he took the throne of Scotland. He was a just king and a lover of good order, who gave new structure to the feudal and legal system. He developed the towns, making trade flourish. His great mistake in the 1138 invasion of northern England was to enlist barbarian troops, who left a sad memory of their atrocities.

A religious and humble man of great generosity toward the poor and the sick, he often recited the Office and frequently received the sacraments, all inherited from his mother Margaret. He created 4 dioceses and numerous monasteries. Personally, he had to mourn the death of his only son and heir. His political and religious influence raised the country to be among the leading ones of the time, making him one of the greatest sovereigns of the Middle Ages. He was never canonized, but the Catholic Church venerates him on May 24.

Born in Anzi (Italy) in 1938, he moved to Viterbo with his family in 1949. After winning a competitive exam for Social Security in Pavia, he attended the Faculty of Economics and Commerce as a working student. Back in Viterbo, he met Maria Pia and they married in 1966.
They came to know the Focolare in 1974 and together embraced its ideals with enthusiasm, becoming actively involved in the Volunteers of God branch.

He was a manager at the INPS (the national social security institute) for 37 years, and from his office for impossible cases he helped many people: “There was always a line, because he really took on people’s problems.” This intense love for people led him into politics in Viterbo and, on a larger scale, alongside Chiara Lubich in the Political Movement for Unity, of which he was one of the main promoters in the country.
He died in Viterbo on December 22, 2001. The following year his biography, “An Extraordinarily Simple Man,” by Paolo Crepaz, was published.
Born in old Prussia, Dorothea married the swordsmith Albrecht, a hot-tempered and violent man.
Living a life of holy patience, through her humility and gentleness she gradually changed her husband’s character.
Of her 9 children, only one reached adulthood, and she became a Benedictine nun.
She and Albrecht made frequent pilgrimages, and in 1390 they planned to visit Rome, but he fell ill and died.
In her last years she had a hermit’s cell built next to the cathedral and lived a very austere life there. She had visions and revelations, and many visitors came to seek her comfort and counsel.
Eduardo strove to fulfill his family duties and also to seek God through his work as a doctor and university professor; he radiated peace and joy around him.
Laurita’s life was one of extraordinary generosity in giving herself to her husband and children, as well as to many others; both became supernumerary members of Opus Dei.
When he was a prominent dean in Granada, Josemaría Escrivá asked him to move to the newly founded School of Medicine of the University of Navarra to set up the University Clinic.
In 2015 the diocesan phase of both causes was closed, and their possible beatification is being studied jointly.

Born in Paris in 1899 to a shopkeeper father. In 1919 the Catholic Youth Association strengthened his faith and allowed him to continue his human and civic formation. An excellent speaker, he was a delegate to the ACJF national congress of 1920 in Paris.

He helped many victims of the Nazis in occupied France, including the Catholic philosopher Dietrich von Hildebrand. In 1943 he was arrested and imprisoned in the Dachau concentration camp, where he cared for other prisoners during a typhus epidemic and became infected himself. When Dachau was liberated he was still helping the sick and was the last to leave, on May 26, 1945.

He was elected to the French Parliament on October 21, 1945. Charles de Gaulle appointed him Minister of the Armed Forces in 1946, and he served as Minister of Justice from 1959 and later as minister in charge of the civil service.
He has been called “the chaplain of France.” He had 44 grandchildren. He died on October 9, 1970, and was named Righteous Among the Nations in 1995.
He was born in 1762 into a well-off Catholic family in Callan, in an Ireland under English rule: to control them better, Irish children were denied education.

Edmund received a limited education until he joined his uncle’s business supplying ships and the Navy. He was respected for his fair dealing, succeeded in business and became rich like many of his social class.

He married the young Mary, and everything seemed to be going better and better, until suddenly, after 4 years, she died in an accident, and their daughter was born disabled as a result. Edmund had to raise the girl with his stepsister Joan.

Discerning in his grief, at 40 he became a religious brother. He sold the business and began teaching poor children. In 1803 he opened a school providing food, clothing, job training and spiritual formation: thus he founded the Christian Brothers.
The congregation was approved in 1820 and today has thousands of members in 30 countries, in educational institutions and in services to the poor.

Son of an Anglican clergyman from Suffolk, after a distinguished career at Cambridge he converted to Catholicism and was employed by the Duchess of York. He was a good linguist, polemicist and writer, with several published books.
In 1675 he offered his services on behalf of Catholicism to the confessor of Louis XIV and to Father Saint-Germain, to prevent a rupture between England and France.

He became a suspect and, in the Titus Oates Plot, devised in 1678 to ruin the Duke of York, who was suspected of being Catholic, he was named as one of the conspirators. Aware of his innocence, he took no steps to protect himself and allowed his papers to be examined.

He was tried on charges of corresponding with foreign powers to subvert the Protestant religion and of consenting to a plan to assassinate King Charles II. He denied any complicity in the plot against the king. His correspondence abroad made him appear before the judges as an instigator, but it contained nothing linking him to plans against the king’s life. Nevertheless he was found guilty, taken to Tyburn in London and executed there.

Hedwig (Jadwiga) was crowned Queen of Poland in 1384 at only 10 years old. Her marriage to the Grand Duke of Lithuania, Jogaila (Władysław after his conversion), changed the history of Europe by bringing Western civilization to the eastern Polish-Lithuanian frontier.

She was very active on behalf of the poor and the sick, founding hospitals and relief centers. But she did not shut herself up in her court; she took an active part in the life of the vast Polish-Lithuanian state. Aware of culture as a vehicle of faith, she founded the Faculty of Theology of the University of Kraków, one of the oldest in Europe, where Copernicus taught and the future John Paul II studied, who canonized her in 1997.
Although she died at only 25 after childbirth, she left a deep mark of admiration on her people that has lasted 6 centuries.

Hedwig was born in Bavaria in 1174 and at 12 married the 18-year-old Duke Henry of Silesia. Together they founded many monasteries. He started the Hospital of the Holy Cross, and she a hospital where she personally cared for women with leprosy.
She always went to church barefoot, even in the snow. As a widow she took the religious habit, without taking vows, so she could keep managing her property for those most in need.

God gave her the gift of prophecy and miracles. She always carried a small image of the Virgin in her hand, and when she died it was impossible to remove it. Years later, when her body was moved, it was found still holding the image, and the fingers that held it were incorrupt.
He was king of the ancient regions of Deira and Bernicia, which would come to be known together as Northumbria (in England), from 616 until his death.
He converted to Christianity and was baptized in 627.

The influence of Queen Æthelburh cannot be ignored: being of the Merovingian line, she was a Christian and an evangelizer by nature. Just as her mother Saint Bertha had done with her father Æthelberht, she would convert Edwin to Christianity.
There are records of letters that Pope Boniface V sent to Edwin and Æthelburh, which show their efforts to Christianize their nation.
Edwin finally faced Penda and Cadwallon at the battle of Hatfield Chase in the autumn of 633, where he was defeated and killed, and from then on the people venerated him as a saint.
She was born in Bologna and given a very Christian upbringing.
Very young she expressed the wish to take a vow of chastity, but her mother persuaded her to marry, and at 17 she wed Benedetto Dall’Olio, who was then 40 years old.
They lived almost six decades of a wonderful and harmonious marriage; it has been said they lived in chastity, though this cannot be proven.
After her husband’s death she spent the rest of her life as an example to her community, until her death on September 23, 1520. She was buried in the church of San Giovanni in Monte.
Her reputation for holiness moved the people to remember her every September 23. Pope Leo XII officially confirmed her cult in 1828.
From a noble Genoese family, Eleonora lost her father as a small child and was educated in a Poor Clare monastery in Florence.
She married Orazio Landi in 1620, and it is said they lived in chastity, alternating periods of living in the city and in the country.

She experienced illuminations and revelations, partly from her guardian angel. In 1626 she began to gather abandoned girls, which would define for the rest of her life her vocation to educate girls, both commoners and nobles.

She called her foundation Angels of the Most Blessed Virgin, wrote a spirituality based on Saint Ignatius and drew up constitutions inspired by the Rule of Saint Clare, with private vows. Her deep faith led her to write letters to Popes Innocent X and Alexander VII.

Eleonora died in 1659 with a reputation for holiness, immediately inspiring great veneration and careful preservation of her writings and memories by her community. In the 20th century the institute became a religious institute and later disappeared. In 1987 John Paul II confirmed her heroic virtues.

She came from a Hispano-Roman family. Around 375 she became the first wife of the future Theodosius I the Great, later becoming Roman empress consort. Theodosius was the first Roman ruler to declare Christianity the official religion of the Empire.

She was a fervent defender of the Nicene Creed against the heresies of that early period. The Doctors of the Church Saint Ambrose and Saint Gregory of Nyssa praise her Christian virtue and speak of her role as “a leader in justice” and a “pillar of the Church.” Others also speak of her works of charity, personally caring for the disabled.

At her death the Palatium Flaccillianum in Constantinople was named after her, and a statue of her was placed in the Byzantine Senate. She is a saint in the Byzantine rite and is generally considered venerable by Catholics.
As a girl she wrote her “rule of life,” based on solid principles of faith.

In 1882 she married Gaetano Foresti, a devout merchant with whom she was happy but had no children. He contracted a serious mental illness that left him in an almost vegetative state. Elisa was widowed at 29.

She was guided by Father Giovanni Battista Piamarta (canonized in 2012) to devote herself to charity toward the most abandoned. With her property she bought a house where she founded the Pious House of Saint Joseph in Gavardo, where she herself cared for the sick and elderly.

She agreed to take charge of the merger with the Artigianelli Institute founded by Father Piamarta and wrote the Constitutions of the new congregation, of which she was superior: the Humble Servants of the Lord.

Elisabetta was born in 1788 in Sardinia. Struck by smallpox at only 3 months, she could no longer raise her arms, only move her fingers and wrists; she could not bring food to her mouth, comb her hair or change her clothes, but she could knead bread and cook, and so she raised her 5 children (2 died early). Her marriage was completely happy, and with her children she taught others, preparing them for the sacraments. In her home she taught several women hymns and psalms. In 1825 her husband died, and Elisabetta took on responsibility for the family and the house.

Growing in the spiritual life, she set out on pilgrimage to the Holy Land with her confessor, but they were forced to change their destination to Rome; because of serious physical ailments she could never return to Sardinia. There she received spiritual direction from Vincent Pallotti. She worked weaving and gave what she earned to the poor or to orphans in two houses founded by Pallotti, who praised her merits; the first Pallottines sought her advice.

She often went to the Hospital for the Incurably Ill and visited private homes to help the sick. She held daily adoration of the Blessed Sacrament with guests in her own home, where many people sought her counsel.
She died with a reputation for holiness in Rome on February 17, 1857. In 2016 Pope Francis promulgated the decree recognizing a miracle through her intercession.
Born in 1899 into an honest farming family; every night her father read them a page of Holy Scripture and explained it. As a girl she was already devoted to the Eucharist.

She met her handsome future husband Giuseppe while he was a soldier in World War I, but she did not respond to him with much enthusiasm. She went to the shrine of Our Lady of the Mount to lay her concern before her, and “meditating on the 3rd joyful mystery, the birth of Jesus, such an intense love for the soldier entered my heart that I ran and told him I would marry him!” The wedding took place in 1921: “Lord, in my marriage I will always do your will and accept all the children you wish to give. I ask that at least half of them give themselves to your service.” Of the 12 children who reached adulthood, 2 became priests, 2 nuns, and the other 8 formed good families.
The children went their ways, and Elisabetta lovingly cared for her faithful, ailing husband during the four years he spent in a wheelchair until he died.

Her life was built on Providence, the Word, which she knew by heart, and the will of God. She died at 79, with a funeral celebrated by her 2 sons and 27 priests. Mamma Elisabetta’s reputation for holiness draws devotees who receive countless graces.

She was born in New York in 1774 into the Episcopal Church and as a very young girl had to go live almost on charity in an aunt’s house. She married William Seton at 20, and in 1803 they set off on a journey to Italy to try to cure his tuberculosis, but as soon as they arrived he died.

Thanks to friends who welcomed her in Italy and introduced her to Jesus in the Eucharist, in 1805 Elizabeth embraced Catholicism, also disillusioned by what she saw in other religions. This brought her many trials, but she devoted herself diligently to the spiritual life. She raised her children with care and, eager to devote herself to charitable and educational work, in 1809 she founded in Baltimore the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph, to educate girls under the rules of the Daughters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul. It was the first women’s religious congregation in the U.S. Elizabeth served both as mother of a family and as mother superior. She also founded the first Catholic parish school.
She died piously in Maryland on January 4, 1821, at only 46. In 1975 Paul VI canonized her, the first saint of the United States.
Ellen Sundström was born in Stockholm and trained as a physiotherapist. In 1890 she married the German orthopedic surgeon Ottmar Ammann, and they moved to Munich.

She worked for women’s rights and was a pioneer in professional training for social work. A convert to Catholicism, she soon became involved in works of charity. In 1895 she co-founded the Marian Association for the Protection of Girls, and in 1904 the Catholic Women’s Association of Munich. In 1914 Ellen received the papal Pro Ecclesia et Pontifice medal for her charitable work. In 1919 she founded an association of Catholic deaconesses.

From 1919 to 1932 she was one of the first women members of parliament, for the Bavarian People’s Party, where she championed professional education for women. With several members of the government she condemned Hitler’s attempted coup and opposed National Socialism until her death. Right after a speech in parliament on aid for large families, she died in Munich of a stroke in 1932, at 62. Her cause for sainthood has been opened by the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising.

Descended from French nobles of Normandy, Eloisa received an exquisite education at court and a solid Christian formation. Her first marriage was to Count Hugh II, but it lasted only a few months because of her husband’s early death. She inherited a great fortune and donated much of it.

Having settled her life and living peacefully on her remaining property, she married a second time, to Alexandre Azzelin, with whom she had several children (one of them, Geoffrey, would become abbot of Coulombs). However, her second husband also died. Then she began to understand the call to give herself totally to God, in prayer, fasting, sacrifice and charity.

So Eloisa gave the rest of her possessions to the poor and to the Church, building a small house next to the Abbey of Coulombs, where she lived. A plague swept through Europe, wiping out almost a third of the population. She devoted herself to caring for the sick personally, without catching the disease.
She died around 1066 with a reputation for holiness, and soon her tomb became a place of pilgrimage, healings and miracles. She is invoked in difficult situations.

Delphine was 16 when she married Count Elzéar, also born in Provence (France) and two years younger. She shared with her husband her wish to remain a virgin forever. He agreed, without binding himself by a vow as she asked. One day she fell gravely ill, and then Elzéar promised to grant her wish. They took vows before their Franciscan confessor and entered the Third Order.

They belonged to the nobility, but amid riches they kept their hearts entirely free and applied the rule of the Franciscan tertiaries to their secular life. Elzéar was charming in his dealings with the poor, yet knew how to face the unrest of his vassals bravely with his skill at arms.

In 1323, at only 38, Elzéar died in Paris. Like Saint Louis the king, he had been seen visiting hospitals and tending lepers with his own hands. Delphine, faithful to Franciscan spirituality, wished to embrace poverty by giving up her property. She left her lands and went to Naples and then to France to live detached from everything. There she managed to intercede against a war. She died at 68 and is buried next to her husband in the Franciscan church.

Émilie was born in a castle at Wégimont, Liège (Belgium), in 1818, the daughter of counts. She married Victor, Baron d’Oultremont d’Hooghvorst, in 1837. The social obligations of diplomatic life did not keep her from developing an intense spiritual life under the direction of the Jesuits. Four children were born, but in 1847 she was widowed and turned her devout life toward religious life.

In 1854 she was deeply moved by the proclamation of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception. Soon the Virgin revealed to her that God wanted a congregation founded to make reparation for the outrages committed against the Blessed Sacrament. This religious family, the “Institute of Mary Reparatrix,” was born in 1857 in Strasbourg. Although Émilie led it, she did not enter the institute while she was responsible for her children’s education.

Later, her daughters followed her in her religious vocation. The Blessed died on February 22, 1879. Her tomb is in the church of the Holy Cross and Saint Bartholomew in Rome. In the beatification homily in 1997, Saint John Paul II said: “Émilie fulfilled above all the mission of every Christian marriage: to make her home ‘a domestic sanctuary of the Church.’”

Émilie was born in Montreal in 1800 to humble parents, the last of 15 children. Her parents died while she was still a child. In 1823 she married Jean-Baptiste, an apple grower 27 years her senior. She found in him a friend of the poor who shared her aspirations. Sorrow soon overwhelmed her, with the death of her young children and then of her husband, with whom she had lived happy years.

Faced with these trials, Émilie did not dwell in her suffering. With the resources her husband had left, she sheltered in her own home the elderly, orphans, prisoners, immigrants, the unemployed, the deaf, the disabled and the mentally ill. They spontaneously named it the “House of Providence.”

The bishop requested nuns to assist her work, and Émilie trained them until she was entrusted with forming a new religious community of charity: the Sisters of Providence. Émilie joined them as foundress and novice in 1844. Today there are more than 6,000 sisters in 9 countries on 4 continents.
She was related to the Holy Roman Emperor Saint Henry II, at whose court she was educated under the care of Saint Cunigunde.
She married Count William, and their union was very happy.
However, in the same year, 1036, their two sons were murdered in an act of revenge and her husband died of illness.
Emma devoted her vast fortune to the benefit of the poor and founded ten churches and several monasteries in present-day Austria, in one of which she later retired.
The ancient cult of Countess Emma, who already had a reputation for holiness in her lifetime, was confirmed by the Holy See in 1938.
Emma was born into the noble Saxon family of the Immedinger, daughter of a count and sister of Meinwerk, Bishop of Paderborn.
She married Liudger, son of a duke and brother of Bernard I, Duke of Saxony. Her only son was Imad, consecrated Bishop of Paderborn in 1051.
In 1008 Emma built a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary, which would later become a popular place of pilgrimage.

After her husband’s early death in 1011, she moved to Lesum (now Bremen) and generously supported Bremen Cathedral with her fortune. She is described as a great benefactor of the Church and founded several churches in the area, though her greatest concern was the poor.

Emma was later venerated as a saint, although she was never formally canonized. She was buried in Bremen Cathedral, and when the tomb was opened her body had turned to dust except for her right hand (the hand with which she gave her gifts). That relic was placed in the Abbey of Saint Liudger in Werden.

Born in Granada, she married the French emperor in 1853 in Notre-Dame Cathedral and donated the sum the city gave them as a wedding gift to build an orphanage for girls. She promoted the creation of monasteries, hospitals and other works of charity. She always visited them personally to see to their needs firsthand.

When her son was one year old, he fell gravely ill. In desperation, she sent for water from Lourdes, and the little boy soon recovered. Empress Eugénie would always defend the authenticity of those apparitions and encourage pilgrimages to the grotto.

Later she lost her husband and her only son, and endured exile in England and terrorist attacks. Despite everything, she never stopped defending the Catholic faith that had made her a charitable and caring sovereign.

Aldo was born in 1937 and through his faith overcame serious illnesses, managing to continue his studies until he graduated in political science and joined the Ministry of Finance. She was born to a father who abandoned the family, with a congenital heart defect, and was consecrated by her mother to the Immaculate Conception; she graduated in accounting.
They married in 1967, never missing daily Mass, with a deep life of prayer, and served as ministers of the Eucharist.

She was widowed in 1997 and, already a grandmother, gave her last decade as a pillar of the Italian Bishops’ Conference National Service for charitable initiatives for the Third World. She traveled to several countries in Asia, Africa and Central America. A village in Honduras destroyed by a hurricane in 1998 was rebuilt thanks to her. She met Archbishop Bergoglio, who praised her charitable sensitivity and her dedication to the Church.

Born in 1911, he graduated in physics at 21. In 1938 he married Enrica, a pharmaceutical chemist he had met at university. He took part for Christian Democracy in the constituent assembly of 1946; he was a deputy until 1953 and again in 1971. He promoted the referendum to repeal the divorce law.

In 1949 he became president of the National Institute of Geophysics, and in 1958, when Euratom (of the European Community) was established, he became its vice president. He resigned in 1965, judging that the interests of member states were prevailing over the common good.

Greatly devoted to the Blessed Sacrament, he was allowed a chapel with a tabernacle in his home; he earned a degree in theology. He was a spiritual son of Padre Pio and narrated his funeral on TV. In 1966 Pope Paul VI named him a lay adviser to the Vatican.

A great speaker, he hosted popular science programs, and in 1969 he narrated the Moon landing for RAI as an expert. He died in 1974. Scientific, technical and educational institutions bear his name, as do streets in 11 cities. In 2024 Pope Francis recognized his heroic virtues.
Henry was born in Valletta, Malta, in 1917. He worked as a draftsman in the Public Works Department, a post he held until his retirement in 1977.

They married in 1944. Inez, a qualified teacher, gave lessons to the poor and needy. A kind, generous and sincere woman, she loved and helped anyone who needed her. She trusted completely in God despite difficulties.
At 38 Henry was diagnosed with diabetes, which later caused blindness, but his miraculous recovery in 1992 baffled specialists.

Henry was exceptionally virtuous, honest and good-humored. He was a peacemaker, able to build bridges among his coworkers. He regularly brought his friends to prayer and reminded them of their religious duties. He never held a grudge or spoke ill of others. He always carried money to give to charities or in response to requests for help. He died in 1999. In her last years Inez suffered serious health problems, which she joyfully accepted until she gave up her life in 1992. She herself wrote: “I thank God for this new bouquet. These are the wonders of life. I am in His hands and accept everything He sends me with joy.”
A carpenter and shoemaker, he led the hard life of a poor craftsman but gave the poor everything he had.
He moved to Treviso (near Venice) with his wife and son.
In his last years, almost without strength, he lived in extreme poverty, accepting alms to survive.

When he died, the hovel where he lived was crowded with visitors who wished to show their veneration and take some piece of his belongings: he had only a tunic, a log for a pillow and straw for a mattress; at least 276 miracles worked through his relics were recorded within a few days.

Henry was born at the beginning of the 13th century and became Duke of Silesia and of Kraków, and thus High Duke of all Poland. Around 1218 his father arranged his marriage to Princess Anne, daughter of the King of Bohemia. This union allowed Henry II to take an active part in international politics.

At his father’s death, Henry II, at about 40, took possession of the duchy, which faced some complications. He supported Pope Gregory IX, which immediately ended his disputes with the Church. After invading Kievan Rus, the Mongols set their sights on the Kingdom of Hungary, but first they had to seize Poland. The European sovereigns, more interested in the struggles between the Empire and the Papacy, ignored Henry’s plea for help, except King Wenceslaus I of Bohemia. Henry was defeated and died in battle on April 9, 1241, and was buried in the Franciscan crypt in Wrocław.

Although he ruled for only 3 years, Henry remained in the memory of Silesia, Greater Poland and Kraków as a perfect Christian knight. In 2015 the diocese presented his cause for beatification, and Pope Francis declared him a Servant of God.
In 1014, together with his wife, he was anointed by the Pope in Rome as emperor of the Holy Roman Empire.

With his upright and just character, he attended to the needs of his people and governed with a firm yet gentle hand. He was understanding and not vengeful. He preferred forgiving to punishing and put the good of his subjects before his own interests.
With his prodigious military genius he knew how to triumph but, unlike others of his time, he did not abuse victory. Justice governed all his acts. His sincerity and nobility were recognized by all.
When Henry breathed his last, Cunigunde left the court to take refuge in a monastery until the end of her days, since, having lived a Josephite marriage, they had no children.

Enzo was born in Scandiano (Italy) in 1951. He took part in the Communion and Liberation movement, which was taking its first steps in the universities in those years. In 1972 he began intense social work in his neighborhood and grew closer to Fr. Luigi Giussani, the movement’s founder.

In 1973 he married Fiorisa, and in 1976 he specialized in vascular surgery. In 1979 his awareness of the need for a clear educational proposal grew, and he set up a cooperative school in Modena run by parents and teachers.
Around the same time, with friends, he created the “La Collina della Poesia Cultural Center,” which became a reliable point of reference for hundreds of young people.
In 1980 he moved to the University of Bologna. His professional passion embraced every aspect of human need, according to testimonies.

On May 26, 1999, Enzo died suddenly in a car accident. More than 7,000 people attended the funeral celebrated by the cardinal. His Foundation still receives letters of gratitude from young people whose lives he marked.

He was born around 1120 in Västergötland, the son of a nobleman. In 1150 he was elected king by the Swedes of Uppland, and with the death of the rival king in 1154, Eric became sovereign of all Sweden.

He codified the kingdom’s legislation in what became known as “Eric’s Law.” His works were directed at consolidating and spreading the Christian faith in Scandinavia. He completed the Cathedral of Old Uppsala and, with the support of Saint Henry, undertook the First Crusade to Finland in 1155 to Christianize the pagan Finns. This bloody war would lay the foundation for a long Swedish rule over Finland until the 19th century.

He died after being knocked off his horse and murdered next to the Cathedral of Old Uppsala as he left Mass on May 18, 1160, Ascension Day. Rebel nobles are said to have wanted to get rid of him because of his unpopular policy of tithes for the Church.

He was venerated as a saint in Sweden during the Middle Ages, but the Catholic Church has never formally canonized him. The coat of arms of the city of Stockholm bears the image of the king, its patron saint.

He studied medicine at the Sorbonne (France), and in 1930 he created the first Chair of Pediatrics at the University of San Carlos (USAC), being its first professor and holding the chair for 24 years. He is considered the father of pediatrics in Guatemala.

Concerned with helping children and the poor, he carried out extensive social and medical work: he created the Children’s Tuberculosis Sanatorium, was medical director of the Society for the Protection of Children and director of the Fight against Tuberculosis. For 3 years he was director of Caritas Guatemala, organizing food distribution to some 90,000 people, and he was also a delegate to the Inter-American Children’s Institute.

He had a strong will, a big heart, social sensitivity, impeccable professional integrity and a broad cultural background. He was a passionate defender of the right to life and love for life, especially of the unborn, being one of the initiators of the pro-life campaigns in Guatemala and giving talks on the subject to thousands all over the country. Ernesto was a supernumerary of Opus Dei. He died in 1991 and was declared venerable by Pope Francis in 2023.

He was born on the island of Cyprus in the 3rd century and spent his early years in the simplicity of a shepherd. His reputation as a saint spread throughout the island, and so he was one of the confessors whom Maximinus, a great persecutor of Christians, ordered to have their right eye gouged out and a leg hamstrung, condemning them to work in the mines.

He was able to return to Cyprus as a shepherd under the peace of Constantine; he married, had a daughter and was widowed; he spread holiness, and the people and clergy acclaimed him successor to the bishop.

He was summoned to the Council of Nicaea, which condemned Arius, as one of the 318 prelates. He put into simple words the sum of the Christian faith on the Trinity and Christ’s redemption of man, and so the rival heretical philosopher was converted. He also attended the Council of Serdica. He was famous for his virtues and his miracles.

The island of Corfu, where his relics rest, was the only territory of Greece not conquered by the Ottoman Empire: in 1716 the image of an old man with a fiery sword appeared in the sky and the Turks withdrew. His incorrupt relics keep the softness and temperature (36.6 °C) of a human body. When his vestments and slippers are changed, they look worn, although the body remains intact all year. It is said that he walks about a great deal, helping people.

Æthelberht, King of Kent in early England, married the Christian princess Bertha, only daughter of the King of Paris. Her piety and gentle virtues greatly impressed her husband, who granted her full freedom to practice her religion. She brought to England Liudhard, a Frankish bishop, and later came missionaries sent by Saint Gregory the Great: Saint Augustine of Canterbury and his companions.

The king went personally to hear them and soon gave them permission to preach to all the people. Conversions began to multiply, and soon the king and his court were baptized at Pentecost in 597. In a short time he became a model for the nobility of his conversion.

His reign was marked by his commitment to improving his subjects’ living conditions; his laws earned him esteem, and his support for the Catholic faith allowed many churches and monasteries to be built. By not imposing the faith on his subjects, he greatly favored the missionaries’ work.
He died in 616 and was buried beside Queen Saint Bertha and Saint Liudhard.

Born in Brussels in 1930, at 21 he became king of a Belgium in turmoil over secularism, social unrest and the end of the colonial era. He stood out for his firm Catholic faith and commitment to public service.

In 1960 he married the Spanish princess Fabiola de Mora y Aragón, a devout Catholic like himself. Although they could not have children, they found consolation in daily Eucharist, the defense of children and the fight against human trafficking.

In 1990 King Baudouin refused to sign the law decriminalizing abortion in his country and, defending his freedom of conscience as a Catholic, abdicated for 36 hours. He had to suffer much in his life, and he would say “Thank you, Jesus,” because he felt that this helped him carry his cross.

He died on July 31, 1993, after 40 years on the throne. He is remembered as a humble leader, a defender of the most vulnerable. Saint John Paul II highlighted his example as a “great champion of the rights of human conscience.” Pope Francis asked for his cause to be opened in 2024.

While studying law he was a member of the Association of German Catholic Students. He was then a deputy of the Center Party in the German Reichstag between 1912 and 1933, and Minister of Justice and of the Interior of the State of Württemberg. He married in 1920.

He was elected president of Württemberg, a mostly Protestant state, in 1933, just as the Nazi party was taking power. A supporter of the Church’s social doctrine, he opposed the new regime and was sent to a concentration camp. On his release he found refuge at Beuron Abbey, where he studied papal encyclicals, questions related to Catholic Action and economic doctrines.

In 1941 he made contact with resistance circles, with whom he planned a new government after an eventual Nazi collapse. Baron von Stauffenberg’s attempt on Hitler’s life in 1944 led to his arrest; he was tried for treason and beheaded in prison on January 23, 1945. The German Bishops’ Conference today awards the Eugen Bolz Prize, given among others to Angela Merkel in 2017 for welcoming refugees and people in need.
Eugenio was born in Mexico in 1900, the eldest of 10 siblings, and studied art with the Augustinian fathers. Out of necessity he gave up his studies and went to work for the oil company PEMEX.

During the Cristero religious persecution, he secretly trained catechists, brought Communion to the sick and imprisoned, and visited the poor and priests in hiding. He stood out as a defender of the faith and of the freedom of the Church and wrote on political, social and economic matters; he spread the Catholic press, producing pamphlets. He took part in popular missions to revive the faith oppressed by persecution.

In 1937 he married Marina, a catechist like himself and a woman of deep piety. She received mystical graces, which she kept discreetly. She expressed her faith in her spiritual diary and in a hundred poems; there are 180 letters from their engagement. The poor found comfort in their home, both materially and by hearing the Word.

In 1942 Eugenio was directing the reconstruction of the church of San José when he had an accident and died. Marina began working in a factory to support her children and obtained scholarships for them in Christian schools. One son became a bishop in Mexico (now retired). She died in 1988; in 1997 their causes for beatification were begun.

Eurosia Fabris was born in a rural area near Vicenza (Italy) in 1866. She completed only 2 grades of primary school because she had to help in the fields and at home. She learned to read and write with the Scriptures, the Catechism, Church History and the Philothea.
She joined the Association of the Daughters of Mary and was an apostle of charity with her family and in her parish, where she taught catechism to children and sewing to girls.

In 1855 a neighbor died, leaving three very young girls. The first died very soon after, and the others were under 2 years old. For 6 months, every morning, she took care of the girls and their home. She decided to marry Carlo in 1886, because she felt called through these babies to a mission. Together with her 9 children, “Mamma Rosa,” as she was now called, gave them a solid Christian formation.

She lived an intense life of prayer; she balanced the family budget while doing great charity toward the poor, sharing her daily bread. Three sons were ordained priests. She became a Franciscan tertiary, seeking to live the true spirit of poverty and joy in her home amid her daily duties. The family home was an ideal Christian community. She died in 1932.

Faro spent his youth at the courts of two kings and led a very holy and edifying life. At 38 he felt he should embrace religious life. His wife Blidechild not only consented but withdrew to a place on one of her estates. She died there a few years later, having urged her husband to persevere in his vocation when he had wanted to rejoin her.

He received the tonsure in the diocese of Meaux. In 628 the see became vacant and he was consecrated bishop. Dagobert I named him his chancellor, and Faro used all his influence to protect the innocent, orphans and widows and to help all those in need. He worked with tireless zeal and vigilance to convert those who still practiced idolatry.

Saint Faro made large donations of his own property to the Church, building parishes and monasteries. In the outskirts of Meaux he founded the monastery of the Holy Cross, which later took his name, and entrusted it to the monks of Saint Columbanus of Luxeuil.
María and Fernando first saw each other when he was 6 and she was brought to be baptized. Two decades later, they became inseparable.

Fernando had not been so devout. After studying in Switzerland, he went to Bolivia without his parents’ permission to get rich in mining and live well. When he fell gravely ill, he returned to his city, and during his convalescence he had a deep conversion; he began working at the family sugar mill.

They married in 1936 and became involved in helping the poor and in Catholic Action. Fernando joined the board of the diocesan radio. They helped establish a Carmelite convent in León, which they supported until their deaths. One son became a Jesuit missionary in Honduras (and wrote a book about them), and 3 others joined Opus Dei, as did their mother, who asked for admission at 61.

In 1976 Fernando died of a heart attack. In 1982 she made the pilgrimage with John Paul II and died of cancer a few months later. Their family, friends and neighbors in León were convinced of the holiness of Lourdes and Fernando’s lives.

Born in the province of Zamora around 1199, cousin of King Saint Louis of France and son of Alfonso IX, to whom he wrote a letter that softened his heart, averting a war between father and son and thus uniting the crowns of Castile and León. In 1220 he married Beatrice and, widowed in 1237, married Joan, breaking the tradition of adulterous kings and illegitimate children.

He devoted his life to freeing Spain and the Catholic religion from Moorish rule, enduring 24 years of incessant war. He did not seek his own glory or to enlarge his domains. He wanted his soldiers to be educated in the faith. His true kingdom was God’s.

A poet and musician, he composed songs and stood out for his honesty and the purity of his conduct. He established Castilian as the official language. A great penitent, he joined the Franciscan Third Order. He spread devotion to the Virgin and built chapels to her for his victories. He raised Burgos Cathedral and made the mosque of Seville a Catholic church.

His death in 1252 was an example of faith and humility: he lay prostrate on ashes, asked for the sacraments, said goodbye to his family and asked those present to forgive any unintended offenses. Sixtus V confirmed his “halo of holiness,” and Clement X canonized him in 1671.
Philetus, a senator, his wife Lydia, their children, a captain and a notary were arrested for being Christians in Illyria (an ancient region in the west of the Balkan Peninsula).
Emperor Hadrian entrusted them to a high-ranking officer named Amphilochius, who ended up converting to Christianity. Likewise the officer of the prison guard, Cronides, followed his example.
When the emperor learned of this, he ordered them all tortured to make them apostatize. Failing to make them give in, they were martyred in the year 121 in a vessel of boiling oil.
A simple woman of deep spirituality, a life of prayer and commitment; she made the Church her family and her family a church at home. She said: “With God there are no coincidences, only Providence.”
She taught in hard-to-reach rural schools in the interior of the state of São Paulo, arriving by carriage, on horseback or by donkey.

She was a Focolarina, leader of the Mothers’ Club of the Loreto Community, a columnist for the Gazeta do Rio Pardo and the Diocesan Bulletin of São João da Boa Vista, and took part in the Congress of New Parishes in Rome. On that trip she met Mother Teresa in Loreto.

“Her joy and humility were contagious; there was no one who did not open their heart to her, for she was greatly esteemed by rich and poor alike” (Paulo Celso, Abbot Emeritus). Her daughter Maria de Lourdes says: “She seemed to have a direct connection with God; it was impressive, always a kind and faithful word for everyone.”

Natuzza (short for Fortunata) helped her mother and siblings and so could not go to school; she never learned to read or write. In 1944 she married Pasquale, a carpenter. From a very early age she had visions of Christ and the Virgin. There are 10 documented volumes of her healings and other graces. She had the gift of bilocation and saw Padre Pio and other saints, her guardian angel and also the dead, and spoke with them.

She became known for the appearance on her body of blood-colored images and words around Easter, which caused her great psychological and physical pain. Some of the words were Hebrew and Aramaic, though she could not even read Italian. For decades, devout Catholics from Calabria and the rest of Italy came to her to ask for advice and prayers, and for news of the souls of their relatives.

From childhood, Natuzza understood that her mission would be to give people a word of comfort. She received hundreds of people a day for years. Taking on their sufferings, she gave everyone a word of comfort, hope and peace. She died in 2007, and her tomb became a pilgrimage destination. Her cause was opened in 2014.

Her father was a wealthy businessman of solid moral principles. From childhood she hid a gift, felt a call within her and used to walk 4 km to the Shrine of Our Lady of Belvedere. As a young woman she was already a spiritual reference.
Although determined to follow a religious vocation, by the custom of the time she was given in marriage to Faustino Zotta, who would support and accompany her in her heavy yet beautiful mission.

In 1956, at 39, drawn by a strange feeling to the back of her shop, she saw a faint light and a heavenly radiance with the apparition of Saint Michael the Archangel, who told her to leave her town and go to Rome, where she had never been. There her great mission would be fulfilled.

They moved, and within a few days lines of people began to form, waiting to be received and heard. From then on, numerous extraordinary events took place, and above all thousands were converted thanks to her example and spiritual simplicity. She died in 2008 and has been venerable since 2023.

Francesco was born in 1912 in southern Italy and learned the hard work of the fields as a child. Teresa was born a year later into a family of fervent Christians. They married in 1942. They lost a baby boy and a teenage girl full of life; an endless grief for both, but faith prevailed. As a consolation, one son became a priest.
Despite financial hardship, Providence led them through unprecedented trials, and they raised their children in God and prayer. She invited them to take part in Catholic Action meetings.

To her son, about to be ordained a priest, Teresa wrote in 1970: “I will let out a deep sigh while you, on that day, in your beautiful and kind hands, lift up the Sacred Host. Don’t worry, sometimes we suffer. That is how we become like Jesus.”
Saints of the home, Teresa and Francesco remained in Jesus every day of their lives and bore much fruit. She died in 1984 and he in 1998.

He was born in 1550 into a family of landed nobles north of Dublin that for generations had distinguished itself in the city’s administrative and commercial life. His wife was the granddaughter of Blessed Margaret Ball, another Irish martyr. Francis remained faithful to the family tradition for some 30 years as an official in municipal bodies.

In 1593 he was elected mayor of Dublin. For Catholics the situation grew steadily worse, especially after the defeat of the Irish Catholic resistance against the Protestant power of England in 1603. Francis was willing to open his home to Catholic priests, knowing that he was risking his life.

Soon Catholics were expelled from public office, and the government began to organize a Parliament made up mostly of Protestants. Francis was elected to the Irish Parliament, but a Protestant mayor annulled the election.

In 1614 he was imprisoned on false pretexts. Francis preferred to suffer rather than deny his faith. He died in 1621, already elderly, after 7 years in prison in deplorable conditions, patiently accepted. He was declared a martyr by Saint John Paul II in 1992.
Francesca Bussi was born in 1384 and at 13 was married to the nobleman Lorenzo de’ Ponziani. They had a happy marriage; she suffered the death of 2 young children.

With her sister-in-law Vannozza she used to go through the streets helping the sick and the poor. They led many Roman ladies to abandon their frivolous lives and join an association linked to a monastery, and even turned their house into a hospital.

During an attack on Rome, her husband was wounded, her son taken hostage and all their belongings looted. God rewarded her work and prayer by granting her the gift of healing the sick, reading consciences and seeing revelations of purgatory and hell, and even revealed to her the Western Schism in advance.
To widen the reach of her charity, as a widow she founded the congregation of the Olivetan Oblates of Santa Maria Nova in 1425.
So unanimous was the devotion the Romans paid her that it is said the whole city came to pay her a final tribute. There is a church in Rome named after her.

Francis was the son of the Duke of Gandía and a descendant of Ferdinand V of Aragon and of two Borgia popes. At the royal court in Alcalá he was deeply impressed by a man being taken to prison by the Inquisition: Ignatius of Loyola.

He married the Portuguese Leonor at 19 and received the title of marquis; at 29 Charles V named him Viceroy of Catalonia, and in 1543 he inherited the duchy of Gandía. He was a great administrator, a model Christian, and enjoyed composing music.

As adviser and friend of Empress Isabella, he was charged with burying her in Granada when she died young. On identifying her body, he was struck by its advanced decomposition and resolved “never again to serve a master who could die!” Soon his wife died; he made the Ignatian Exercises, took Jesuit vows and was ordained.

Crowds gathered to hear the holy duke preach. He did not want positions, but because of his management experience he was elected the 3rd Superior General in 1566. Hundreds of schools and the spread of the Society beyond the Alps are owed to him. Today he is considered among the 3 most important Jesuits of all time.

Francis, of peasant origin, was kind, sincere, helpful and of upright faith. He married Józefa Kobyłka and they had 7 children; however, he was soon widowed with young children and, needing someone to care for them, married Józefa Leiman, also widowed.

With the Nazi occupation of Poland he saw the need to give catechesis to the children, since the parishes had been closed and most priests arrested. Despite the danger, he organized catechism classes for children in his home, and later in catechetical centers in various villages. In 3 years he prepared 300 children for First Communion.
In 1944 he was arrested by the German police and subjected to such torture that he died in the prison of Kalisz (Poland) 10 days after his arrest.
He was beatified by John Paul II on June 13, 1999.

Franco was born in 1948 in Calabria. Specialized in cardiology, anesthesia and resuscitation, he accompanied the terminally ill with great skill and deep faith. With Rosaria, a medical student and member of Catholic Action like him, they asked in their wedding rite in Assisi, in the saint’s crypt, that they might become saints together.

Rosaria lived her medical vocation as a mission: “In my profession I try to live the Gospel. Seeing Jesus in the least leads me to give myself to each person beyond mere professional duty; it comes back to me multiplied in gratitude and joy.”

He became diocesan president of Catholic Action for 9 years and founded the Ecclesial Movement of Cultural Commitment (MEIC). She took an active part in the Focolare Movement, taking responsibility for the Locride region.

In 1993 Franco was elected mayor, but pressure from the old political guard was so strong that within 6 months he decided to step down. In 1996 he had an accident, saved the life of his youngest son and died after 18 days in a coma. In 2000 a tumor took Rosaria in 39 days. They left before turning 50, leaving their mark.

Born in 1886, he studied law at Charles University in Prague, earned his doctorate in 1910 and went on to study financial administration. In 1917 he married Anna, whom he had known since childhood and who later became his student.

He truly lived his faith in his educational, social, political and charitable activities. He took an active part in Catholic works and was a member of the Secular Franciscan Order. He told young Catholics thinking of entering politics that the mere idea of using power and influence for personal gain is a conspiracy against the foundations of the state.

From 1918 he worked at the Ministry of Finance. He co-founded the Czechoslovak People’s Party and was its president from 1920 to 1930. In 1920 he became a member of the National Assembly, serving until 1935. He was Minister of the Interior and of Posts and Telegraphs. He promoted the creation of credit cooperatives for farmers.
He was known for never lying, not even in politics. He personally funded land for several churches and died in 1935 in Prague, without wealth, in a rented apartment.

Franz was the illegitimate son of a peasant woman and in his youth fathered a daughter out of wedlock. But in 1936 he married Franziska and wholeheartedly embraced the Catholic faith; they visited Rome on their honeymoon.

In 1941, as sacristan of his parish, he was horrified to see Nazi party members receiving Communion, children in the Hitler Youth and neighbors sacrificing lives to Fascism, all with the connivance of the Austrian Church.

Called up in 1943, he refused to serve the Führer: for him, being Catholic was incompatible with defending Nazism. His wife supported him despite her pain. He was finally sentenced in Berlin and guillotined.

Neighbors stopped greeting her, accusing her of turning him into an intransigent Catholic sacrificed in vain. Years later he was vindicated, and Benedict XVI proclaimed him a martyr in 2007. She died in 2013 at 100.
They married in Munich in 1902, and Fritz, born a Calvinist, began as a journalist and rose to editor of the main Bavarian newspaper.
In 1927, as a skeptical journalist, he approached the stigmatic mystic Therese Neumann, also an opponent of the regime; he became personally involved to the point of converting.
His ideological distance from the publishers led him to found his own Catholic weekly, “Der Gerade Weg” (The Straight Path), with Father Naab.
His opposition to Nazi ideology was absolute, and he publicly advocated active participation by Catholics in political life.

In 1933 Hitler came to power, and Fritz was immediately arrested and his newspaper banned. After 15 months of torture without any trial, he was sent to Dachau and shot there on the Night of the Long Knives.

Gaetana Sterni lived all her life in the province of Vicenza (Italy). At 16 she married Liberale, a widower with 3 children. She filled the new home with vitality and joy and was expecting a child, but in prayer she sensed his death in the prime of youth and health; the much-desired child died shortly after birth. At 18 her older sister died, then her father, and her brother drifted away from the family, which faced a critical financial situation. She lived these difficult moments in surrender to the Lord.

Her in-laws hounded her with suspicion and slander until they separated her from her stepchildren and drove her from the home. At 19 she returned to her mother’s house, defended her children’s rights, forgave and managed to reconcile. Suffering did not make her despair.

She had never thought of becoming a nun; she asked God to meet a future husband, but in prayer she saw that He wanted “to be the only spouse of her soul.” She entered the Canossian Sisters, where she lived happily for only 5 months; her mother died and she had to care for her younger siblings. Years passed facing difficulties and illnesses.
