God was preparing her to give her whole life. In 1853 she took vows and lived in the hospice for victims of disordered lives and vice. She spent 36 years there, during which her congregation, the Daughters of the Divine Will, was born; it spread to Europe, America and Africa.
She was born in Ravenna in 1471, and around 1496 she married the Venetian tailor Giacomo, nicknamed Pianella. Of their children, one died young and the other, named Leo, became a priest.

The marriage was unhappy because of the mistreatment she received from her irascible and dissolute husband, who went so far as to denounce her as a witch. But the bishop’s vicar could see the falsehood of the accusations. In despair at being abandoned, she went to Padua in poverty and endured great hunger. Many years later her husband arrived and began to notice the signs of Providence, which miraculously ensured she never lacked divine help; repentant thanks to her prayers, he died in 1511.

As a widow she devoted herself to charity and care of the sick, and helped those afflicted in Ravenna during the plague that swept the country. She helped transform the “Brotherhood of the Good Jesus” after the death of its foundress Margaret Molli.

Gentile also had the gift of prophecy and of miraculous cures. She died a holy death in 1530, and as early as 1537 Pope Paul III authorized a process for miracles attributed to her intercession and Margaret’s.

From one of the noblest families of Gaul at the end of the 4th century, he received the best education and went to Rome to study civil law, where he married Eustachia, a lady highly esteemed in imperial circles.
The emperor sent him as a duke to govern the Gallic provinces. Meanwhile Germanus gave himself over to all the pleasures that came his way, and so earned the displeasure of the bishop, Saint Amator.

One day the bishop confronted him and asked him to live as someone destined to be his successor. He promptly made him a deacon; a wonderful change took place instantly, and he accepted everything that had happened as God’s will. He gave himself to prayer, study and charity, and when Amator died he was unanimously elected to the vacant episcopal see.

He distributed his property among the poor, built a large monastery and practiced great austerities, becoming an admired bishop. Saint Patrick, the great apostle of Ireland, is said to have been part of Germanus’s entourage.
She was born at the beginning of the 7th century, the daughter of Theobald, Count of Douai, related to the Franco-Germanic Merovingian dynasty.

She was married to Rigomer, a Frankish nobleman who died soon, after a few years of marriage and several children. Among her children were Sigefrid, married to Saint Bertha of Blangy, Saint Adalbald, married to Saint Rictrude, and Saint Gerberta; her best-known grandchildren were Saint Mauront, Saint Eusebia, Saint Clotsend and Saint Adalsend.
Around 640 Gertrude founded the Benedictine abbey of Hamage where, now a widow, she took the habit and became the first abbess.

During a journey to Périgueux, her son Saint Adalbald was martyred by relatives of his wife Saint Rictrude. Grandmother Gertrude claimed the little orphan Eusebia and took her to the monastery of Hamage.
Gertrude died in 652, and her granddaughter, the future Saint Eusebia, succeeded her as abbess.
On vacation with his family he met Anna. Although from Catholic families, they did not practice, except for her devotion to Padre Pio.

Anna came into contact by chance with the Charismatic community. This awakened his interest in seeing for himself what his wife and daughters were experiencing. In 1976 he began his path of conversion and radical change of life.

At 45 he was ordained a permanent deacon of the Diocese of Rome. In 1987, with his wife and two other couples, they founded the “Community of the Risen Jesus” in the spirit of the Charismatic Renewal.

In 1991 he developed a serious multiple myeloma, which he faced with great courage and faith. He offered his pain to the Lord for the Church and, with great determination, kept evangelizing, offering everything for the World Congress of Ecclesial Movements. He was born into heaven in 1998, at 46.

Born in Pescara in 1933, as soon as he graduated as a surgeon in 1957 he joined the Parma clinic. His charity toward patients surprised everyone. He won a fellowship at the Mayo Clinic in the U.S. in 1961 and soon became head of cardiovascular research.
In 1964 he returned to Italy to marry Anna, whom he had met skiing in the Alps.
Hundreds of Italian children with congenital heart disease crossed the ocean with their families for him to operate on them. He helped pay for their travel and offered his home to many.
In his last 5 years he was diagnosed with Hodgkin’s disease and spent them doing research: he authored 100 scientific publications and received 3 gold medals.
Although he died at only 36 in 1970, surgeons around the world today save lives with his Rastelli I and II surgical procedures for congenital heart disease.
In the late 1980s, the Jesuit Father Castelli of Parma took an interest in him and proposed him as an example of holiness for young people, researchers and doctors.
Giovanni, president of Catholic Youth Action, was called “the peacemaker” in his town because he spoke to everyone about peace and forgiveness in a deeply convincing way.

Rosetta was a woman of peace who helped the poor and people in difficulty. Together they shared a humble family life based on prayer, reading, and daily Mass and rosary. She died young of pneumonia during a pregnancy. Her body is preserved intact.

In 1942, serving at the front in World War II, Giovanni told a comrade: “You are young and have a life to build; my children are in good hands. Escape, and I’ll stay.” The soldier later tracked down his children to thank them.
He was born in Bitonto (Bari, Italy) in 1880. In 1909 he ran in the municipal elections and managed to create a cultural school for workers.

In 1911 he graduated in philosophy and pedagogy in Naples. In 1919 he began to distance himself from political commitment and from the socialists, disappointed by their “tendency to oppress.” He then devoted himself to study and to teaching young people. He would say: “I am too much of an educator to do politics.” He believed that “Catholic Christianity belongs to the weak, to the oppressed, to help them claim their rights.”

In a 1919 lecture he set out the aims a school should have: “to form the personality of the students and guide them toward self-education, so that they acquire the ability and habit of judging their own actions and those of others correctly, of weighing consequences with criteria of justice and responsibility.” Between 1925 and 1934 he drew closer to the faith, above all through reading. In 1943 he founded a school of political formation for young people and courageously denounced the devastating aspects of the dictatorship spreading in Italy.
With Aldo Moro, later prime minister and Servant of God, he would see the dangers of entrusting political tasks to Catholic Action and of confusing it with the Christian Democrats. He died in 1957.

Born in 1909 in a village near Modena (Italy), the second-to-last of 9 siblings. By 16 he was already working as a cheesemaker with his parents. In 1933 he took over the family dairy, while being very active in Catholic Action.

Drafted into the army, he went on pilgrimage to San Giovanni Rotondo to recover from a stomach illness that tormented him; from then on Padre Pio guided his path and was part of his most important decisions.
In 1939 they married and shared the management of the dairy he already ran.

In 1945 he was appointed mayor of Prignano and held office for almost three terms, until 1959. He inherited a town devastated by the war with empty coffers, but he invited the people to roll up their sleeves, and they managed to build an aqueduct, an electricity network, roads, a post office, the town hall and schools.
To guard against pride, he swore before Padre Pio to wear sandals throughout his term.
Godfrey was Count of Cappenberg (Germany) and lord of a large district in the diocese of Münster. His wife came from another distinguished family.

Under the influence of Saint Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian canons, he decided to turn his castle of Cappenberg into a monastery of that order. He persuaded his wife and his brother to renounce the world as he did and become religious under Saint Norbert’s direction. His father-in-law violently opposed him and even threatened him with death, but he still donated all his possessions to the Premonstratensians.
Near Cappenberg he built a convent in which his wife and two of his sisters took the veil. He also founded hospitals and charitable institutions.

As a Premonstratensian novice, he took on the humblest tasks and washed the feet of the sick and pilgrims lodged in the hospital. He received minor orders but did not live long enough to be ordained a priest.
On January 13, 1127, at 30, he joyfully gave up his soul, declaring that he did not want to live a moment longer, not for all the gold in the world.
In Nazianzus, in Cappadocia (today Turkey), Nonna married Gregory, a member of a pagan sect, a magistrate and wealthy landowner.
With her gentle manners, education and fervent prayer, by God’s grace she brought about his conversion to the true faith.
He took his conversion so seriously that he was ordained a priest and later, at 60, elected Bishop of Nazianzus; Nonna was always at her husband’s side serving the poor.

Their 3 children would be saints: Saint Gregory “the Theologian” (baptized by his own father and later Doctor of the Church), Saint Caesarius (physician to the imperial court of Constantinople) and Saint Gorgonia.
Nonna died while praying in church, shortly after Gregory.

Gregory was born in Caesarea in Cappadocia, son of Saints Basil and Emmelia, and brother of Saints Basil the Great, Peter of Sebaste and Macrina. He was probably orphaned very early. After completing an excellent education in letters with his brother, he took up the profession of rhetorician.

He married the young Theosebia. He was a professor of rhetoric and was later ordained a priest (priestly celibacy was not yet required). Saint Gregory of Nazianzus held Theosebia in the highest respect and called her “the glory of the Church and the blessing of our generation.”

He became Bishop of Nyssa (today in Armenia) in 372 and Archbishop of Sebaste. He fought the Arian heresy. He was known for his writings on contemplation and Christian mysticism, his commentaries on Scripture and his Trinitarian theology.

He spent some time in exile in the mountains of Cappadocia; wherever he went, he was asked to restore peace and regulate orthodoxy and discipline. An illustrious Doctor of the Church, he was a leader at the Councils of Constantinople and Antioch. With his brother Saint Basil the Great and his close friend Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, they are the so-called “Cappadocian Fathers,” known by this formula: “Basil is the arm that acts; Gregory of Nazianzus, the mouth that speaks; and Gregory of Nyssa, the head that thinks.”

He graduated as an industrial engineer and worked for the Tramway Company of Madrid and Alicante. To his strong personality he joined a deep Christian faith made luminous by the brilliance of his works. His family went to daily Mass, and on the way back he generously helped a group of poor people. He took older and younger friends to the mountains to talk about religious and social topics while enjoying nature.

Three things pained him about the years before the Civil War: the poverty and destitution of so many families, the ban on religion in schools, and politics without God. So he created a cooperative espadrille factory so workers could have jobs and built a road to employ the unemployed. He founded a private school so religion could be taught.

On Corpus Christi of 1936, when the town council banned the procession, he put up a large wooden banner: “Long live Christ the King!” The Republicans jailed him for several hours. When an uprising against the bans began, he was arrested. His wife visited him often, until he was shot together with 6 companions for an alleged illegal meeting. He prepared them all to die for God. His town named the street where he was born after him. His eldest son, an industrial engineer like him, is an Opus Dei priest.
Guillem was born in 1897 in a coastal town in southern Catalonia. He was a brilliant student, and in Barcelona he earned the regard of Albert Einstein himself.

Meeting Christ meant the radical gift of his life, for him and for Caterina. When the Civil War broke out they lived in a suburb of Madrid that became a battlefront. They were forced to move into the city and ended up in a basement where social books of the Jesuit fathers had been left to be burned. For 2 years he immersed himself in this social reading, discovering that his best service would be the apostolate to the working world. Without belonging to any political party or union, he was unanimously elected president of the workers’ council in his company. For that General Franco sentenced him to 12 years in prison, but his scientific and technical skills spared him many of those years, allowing his sentence to be reduced.

In 1946 he promoted the Workers’ Brotherhood of Catholic Action (HOAC), which would build bridges between the Church and the working class. He traveled across Spain several times in third class, lodging as a poor man among the poor, kindling enthusiasm without assemblies or anyone’s support. He died in 1964, and in 2003 his beatification process began.

Born in 1800, he was a volunteer army surgeon. As a longtime member of the Aachen city council and of the parliament in Berlin, he shaped the political, social and religious life of the city. He was concerned with social, educational and health issues, and in an increasingly secularized age he made Catholic principles heard.
He married Barbara in 1826, and their marriage was happy, blessed with many children, though struck by the death of 4 of them and then of his wife in 1866.

He promoted the settlement of religious orders and the founding of several Catholic associations. The Saint Francis Xavier Missionary Association (today Missio, International Missionary Society), which he founded in 1832, has been a blessing for 175 years. After World War II other organizations based on his work emerged: Misereor, Adveniat and Renovabis.

As a doctor and scientist, he published a study on tuberculous meningitis, a major concern in children. He was committed to the physical and mental well-being of his patients, always open to the poorest, whom he often treated free of charge. He died in 1882, and Pope Francis decreed his heroic virtues in 2015.
Born in 1396 in Udine into the family of the lords Valentini of Maniago.
Around 1414 she married the nobleman Antonio, with whom she had six children.

Widowed in 1441, she decided to withdraw from the world and, under the influence of the stirring preaching of the Augustinian Angelo da San Severino, became an Augustinian tertiary. Even after making her profession, she continued living in the house her husband left her until 1446, when she went to live with her sister Perfetta, also a new Augustinian tertiary.

She always led a life of penance and mortification, had ecstasies and heavenly visions, and was favored by God with the gift of miracles and knowledge of hidden things. Having broken both thighbones, she spent her last years always lying on her poor, hard bed, serene and patient.
She died on April 23, 1458, and her cult was confirmed in 1848 by Pius IX.

Son of the Arian king Leovigild, he was sent to Seville with his brother to be educated in the school run by their uncle Saint Leander. There he married the Catholic Ingund. Despite all the pressure Queen Goiswintha, his father’s wife, put on her to embrace Arianism, she refused and brought about Hermenegild’s conversion to Catholicism in 579, when he governed Baetica.

His father fought against him, and Hermenegild sent his wife and son to Byzantium, where they died. Taken prisoner as a result of a complicated political conflict between the Hispano-Romans (Catholics) and the Hispano-Goths (Arians), on his father’s orders he endured a harsh imprisonment, sunk in misery, bound hand and foot under a jailer who mistreated him.

To avoid even the appearance of complicity with Arianism, on Easter Day he refused to receive Communion from Arian hands. He was murdered in prison. Pope Saint Gregory the Great wrote an enthusiastic eulogy of him, attributing to Saint Hermenegild’s merits the conversion of his brother, King Reccared, and of all Visigothic Spain.
Herminia was born in 1887 in Puzol (Valencia). She married Vicente Ferrer in 1916; they had no children.

She belonged to several religious associations. She stood out for her charity and her many works of mercy. Her comfortable social position allowed her to be more generous in giving alms and in visiting and taking in the sick.
She often offered her home to do good, especially to young mothers, whose medical expenses she paid. She founded a society for the sick poor. Her life of piety was intense.

She was arrested by militiamen during the religious persecution and shot for her public profession of faith, together with her husband and the Blessed nun Francisca Javier Fenollosa, in Gilet (Valencia) on September 27, 1936.
She was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 2001.

He was born in Poitiers (France) into a pagan family and was a noble landowner. His search for an answer about man’s ultimate end led him to read the Bible, where he finally found what he was looking for; then he converted to Christianity.

At his conversion he was married with a daughter, and shortly after his baptism the people acclaimed him bishop of his native city. There were 6 years of intense study and preaching before he went into exile, which perfected his cultural and theological formation.

He was banished to Phrygia by Emperor Constantius, who sided with the Arian synod of 356. Contact with the East was providential for Hilary. During those 5 years he learned Greek and discovered Origen, as well as the great theological output of the Eastern Fathers, gathering critical material for the book that earned him the title of Doctor of the Church: De Trinitate (or De Fide adversus Arianos).

He was called “the Athanasius of the West,” of whom he was a contemporary. Both fought Arianism in theological debates and above all in their writings. Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine called him “the most glorious defender of the faith.” The most illustrious of his followers was Saint Martin of Tours. He died in Poitiers in 367.
Hildegund was born between 1110 and 1115, the daughter of a count.

She married Count Lothar of Are, and they had 3 children. After her husband and, shortly after, one son had died, she visited the tombs of the Apostles in Rome, seeking God’s will so she could follow Him.

Then in 1165 she founded the Mehre monastery, supported by her children Hedwig and Hermann, and was its first abbess. She stood out for her humility. She did works of charity and mercy inside and outside the monastery.
She died on February 6, 1183, and her daughter Hedwig succeeded her as abbess.

Hildegund was never officially canonized; however, together with her daughter, she has always been considered venerable within the order and is regarded as blessed in the region. Her belt and comb used to be placed on women about to give birth and on the sick to obtain divine protection. Two streets and a nursing home in Meerbusch bear her name.
A tailor and cloth merchant, he converted and became a builder of reconciliation and peace.

He turned his house into a shelter. He opened his heart and his purse to all those in need. He saw to the burial of abandoned dead. He put all his effort into settling the disputes that divided groups and families in his city. He also protected the integrity of the Catholic faith against heretical infiltration.
He faced obstacles: at home, his wife did not share all his devotions; in the parish, his great austerity was viewed with some suspicion; and at work, from competition and the bad faith of some.

In his family he was an exemplary father and showed holiness as a husband; he lived the liturgy with the community and took part faithfully in catechesis. In civic life he radiated the charm of his goodness and peace.

He died during Mass, stretching out his hands toward the altar and falling with his arms in the shape of a cross before the Crucifix. Because of his reputation for holiness, a few months later his statue was already being carved for the church “Saint Homobonus of Cremona,” and 2 years later the Pope canonized him, the first layman who was neither noble nor royal to be canonized in the Middle Ages. In 1592 the cathedral was dedicated jointly to him and to the Assumption of Mary, and in 1643 he was chosen patron of his city.

From a noble family, her father was a knight. When her mother was pregnant, she went to church and, as she prayed devoutly before the cross asking God to help her through the dangers of childbirth, a voice told her: “You will give birth to a light that will greatly illuminate the world.”

Her married life with Favarone was presumably like that of all the wealthy ladies of the time: in charge of the house, the servants and the daughters’ education, and kept away from business. Because of wars from 1200 to 1208, she had to go into exile in Perugia with her 3 daughters.

In March 1211, on Palm Sunday, her daughter Clare ran away from home to San Damiano, where Francis of Assisi consecrated her to Christ. Her uncle opposed it so fiercely that he tried to drag her from the altar, without success. We do not know how Ortolana reacted, but we can imagine her bewilderment and fear at the extremely poor life her daughter chose.

One day, now widowed, a sermon on, of all days, Palm Sunday moved her deeply and she decided to change her life. She made her will, left everything to the poor, gave her jewels to the needy and went to San Damiano with her daughters. Clare embraced her, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Monastery life would be hard for her at first, being subordinate to her daughter, but love and monastic obedience did their work.
He was born around 1160 in Bohemia (today’s Czech Republic). He became an important figure at the court of King Ottokar I in Prague, evidently destined for a successful military and political career.

But after the sudden death of his young wife and small son, he was so overwhelmed by grief that he left the court. He built a Premonstratensian abbey in his native Teplá and vowed to go to the Holy Land, taking the Cross as a crusader. However, the crusade was canceled and the Pope released him from his vow.

He entered Teplá as a lay brother. In time he was put in charge of the abbey’s temporal affairs and property. He was captured while trying to recover lands seized by bandits. The kidnappers demanded a ransom, but Hroznata would not let the abbot pay it, and he died shortly afterward from hunger and mistreatment. Pope Leo XIII confirmed his cult in 1897.

Hunna was born in the 7th century in Alsace, today’s France, the daughter of the Duke of Alsace and later wife of Huno of Hunawihr. She was devoted to the Lord, living the virtues of faith, caring for her home and praying while her husband traveled on diplomatic and political missions. Her son was baptized by Saint Deodatus of Nevers and was also named Deodatus.

She donated property to monasteries and funded the building of churches. Devoted to the poor of Strasbourg, she helped them with any task. She took special care to help her neighbors with their laundry, regardless of class. That is why she was nicknamed “the holy washerwoman.” She went from house to house collecting dirty clothes and then spent most of the day washing. When clothes were too dirty or damaged to repair, she replaced them with new ones. Her service expanded to any task they needed: cooking, cleaning, caring for children and doing even more demanding physical work, and she even bathed those who could not do so themselves.
She began making daily trips to the local villages and fields, visiting her poor neighbors, offering them religious instruction and working for them.
She died of natural causes in 679 in Alsace and was canonized in 1520 by Leo X.

Ida was born in Boulogne in 1040, the daughter of Godfrey, Duke of Lower Lorraine. At 17 she married Eustace II, Count of Boulogne, a childless widower. His possessions stretched from Luxembourg to the Atlantic, through the Ardennes and the Pas-de-Calais.

She was a very devout woman and received spiritual direction from Saint Anselm, with whom she kept up a spiritual correspondence that has survived to this day. Her favorite occupation was making beautiful liturgical vestments.

Two of her sons took part in the glorious First Crusade and were the first Christian sovereigns of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which lasted almost a century: Godfrey of Bouillon, defender of the Holy Sepulchre, and King Baldwin I of Jerusalem. She prayed so fervently that a historian attributed much of that Crusade’s success to her prayers. Her other son was Eustace III, Count of Boulogne.

Widowed, she devoted herself to richly endowing the old abbeys and also founded three others. She died in 1113, and her remains were buried in one of the abbeys she built, where miracles soon began to take place.

Daughter of a German count and educated at the court of Charlemagne, she was given in marriage to Count Egbert with a large fortune in land. They had a happy marriage; one of their sons became an abbot and a daughter an abbess.

She always kept a humble spirit, with a life devoted to prayer and works of charity. She made sure the income from her estates helped relieve the hunger of the neediest in Saxony. It is said that every day she filled a bin with food for the poor of the area.
She had a dream in which an angel appeared to her saying she should build a church in Westphalia, which she did years later.

Ida is one of the pioneers of the German Church. The monk Uffing wrote her exemplary life in 980; in one passage he describes her marriage as a reflection that: “At the moment the spouses unite, there is a physical unity in them, an indivisible action of the Holy Spirit, who kindles them with a powerful inner love directed toward heavenly realities.”
It has been suggested that she came from a senatorial family from Aquitaine, France. She married Pepin of Landen, mayor of the palace of the Merovingians, the royal house descended from King Clovis.

After Pepin’s death in 640, Itta and her daughter Gertrude withdrew from the capital to live a life of religious reflection. Around 647, on the bishop’s advice, Itta founded the abbey of Nivelles (present-day Belgium). It was originally a community of nuns, but it later became a double monastery when a group of Irish monks joined them and offered help in running the abbey.

Itta may have appointed her daughter as the first abbess, while she lived there as a simple nun, helping her daughter with her advice. Her other daughter also later joined the abbey. Both daughters were canonized as well.
Her sons were Grimoald I the Elder, mayor of the palace and father of King Childebert the Adopted, and Bavo of Ghent (or Allowin), who became a hermit and was later canonized.
Itta died at the abbey on May 8, 652, at 59 or 60.
Igino was born in Tivoli in 1894 to a humble Catholic family. His wealthy employer, moved by his intelligence, paid for his seminary studies, where he was one of the most brilliant graduates.
He spent World War I in the trenches without firing a shot because he refused to kill, and came out seriously wounded. In the military hospital he managed to graduate in letters and philosophy.

He was a director at the Vatican Library and edited the magazines Fides and later Città Nuova. Fascism persecuted him. After the war he helped relaunch Christian Democracy and served in parliament. Because of his stance for pacifism and unity, he was not reelected.

In 1948, at 54, he met 28-year-old Chiara Lubich, in whom he saw an extraordinary spiritual inspiration. He played an important role in building the movement, to the point of being considered a co-founder. With Mya he would be one of the first married Focolarini.

He published numerous works and presented theses on the mission of the laity that were taken into account at the Second Vatican Council. Widowed in 1974, and with his children’s consent, he spent his last years in a Focolare community. He died on April 18, 1980.
She was born with the name Piroska, daughter of King Saint Ladislaus of Hungary.
The Eastern Roman Emperor Alexios I Komnenos and his wife asked for her hand for their son, so she took the Orthodox name Irene and in 1105 married John II, emperor from 1118.

She is described as rich in virtues, especially in charity toward the poor. While her husband was at war against the Turks, she had the famous monastery of Christ Pantokrator built in Byzantium (today the Zeyrek Mosque), with 3 churches, a hospital of more than 50 beds for all social classes, and a hostel to feed the destitute.

She was the mother of 2 Byzantine emperors and died on August 13, 1134, and was buried in the Pantokrator beside John II. She is a saint for the Orthodox Church and blessed/venerable for the Catholic Church.

Irving was born in 1925 in Wilson, Michigan. At 6 he fell from a horse, breaking ribs and puncturing a lung. The injuries were thought to be fatal. His aunt, a Franciscan sister, held a community prayer vigil for his recovery. That morning they found him greatly improved, and he no longer had trouble breathing. Irving said that a beautiful man in a white robe stood beside the bed and raised his hand.

In high school he went to daily Mass even though he was the only one from his school. It was not unusual for him to weep at the consecration and on receiving Jesus. He joined the army and served in World War II in Europe. His letters often mention his faith, the Eucharist and his wish to go to Mass and share his faith with his comrades. In 1948 he married Gail and worked in stores and factories, becoming a plant manager. He prayed the Stations of the Cross every day after work and became a 4th Degree Knight of Columbus.

On Good Friday 1993, Irving received the stigmata. They appeared first on the palms of his hands, and he suffered the pains of the Passion every night between midnight and 3 a.m. for the rest of his life. Extraordinary physical and spiritual healings took place through him, which he always made clear came from God. Because of this special charism, they suffered as a couple but later found peace. He died in 2009.
She was born in Rome in 1774 into a well-off, deeply Christian family and studied with the Augustinian Sisters, where she stood out for her intelligence and deep interior life.

In 1796 she married the young Roman lawyer Cristoforo, but after a few months Cristoforo’s psychological fragility put the family at risk. He took a mistress, humiliated and abused his wife in various ways, and spent so much money on his affairs that it led them into extreme poverty and growing debt. Elizabeth always responded with gentle patience, offering penances and prayers for his conversion.

In 1801 she suffered a mysterious illness that brought her to the brink of death. She was inexplicably cured and had her first mystical experience. She received several prophecies about the tribulations of the Church in the last times and bore the stigmata of Christ.

Her home soon became a point of reference for many people seeking material and spiritual help. She devoted herself to caring for families in need. In 1807 she joined the Trinitarian Third Order. She gained a great reputation for holiness and died in 1825. Five years later, as she had predicted, her husband converted and was ordained a Franciscan priest. John Paul II beatified her in 1994 as a protector of the institution of marriage.

Her father, King Andrew II of Hungary, had promised her as a wife to Louis, son of the Landgrave of Thuringia, when she was only 11. Though it was an arranged marriage, they lived it in love, joining Christian asceticism, human happiness and an aura of holiness. She angered her mother-in-law and sister-in-law by not wearing the precious necklaces of her rank to church.

They grew in mutual self-giving, sustained by the conviction that their love and the happiness that came from it were a sacramental gift. Her husband, tenderly in love, wanted to prove himself worthy of a creature so beautiful in soul and took as the motto on his coat of arms the program of his public life: “Piety, Purity, Justice.”

He died young on his way to a Crusade, and then the hostility of her in-laws, who could not bear her generosity to the poor, broke out. Deprived also of her children, she was expelled from the castle at only 20. So she fully lived her Franciscan ideal of poverty in the Third Order until her death at 24, in 1231. In just 4 years she was raised to the altars by Pope Gregory IX.
At 15 her parents had already married her to the King of Portugal, Denis, who admired his wife’s qualities but had a violent temper and was unfaithful to her.
Elizabeth bore it with heroic patience, prayed for him, offered him kind words and made sacrifices for his conversion.
She devoted herself to visiting the elderly and the sick and to building convents, shelters for children, the destitute and pilgrims, a hospital for the poor and a free school for girls.
When the armies of her husband and her son were about to clash, Elizabeth crossed the fields dressed as a peasant and, on her knees, made them swear forgiveness, winning peace again and again.
Her husband died deeply repentant, and Elizabeth then devoted the rest of her life to prayer and to helping those in need.

She received a careful education for governing and for a life of faith. A woman of great inner strength, she was fond of grammar, painting and philosophy, knew history like no one else, and learned Latin to understand what she signed. She was austere and prudent and listened to advice. She lived devotion to the Eucharist intensely.

She insisted on traveling to meet her cousin and betrothed Ferdinand beforehand, and it is said they fell in love at once; they had a “clandestine” wedding because of possible opposition. She loved her husband faithfully and made him co-ruler of Castile and León. To avoid suspicion, she slept with her ladies or daughters when he was away. She rushed to care for him after an assassination attempt in Barcelona in 1492.

To restore religious unity, they freed Granada from the Muslims and purged Christendom of foreign influences. Isabella also laid the foundations for the evangelization of the New World with her determination, resolve and financial support. She thought not of conquests but of spreading the Catholic faith. She defended the natives as her subjects, not slaves. Her will is a pioneering declaration of human rights and the abolition of slavery. She died in 1504 and asked to lie beside her husband. Her process was opened in 1958.

Orphaned at 10, Isidore worked as a farmhand on the estate of Don Juan de Vargas near Madrid. There he spent many years plowing and harvesting. At dawn he went to Mass before work; his envious coworkers denounced him to the master.

He married the simple peasant María Toribia. What he earned as a day laborer he divided: part for the church, part for the poor and part for his family. On Sundays they went to Mass, visited the poor and sick, and went for family walks in the fields. One day their little boy fell into a deep well. The couple ran but, unable to rescue him, knelt to pray with all their faith. The water in the well rose and the bucket brought the child back to them safe and sound. They never tired of thanking God for this wonder.

Tradition says they later agreed to take up contemplative lives. María had to endure the slander of some neighbors who accused her of adultery, but he found out it was slander. The saint was called “de la Cabeza” (of the Head), since for several centuries her main relic was her skull, which was carried in procession when it did not rain.

Isidore died a holy death in 1130. Forty-three years later his body was exhumed and found incorrupt. Because of the miracles, in 1622 he was canonized together with Saints Teresa, Ignatius, Francis Xavier and Philip Neri. The Toledo Bridge in Madrid displays sculptures of these holy spouses.
Zapotec natives of the Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, they were born in 1660 and belonged to the Vicariate of San Francisco Cajonos, run by the Dominican fathers.

We know they were people of integrity in their personal, married and family lives, as well as in fulfilling their civic duties, holding various civil offices such as topil, judge of communal labor, mayordomo, councilman, president, trustee and mayor.
Both were baptized and catechized, also serving as acolyte, junior and senior sacristan, and topilillo.

Finally they held the civil and Church office of Fiscal and discovered that a large group of townspeople were practicing an ancestral cult. They alerted the Dominican fathers and caught those responsible, but the town rioted and seized these Fiscales, who were flogged and executed for refusing to renounce their faith: “Once we have professed baptism, we will always continue to follow the true religion.”

James was born in Westmorland, England. He seems to have been raised Protestant and converted while an apprentice in London, after reading a Catholic book. He was jailed twice for not attending Protestant services and was forced to start his Anglican apprenticeship over and leave his master. Finally he received the sacrament of reconciliation and entered the Catholic Church thanks to a venerable priest.

A bookseller and publisher in London, he married the Catholic widow Anne. Of his married life he spent no less than 9 years in prison, because of his zeal in spreading Catholic literature and prayer books and his perseverance in his newfound faith.

A bookbinder betrayed him to obtain his own release from prison. His house was searched in 1601 and Catholic books were found. The jury did not find him guilty, but the judge sent them back to reconsider because he had a controversial book hated by the Anglicans, and they changed the verdict to treason. The bookbinder Bullock was not spared; with Duckett and 3 priests he was taken to Tyburn to be executed on April 19, 1602.
His son, a Carthusian prior, tells that at Tyburn he offered Bullock forgiveness with an embrace, begging him to die in the Catholic faith, without success. In 1929 he was beatified with 105 martyrs.

In the time of Emperor Theodosius, in Persia (today Iran/Iraq), the young James enjoyed great favor with King Yazdegerd I. When the king launched a persecution of Christians, James did not have the courage to give up his friendship, so he concealed his faith in the true God, which he had professed until then.

But soon, harshly rebuked by his mother and his wife, who reproached him for his cowardly conduct, James began to understand his fault; he stopped going to court, renounced all honors and repented publicly. Bahram, the next king, summoned him, and this time James confessed that he was a Christian. Bahram reproached him for his ingratitude and, in a rage, sentenced him to death by being cut to pieces.
The saint replied: “May God grant that I die like the just. This death that seems so terrible is a very low price to pay for eternal life.”
Christians venerated him and gave the martyr the name “Intercisus,” meaning “cut to pieces” or “divided.”

He was born in 1930 in France, the son of a divorced, atheist Belgian banker; he was raised Catholic by his mother but abandoned the faith at 17. He married Pierrette, his pregnant girlfriend, and had another child outside marriage who was given to an orphanage. After working in a bank, he decided to leave everything, even his family, and buy a boat to sail around the world. But to get the money, he robbed a currency exchange office in 1954 and, while fleeing, was found by a police officer, whom he killed with three shots.

Sentenced to death, he told the chaplain he was not a man of faith, but in 1955 he experienced his conversion: “Lying down, suffering for the first time, suddenly a cry came from my chest, ‘My God!’, and like a rushing wind the Spirit seized me by the throat. An infinite power and goodness convinced me that I had never been abandoned.”

He read Saint Francis, Saint Teresa and Saint Thérèse and adopted a monastic way of life in prison. He passed on his faith in writings for his daughter and in letters evangelizing friends and Pierrette, while awaiting his execution in peace and prayer, as a means of sanctification. “May every drop of my blood wipe away a mortal sin,” he said. “Five more hours and I will see Jesus!” he wrote on the eve. On October 1, 1957, he greeted the dawn on his knees praying in his cell: “Lord, do not abandon me, I trust in You.”
In 1852 Jadwiga (Hedwig) married the politician and general Zamoyski, and they moved to Paris, from where she accompanied him on several official trips.

After her husband’s death in 1868, she stayed in France and drew close to the Oratorian order. In 1881 she moved to Kórnik, Prussia, and founded a “school of home work for women.” But in 1885 she was expelled from Prussia under Bismarck’s law as a French citizen, and she moved the school to properties her son bought.

Jadwiga’s school won the support of Church authorities and aroused great interest in society. The curriculum included religious education and practical classes in sewing, embroidery and cooking, as well as classes in drawing, literature, geography, Polish history and singing.

She published works on religious and educational topics and prepared for publication the six volumes of her husband’s diary. She spent the last years of her life with a son in Kórnik, where she died. In 2012 her beatification process began.
Born a count into an aristocratic Hungarian family. He married in 1924 and, with the Provincial Christian Socialist Party, was elected a Czechoslovak deputy in 1935.

During World War II he denounced the government’s plans to get rid of Slovakia’s Jews and told a collaborationist monsignor: “our sign is the Cross, not the swastika.” He then used his parliamentary immunity to drive the persecuted across the Hungarian border in his car, saving Slovak, Czech and Polish Jews.

After the war he criticized the persecution of the Hungarian minority and, in a fierce speech, condemned Stalin as the perpetrator of the massacre of some 28,000 Poles in the Katyn Forest. He was deported by the Soviets in 1945 and, on fabricated charges, sentenced to 10 years of labor in Siberia. In the camps he became famous for his piety and his help to prisoners. They called him “Father” and could not believe he was not actually a priest. He was moved from one Czech prison to another until his death at 57.
The Federation of Hungarian Jewish Communities called him a hero. In 2009 the Polish president awarded him the Order of Polonia Restituta for rescuing Polish refugees.

Born in 1597 in France, Jérôme studied at the Jesuit college in his town and succeeded his father as tax collector. A man of prayer, deeply devoted to Christ, he had a single aim: to do God’s will. For this he believed in the impossible, showing great docility to the Spirit.
In 1630 he felt called to found the congregation of the Hospital Sisters of Saint Joseph to serve the sick poor, and he fitted out his town’s old, run-down hospital for the future community.

In 1635 at Notre-Dame he found himself in the presence of the Holy Family and heard Jesus say: “From now on you will be my faithful servant. I will clothe you with strength and wisdom, and your guardian angel will guide you. Work hard at my work; my grace is enough for you, and it will not fail you.” The inner voice called him to found an evangelizing colony on the island of Montreal. Although he never went to America because of his family and his office, he devoted his efforts to it, chose the leaders and was the main founder of the colonization society that gave rise to the city.
Jérôme and the Societies of Gentlemen and Ladies of Montreal consecrated the island to the Holy Family; in 1659 the first 3 Hospital Sisters set out for Canada.

The engineer Jerzy from Kraków married Danuta Plebaczyk in 1957; they were married by the then priest Karol Wojtyła, their friend from the parish, who would accompany them in their spiritual growth. As John Paul II, he would say in Crossing the Threshold of Hope: “Jerzy knew he had been created for great things, but at the same time he had no doubt that his vocation was neither the priesthood nor religious life. He was passionate about his professional work, engineering. He looked for a life companion ‘on his knees,’ in prayer.”

After his doctorate, as a university lecturer, he joined the intellectuals who, with the Cardinal, carried out cultural and spiritual formation. In 1968 he came into contact with the Focolare. Impressed by the Gospel life among the members of the first community, he embraced this spirituality and, at a “clandestine Mariapolis,” felt called to give himself as a married Focolarino. But in 1970 an accident on the Nile in Sudan took him and two of his children. Karol Wojtyła presided at the funeral.

His passionate love was the Eucharist, celebrated, adored and lived. He had a deep devotion to Our Lady of Remedy and a great interest in the Word. As standard-bearer of the Nocturnal Adoration section of Monóvar (Spain), he took part in the Eucharistic Congress of Barcelona in 1952.
He served as a town councilor from 1941 to 1944. Persecuted for his faith, he did not retaliate and answered those who mistreated him: “people must be saved through repentance and brotherly love.”
He stood by his coworkers, defending their rights and looking for work for those who had none.
“Chimorrata” Llorente died with a reputation for holiness on October 31, 1964, and a street has been named after him in his town of Monóvar, Alicante.

His favorite field of apostolate was the sick and the poor. He visited them, spoke to them of God and often left them a small contribution with the message: “In the name of Jesus Christ, receive this help” (Joaquín Llorente Llorens)

Their names have been preserved by Tradition, beginning with the Protoevangelium of James; they apparently lived first in Galilee and later settled in Jerusalem, where the Virgin was born and grew up; there they also died and were buried.
It is said that, each in their solitude, they found an answer to their prayers for a child, and little Mary came to them.
In 1879 Pope Leo XIII raised the rank of the feast of these spouses.

Born in Barcelona in 1773 into a very Catholic family; her father was a wealthy senior government official. At 16 she married the wealthy landowner Don Teodoro. At first she had scruples, but her husband reassured her that one can reach as high a holiness at home as in a convent. When Napoleon invaded Spain, he fought bravely in five battles. Joaquina and her children had to flee Barcelona, and suddenly a mysterious lady appeared and led them to the house of a family who received them with great affection. The lady disappeared, but Joaquina always believed it was the Blessed Virgin.

One day a voice told her: “Soon you will be a widow.” She prepared herself for God’s will, and two months later, at 42 and in good health, he died unexpectedly. Joaquina was widowed at 33 with 8 little children. From that day on she put aside the dresses of a rich lady and devoted herself to helping the poor and the sick. People thought she had gone mad, but they soon realized she was becoming a great saint. Four daughters became nuns and the others married, and so she felt free of household responsibilities to become a religious.

At 47 she founded the Community of the Carmelite Sisters of Charity. When she died in 1854, at 61, after a paralysis that left her immobile, she had founded convents, schools and hospitals. Today there are 290 houses around the world with 2,700 sisters and 40,000 girls in their schools.
John belonged to the English nobility and married a woman also of noble birth, a personal friend of Queen Elizabeth of England.
But... in 1570 Pope Saint Pius V decided to take the definitive step to break with the Anglicanism begun by Henry VIII, excommunicating Elizabeth with a bull and denying her right to the throne.

Before dawn, the bull appeared boldly nailed to the door of the Bishop of London... and the first man arrested confessed that John Felton had helped him; he was arrested, and they wanted at all costs to make him confess that he had acted under Spain’s political influence, but three times he heroically affirmed that he had no motive other than a strictly religious one.

On August 8 he was handed over to the executioner; as he walked to the place of execution he recited psalms, and as he was being quartered his daughter heard him say the name of Jesus; his son Thomas, a cleric, died 18 years later, also a martyr for his fidelity to the Church.
He was born in northern England and studied at Oxford, where he earned a doctorate in law and was named the first Regius Professor of Civil Law.

After 1547 he married and was elected a member of parliament. He opposed the Act of Uniformity and the Protestant liturgical reforms of Edward VI. He dared to recite in Parliament this verse from Ecclesiastes: “Woe to the land whose king is a child,” which earned him a few months in the Tower of London.

He emigrated to Louvain and did not return until Mary Tudor took the throne. He was appointed chancellor of the dioceses of London and Oxford. Under Elizabeth I he opposed the “Act of Supremacy” (as Saint Thomas More had), which led to his arrest twice; he managed to escape to Louvain (Belgium) in 1563.

Philip II named him censor of books, and he boarded English ships to inspect the books they carried. But Queen Elizabeth’s spies followed him, kidnapped him, and he was hanged in London on a false charge of treason.
In 1886 Pope Leo XIII confirmed his cult, which is equivalent to his beatification.

Born in Málaga in 1866, he excelled in his medical studies in Granada on a scholarship from King Alfonso XIII and earned his doctorate cum laude in obstetrics and gynecology. He and María married at the Noble Hospital in 1904.

He introduced new sterilization techniques in his clinic and at the Civil Hospital of Málaga, where he practiced for 58 years. The lepers called him “Saint Joseph.” In 1898 he performed one of the first post-mortem cesarean sections. In 1923 he was named director; he left his salary to poor patients and never let anyone go without medicine.

He was president of the College of Physicians and mayor of Málaga for 3 years, but he resigned because it kept him away from patients. He gave his estate for a school for vagrant children and presided over Nocturnal Adoration during the church burnings of 1931.

His selflessness in helping the wounded of the Moroccan War earned him the Grand Cross of Merit. During the Civil War he helped people on both sides. His hardest moment was seeing his pregnant daughter taken hostage and jailed by the Civil Government after the war. In 1932 he was imprisoned, but he was released when the lepers threatened to pour out into the streets. When he died, the people said: “A saint has died.”

He was born in Lebanon and raised his large family in the province of Mendoza, Argentina. Freedom, sincerity and harmony reigned in the family. He gave his children a Christian education by his example and his words. He went to Mass in the mornings before work, sometimes with his older daughters.
The couple used to repeat to each other: “Let not the sun go down on our differences,” and they put it into practice.

Kind and good-natured, he had a great religious sense that showed in his words and conduct. His love for Eucharistic Adoration was evident. He radiated peace and happiness to everyone and was always ready to lend a hand.

Even with the marital problems of those close to him, he knew how to guide them with the wisdom and holiness of his teaching. A few minutes of conversation with him healed depressions where medicine had failed.

He was born in Cheste (Valencia) in 1904 into a farming family. He trained as a teacher and earned a law degree. He was elected president of the Regional Federation of Catholic Students. He joined the Catholic Association of Propagandists (ACdP) and Catholic Action, and was its president in Valencia. He became senior judge of the Labor Courts.

In public life he focused his activity on the most disadvantaged, especially children and workers, working closely with the archbishop in the Housing Trust, in the Bank of Our Lady of the Forsaken and in launching the Catholic Teachers’ Association.

He received the Order of Civil Merit and the Silver Medal of School Welfare. In 1961 he entered the Valencian Academy of Jurisprudence, and the Holy See named him a knight of the Order of Saint Gregory the Great. He died with a reputation for holiness in Valencia on August 6, 1965. Streets and schools were named after him in Valencia and Cheste.

He graduated in law in Padua in 1867 and worked all his life as a professor. In 1878 he married Maria, and their family was a rich experience of tenderness and prayer, where the Word of God was at home.

He worked to ensure Catholics were present in society: he founded and presided over the Catholic Union for Social Studies and the “International Review of Social Sciences and Auxiliary Disciplines.” He developed a sociological theory on the primacy of ethics and the Christian spirit over the harsh laws of economics, reconciling faith and science.

From 1894 he became a leader of the Christian Democratic movement. He defended the economic and social value of religion. In 1908 he published his Treatise on Social Economics. He carried on his profession and family life in fidelity to the Church, esteemed by the popes of his time. He collaborated on Leo XIII’s encyclical Rerum Novarum, which began to set out the Church’s social doctrine. He was beatified in 2012.

Born in 1841, he had a brilliant legal career. In 1867 he moved to Brescia to work as a lawyer for his future father-in-law. He married Emilia and was a devoted father, a responsible educator of his children, a caring husband and an exemplary Christian.

In 1871, when he was appointed mayor of his hometown, he began his political career, promoting social organizations and seeking a greater presence of the Church in the world of work. He founded and edited a magazine and held political offices, working to imbue society with a Christian spirit.
He was president of the “Work of the Congresses” and a city councilor in Brescia, and he founded the Bank of Saint Paul and, in Milan, the Banco Ambrosiano, among others.

In education he defended religious instruction in the classroom, created Catholic university circles, helped found the Leo XIII Union (the seed of the Federation of Catholic University Students) and created an educational magazine.
He died in 1897 at 55 and was beatified by Pope John Paul II.

Josef, an Italian, was a leader of German-speaking Catholic Action youth and had written publicly that Nazism could not be reconciled with the values of Christian ethics. As president of the Saint Vincent de Paul Conference, Josef never stopped visiting the poorest and bringing them material and spiritual help.

He was forcibly enlisted in the SS and made to leave his wife and their son, just a few months old, for training in Prussia. At the end he was to take this oath: “I swear to you, Adolf Hitler, loyalty and bravery; I solemnly promise you and the superiors you appoint obedience unto death, so help me God.” In 1944 Josef refused because “his faith and his conscience do not allow it.”

Hildegard shared his stance; he wrote to her from prison: “You would not be my wife if you expected anything different from me.” Convicted of treason and sent to the Dachau concentration camp, he was found dead of dysentery on the train on February 24, 1945. He held a rosary and a Gospel book in his hands. His liturgical memorial was set on October 3, the day he chose to obey Christ and not Hitler.
Born in Córdoba in 1823 into a Christian home. By 9 she had lost both parents. At 17, during a spiritual retreat, her vocation was born, but she did not want to be a contemplative.

In 1852 she married Colonel Zavalía, a widower with 2 children. It took 8 years for her to become pregnant, and her daughter was stillborn; she devoted herself to being a true mother to the children. She always accompanied her husband, spiritually and with unconditional dedication. In 1861, through her cousin President Derqui, she sought the return of the Jesuits to Córdoba.

Zavalía, having finished his public service, devoted himself to a ranch and died in 1865. That year, before the Blessed Sacrament, she glimpsed her golden dream: “to build a House of Spiritual Exercises and form a community of women at its service, under the Ignatian Rule.” At 49, after years of struggle, she managed to found the congregation (the first in Argentina): the Handmaids of the Heart of Jesus. From then on she would be Mother Catalina de María.

In 1877, crossing the mountains by mule, she settled in Villa del Tránsito as a friend and mission partner of the Cura Brochero. From 1880 she opened 12 houses across the country. She died in 1896, and today her sisters number more than 200, with schools throughout Argentina and other countries. In 2017 the miracle for her beatification was approved.
Józef and Wiktoria were deeply religious and active members of their parish in a village near Kraków.
In 1942, despite the danger, they agreed to hide two Jewish families in their home, who willingly worked on the farm in return for shelter.

In March 1944, acting on a denunciation, the Nazi police burst in at dawn. The first to be executed were the 8 Jews. Then came the couple, and finally each of their 6 children. Later, when the bodies were exhumed, it was discovered that Wiktoria was close to giving birth.

In 2017 their process was separated from that of the other Polish martyrs. In 2022 Pope Francis declared the whole family venerable, and on September 10, 2023, he made them the first to be beatified as an entire family. The Ulmas’ beatification is unique in the Church, also because their unborn child is the first unborn Blessed, having received a “baptism of blood.”

Born in 1552, three years after the Jesuit missionary Saint Francis Xavier arrived in Japan, Takayama was baptized at 12 after his father’s conversion. As feudal lords, they used their power to protect the Catholic missionaries.

In 1587, when he was 35, the chancellor expelled the missionaries and launched a harsh campaign forcing Japanese Catholics to abandon their faith. Although many obeyed, Justo and his family chose to leave their lands and live in poverty rather than renounce their religion. He focused on preaching the Gospel among Buddhists and Shintoists.

After 20 years under the protection of other nobles, in 1614 the “evil religion” of Christianity was finally banned in Japan. He was forced into exile in Manila, Philippines, with his wife, daughter and grandchildren and 300 other Catholics.

Gravely ill from the effects of his persecution, he died 40 days later, in February 1615, with a reputation for holiness. Beatified in 2017, he has been called “the Japanese Thomas More.” At the port of Nagasaki he had exclaimed to the laypeople going into exile with him: “God says that whoever takes up the sword will perish by it. Return to Japan as envoys of peace.” (Justo Takayama)
He learned the trade of pyrotechnics from his parents and was considered one of the best in the region, always standing out for his moral integrity in his profession.

In his marriage to Patrocinio he authentically lived his lay vocation as a father and Catholic citizen. A man of deep faith, he received Communion daily, prayed the rosary as a family and was devoted to the Sacred Heart and the Virgin.
He belonged to Catholic Action, the Franciscan Tertiaries and Nocturnal Adoration. He practiced charity by helping the poor in their needs.

Because of his intense apostolic activity, the enemies of the Church regarded him as a “fervent Catholic,” and for that he was arrested and executed. On March 11, 2001, Pope John Paul II beatified him as one of the 233 martyrs of the religious persecution in Spain.
Zapotec natives of the Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, they were born in 1660 and belonged to the Vicariate of San Francisco Cajonos, run by the Dominican fathers.

We know they were people of integrity in their personal, married and family lives, as well as in fulfilling their civic duties, holding various civil offices such as topil, judge of communal labor, mayordomo, councilman, president, trustee and mayor.
Both were baptized and catechized, also serving as acolyte, junior and senior sacristan, and topilillo.

Finally they held the civil and Church office of Fiscal and discovered that a large group of townspeople were practicing an ancestral cult. They alerted the Dominican fathers and caught those responsible, but the town rioted and seized these Fiscales, who were flogged and executed for refusing to renounce their faith: “Once we have professed baptism, we will always continue to follow the true religion.”
Born to a patrician family of Siena, he soon became a rich wool merchant, building connections that led him to become a government magistrate.
He had a happy marriage with 2 children, but went through bouts of anger followed by periods of mortification and self-loathing.

At 50, thanks to his wife, he read the life of the hermit Saint Mary of Egypt and entered a deep spiritual crisis. He wound up his businesses, persuaded his wife to embrace austere poverty and to make the Gospel “visible,” working as a dishwasher where he himself had been a magistrate.
After his son died and with his daughter in a convent, he gave his fortune to support his wife, a hospital and two convents, and embraced complete poverty.

Wealthy young men disillusioned with their way of life began to follow him in the call to give everything to the poor and strip off their clothes in public, and they were banished by the elite. But they obtained papal approval as a lay order of consecrated men, days before John died.

Born in Santiago de Compostela. While studying medicine he received the National Prize for academic record. He was the 5th generation of doctors, and a son and two grandchildren have followed him. He won the Chair of Anatomy at the University of Salamanca and in 1927 became head of the La Fe Provincial Hospital in Valencia. Until his retirement in 1971 he was professor, dean and rector at the Faculty of Medicine. He was also president of the Royal Academy of Medicine of Valencia. He is considered the father of Spanish neuropsychiatry for his vast academic work.
He promoted the Catholic Association of Propagandists in Valencia and for decades led Diocesan Caritas and Catholic Action. As a politician, he was president of the Provincial Council of A Coruña.

Jón Ögmundsson was born in southern Iceland into a powerful family. As a young man he entered the seminary and, as a deacon, traveled to Rome to complete his studies. He was ordained a priest and, since celibacy was not the rule for the Icelandic clergy in his time, he married twice (having been widowed).
A new diocese was created in northern Iceland, where in 1106 John was elected bishop, with a papal dispensation because he was married.

He built the cathedral and a cathedral school that soon became a cultural center for all of Iceland. He founded the first monastery on the island and played an important role in strengthening the Christian faith among Icelanders, banning witchcraft and pagan beliefs. To erase the Norse pagan heritage, John changed the names of some days of the week.

He died after a long illness on April 23, 1121. His canonization is unusual in that it was carried out by the Icelandic parliament in 1200. The Holy See has not officially recognized it but accepts his veneration.
Around 1140 Joan was born in the town of Aza into a noble family linked to the house of Castile, inheriting the lordship of Caleruega on marrying the nobleman Don Félix Ruiz.
They were known as a family compassionate toward the poor: every day the Guzmán Tower opened its doors to give relief and affection to the poor, travelers and pilgrims.

Félix and Joan’s children were raised as Christians, in their mother’s virtues and the exemplary life of the home, and so their vocations were born: the great Saint Dominic, who founded the Order of Preachers (the “Dominicans”), Venerable Anthony, a priest who devoted himself to pilgrims and the sick, and Blessed Father Mannes, a Cistercian who later became a Dominican.
Jeanne was born in Bordeaux in 1556 into a society family and, a woman ahead of her time, received a careful education.
In 1573 she married Gaston, and they lived many years of happy marriage, though 3 children died young. Widowed at 41, she managed her lands and people with tenderness and clear judgment.

She decided to enter a contemplative monastery: the Feuillantines. The rigors of this reformed Cistercian rule damaged her health and forced her to give up that life. In crisis, she had a profound experience of God and discerned a new future: educating the women of her time.
The plague struck Bordeaux, and she risked her life to care for the sick. There she met those who would be her first companions.
She felt called to found an order: the Company of Mary was approved by Pope Paul V in 1607. The first school opened in Bordeaux, and many more would follow.
She died in 1640, having founded 30 houses, and over the centuries the Company of Mary spread throughout the world.
Born into a fervent Catholic family of the French aristocracy, she received a very thorough education and stood out for her piety from childhood.

In 1593 she married Christophe II, Baron de Chantal, forming a harmonious family with Catholic ideals. When she was widowed, her father-in-law demanded that she move to his castle, and there he humiliated her constantly for 7 years, but she showed only gratitude and created an atmosphere of family joy.
In 1604 in Dijon she met Francis de Sales, Bishop of Geneva. Impressed by her piety, he became her spiritual director, always insisting that she put her duties as mother and educator first.
In 1610, with several of her children grown, she founded with Francis the Order of the Visitation of Our Lady and became its first superior.
After Francis died, Saint Vincent de Paul became her spiritual director. In her last years, between 1635 and 1636, she managed to visit all of her... 60 convents!
He discovered the Marian Congregation of the Immaculate and joined as a soldier of Mary. In 1920 he married his first love, Glorita, in Madrid, and they had 9 children.

In Barcelona the Sindicato Único and the Sindicato Libre were competing, with opposite political leanings. Julio tried to set up a third, apolitical union based on the Church’s social doctrine. It reached 20,000 members, but internal disputes frustrated his project, and the very people who had proposed it dismissed him.
He accepted the post of Court Clerk of Esplugas. His work at the court could have made him rich had he listened to shameful offers, but he rejected them, seeing his role as a means of apostolate.

On September 11 militiamen came in and took him away on charges of being a fascist. He said goodbye to his wife and children: “pray for Daddy, he is going to need it.” His body was found only months later.

Born in Quito in 1894. He presided over the Catholic Workers’ Center and wrote for El Republicano, El Porvenir and La Corona de María. He joined the Congregation of Knights of the Immaculate. In 1926 he wrote a series of biographies of illustrious nineteenth-century Catholics.
In 1919 he married Ángela, grandniece of former president Gabriel García Moreno.

From 1915 he was a member of the Conservative Party and became an activist and leader. In 1917 he earned a Doctorate in Jurisprudence. He rose to head Ecuador’s diplomacy, and in 1942, as foreign minister, he led the delegation that signed the Rio de Janeiro Protocol.
In 1946 he founded the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador with Fr. Aurelio Espinosa Pólit, where he served for 25 years as dean and law professor.

A scholar of social and political science, in 1951 he was elected President of the Institute of Hispanic Culture of Quito. He published his finest work, “The Church, Shaper of the Nation,” for which the Council of Quito awarded him the Tobar Prize in 1956. In 1965 he was elected Director of the Ecuadorian Academy of Language. He died in 1981.
Born in 1922, the son of a village chief in Tanganyika (a British colony). At 26 he was the first local selected for a master’s degree in history and economics in Edinburgh.

He returned as a teacher and in 1953 married Maria. He entered politics and soon became the first president of the independent nation in 1962, which united with Zanzibar as the Republic of Tanzania. As president he refused privileges and enjoyed a simple life, attending Holy Mass wherever he was.

He created a plan to recover local traditions of communal ways of working, producing and relating to the land. He was one of the main thinkers and founders of the Organization of African Unity (OAU). After nearly 30 years he stepped down voluntarily and pursued an international career as an African thinker and leader, facilitating UN peace negotiations in Burundi.

When he retired he returned to his small village to live a simple life, attending daily Mass. He died of leukemia in 1999. He was a model of a leader devoted to the development of the people he was called to lead.

Emilia was born in 1884 in Kraków into a family of craftsmen with 9 children. Her mother died when she was only 13. Karol was born in 1879 in Lipnik into a family of tailors and lost his mother at 2. In 1900 he was called up for military service in Wadowice. He finished with the rank of sergeant and could have gone home, but he stayed on as a professional non-commissioned officer. They married in 1906 in Kraków.

Their second child died right after birth, and a well-known obstetrician, Dr. Moskała, said her third pregnancy was high-risk with no chance of a live, healthy baby. She bravely went ahead, knowing these might be the last months of her life, and spent most of them in bed. In the end she survived the birth, and little Karol was born healthy: the future Pope Saint John Paul II.

Emilia died in 1929, having received the last sacraments in her husband’s presence. From then on he cared for the children, moving to Kraków in 1938. He died in 1941 at 63 and is buried next to his wife.

Born in Poland, during the Second World War he served in medical units and married Maria Rochalski. In Warsaw in 1941 the Nazis arrested him in a street roundup, and he miraculously escaped before being sent to Auschwitz.

In 1951, under the communists, he became Director of the District Hospital. He was known for his social concern, helping the poor beyond the call of duty and fighting for their lives in desperate cases. Faced with his firm opposition, the local party authorities withdrew the decision to remove the crosses and the nuns from the hospital, granting him a rare “exception” of religious freedom.

He was a model of medical self-sacrifice, above all for his spiritual values, impeccable character, high medical ethics and great heart. Before every operation he prayed “We fly to thy protection.” True to his principles, at a time when abortion was permitted, he talked women out of the decision and even offered to adopt an unwanted child or support its upbringing financially. He died in 1958.

His piety, as fervent as it was balanced, showed in his zeal for the faith, his scrupulous fulfillment of his religious duties, his strict morals and the austerity of his life; he had stripped himself of all personal ambition and accepted the dignity placed on his shoulders only out of a sense of duty.
Ladislaus restored the Christian laws issued by King Saint Stephen, reformed customs, setting an example of virtue himself, and spread the Christian faith into Croatia and Bosnia.
With Adelaide he had a son and 3 daughters; one, a Byzantine empress, is venerated by the Orthodox as Saint Piroska (or Saint Irene).
He died in 1095 on his way to take part in the First Crusade; the whole nation mourned for three years and remembered him as a saint.

He was born on October 28, 1870, in Dunakiliti (Hungary) into a family of the old Hungarian nobility. In 1896 he graduated in medicine from the University of Vienna. In 1898 he married Countess Maria Theresa, a deeply religious woman, and they were very happy with... 13 children! Every day the family attended Mass and prayed the rosary.

In 1902 he founded a hospital in Kittsee, which during the First World War was expanded to 120 beds for wounded soldiers. On his uncle’s death in 1915 he inherited a castle and the title of “prince.” He set up a hospital there. He was a famous eye doctor in his country and beyond.

He treated many poor people and gave them medicine for free; as “payment” he asked them to pray an Our Father for him. He often even gave them money for their needs. Before operations he invoked God’s blessing together with the patient. He was convinced that as a doctor he only directed the operation, since healing was the Lord’s gift; he felt himself an instrument in His hands. He gave patients holy cards and the booklet Open Your Eyes and See, to help them in their religious life. Many patients already considered him a saint. He died in 1931 after a long illness.

He was born Neelakanda Pillai in 1712 in Tamil Nadu, India. His family was of high Hindu caste. He chose a military career and became a minister of the kingdom of Travancore, as an official of the royal palace.
Through a Dutch Catholic prisoner he came to know Catholicism in 1741, and the prisoner put him in touch with Giovanni Battista Buttari, a Jesuit who would become his friend and spiritual adviser.
Four years later he decided to become a Christian and was baptized, changing his birth name to Lazarus. His wife also converted and took the name Teresa in Tamil.

Lazarus sought and fought for equality among people, regardless of caste or origin, which earned him many enemies. In 1749 he was arrested and accused of treason. He never abandoned his faith, and on January 14, 1752, he was shot. He was beatified in 2012, with more than 100,000 Catholics in attendance.
On May 15, 2022, Pope Francis declared him India’s first lay saint.
In Déols (France), in the region of Bourges, Leocadius was a still-pagan Governor and senator of the Gauls.
There he welcomed the first missionaries of the Christian faith among the Bituriges and made his house the first church, sheltering these preachers.
He later died a martyr with his son Ludre, a newly baptized child.
Lucio León was born in 1932 in the Diocese of San Cristóbal (Venezuela).
He was a hard worker who sold goods at the San Carlos market in the city and later became a bricklayer.

His religious life was that of ordinary people: love for the Eucharist and Confession, and faithfulness to praying the rosary every day. He carried out his apostolate with the Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament.
One of his sons became a priest. Lucio died in 2010, and his beatification process is being opened.
Born in 1075, he was pious from childhood. As a teenager he began to discipline himself, to pray and meditate assiduously, and to study Scripture and theology.

His father died, and at 21 he took the reins of government. In an Austria steeped in paganism, superstition and indifference to the faith, he undertook a work of evangelization and culture. He changed laws in the light of Roman Law and Christian mercy. He lowered taxes, endowed churches so they would teach children, fought impunity and promoted the building of infrastructure.
When the Black Death ravaged the region, he organized charity for the sick and orphans so well that he was called the “father of the poor.”

In 1106 he married the widow Agnes, daughter of Henry IV. They lived an intense piety, praying with the castle’s priests and acting with charity. Among their 11 surviving children were his successor Leopold IV and 2 eminent bishops.

After a good reign full of piety, faith and works of charity, he was wounded while hunting and went to heaven in great peace on November 15, 1136. His tomb soon became a source of many miracles, and in 1663 he was named patron of Austria together with Saint Coloman.

Born in Manila to a Chinese father and a Filipino mother. He was educated by the Dominicans, served as an altar boy and later as a sacristan. He was a member of the Confraternity of the Rosary and earned his family’s bread as a clerk.
Implicated in a crime, he joined Fr. González to save himself.

In 1636 the Dominicans of Manila organized an expedition to help the Christians of Japan. An imperial edict of 1614 had ordered: “Let these Christians be exterminated without delay in every region of Japan, let them have no place to set their feet. If anyone dares to disobey this order, let him be punished with death.”

On the island of Okinawa they were arrested and jailed for over a year before being sentenced by the court of Nagasaki. Lorenzo declared himself ready to give his life for Christ, and he was then hung by his feet. Pope John Paul II beatified this group of martyrs in 1981 in Manila.

He was born in 1877 in northern Ivory Coast and had an ordinary childhood until his village was destroyed by the Dyula tribe. The inhabitants scattered, and many, like his mother, were sold as slaves. He was saved and met the missionary Fr. Bedel.

He was baptized at Christmas 1898 with the name Louis. He went to work for the nuns in Dabou, where he met his future wife Valérie, six years younger, who as a teenager had been the slave of a rich merchant and suffered mistreatment. She fled under the protection of a European lady and asked the nuns to take her in.

They married in 1903 and, with Fr. Bedel, promoted the building of the church of Korhogo in 1904, where she was godmother to the first baptized. They led that small community and worked as catechists in a settlement of freed slaves. Louis became the community’s delegate to the social leaders and the Muslims. In 1925 Pope Pius XI awarded him the “Bene Merenti” medal.
They lost their children as adults, one of them already a priest. The spouses died in 1948/49, 3 months apart. Because of their reputation for holiness, their cause was opened in 1994.

Lucia went to school up to third grade; from a young age she showed great love for the needy, comforting the sick in the hospital and ignoring relatives who feared she would catch tuberculosis. In 1912 she married the fruit merchant Carlo, who was later badly wounded in the First World War.

Toward the end of the Second World War, in 1943, after hard battles at Salerno, Lucia was moved to see children kicking a soldier’s skull. She dreamed of 8 soldiers and their crosses, begging her to return them to their mothers.
