So she obtained permission and the help of 2 gravediggers, and went among mines and grenades wherever there were bodies, to place them in coffins she ordered.

When her work became known in Germany, many mothers wrote to beg her to find their sons’ remains. One told her she had lost 4. In the end she was honored with the Orders of Merit of Germany and Italy: Mamma Lucia had recovered some 700 bodies.
Lucy lived in Hebei province (China) when the violent Boxer uprising began, out of hatred for every foreign faith.
It was the year 1900 and she was 31 when the militiamen entered the village and set the church on fire, and the gang leader gave the Christians the choice of apostasy or death.

Lucy was at the school with her two children and other Christians; since they would not deny their faith, the Boxers separated the mothers from the children and took them to a room with two signs: one offered “Liberation,” with goods and tempting delicacies, in exchange for renouncing their faith; the other said “Death.”
Several gave in, but after a night of prayer Lucy chose true “liberation” and gave herself up with a smile to be beheaded together with her children.
Lucien was born in 1908 in Vohipeno. In 1928 he earned his teaching diploma and became a parish teacher. He spoke French, Latin, English, German and Chinese.

In 1930 he married Suzanne. He became a Franciscan tertiary in 1944. He was also a musician and singer. He was an extraordinary model of Christian and social life, a father of incredible faith. He always went about smiling, with a rosary in his hands. He never lost his patience and seemed immune to anger.

On Palm Sunday 1947 the churches were burned, beginning a persecution of Christians. King Tsimihono wanted to seize the famous teacher and control him with the threat of massacring his family. Lucien sent them away into his brother’s care and was handed over by relatives under threat of death. The king condemned him, and he was beheaded beside a river at 39. Before dying he forgave his executioners, some of whom he had taught. He prophesied the king’s conversion, which came true 17 years later.
Ludmila was born around 860 and at 14 married Prince Bořivoj of Bohemia. They settled north of Prague, and both were baptized by Saint Methodius, the apostle of the Slavic peoples.

She was pious and measured, generous in almsgiving and persevering in prayer. She helped the poor, fed the hungry and clothed strangers. The priests she cared for so selflessly also bear witness to this.
Ludmila played a notable role in spreading Christianity in the Czech-Slovak region. Two of her sons continued her leadership and anchored the country in the Christian world.

Bořivoj died before 40. Ludmila gave her possessions to the poor, which set off a clash with her pagan daughter-in-law Drahomíra, who later had her murdered while she was protecting her grandson. She was 61. It was said that her tomb gave off a pleasant scent and that miracles occurred there. John Paul II proclaimed her patroness of Eastern Europe.

From a well-off family with a solid Christian formation, at 19 he earned his law degree in Santiago de Compostela and the following year was teaching there; he practiced law and defended the poor free of charge.
At 43 he married Adelaida, a widow with one son, and they later had 3 more. He loved his wife deeply and wrote about the quality of the love he had for the women close to him in his life.

A humanitarian activist, he founded a commission of 300 lawyers to defend political and religious prisoners, and he personally mediated in wars: some 20,000 prisoners owed him their freedom and even their lives.

In 1877 he brought Nocturnal Adoration from France to Spain, a lay prayer group that keeps vigil through the night praying to Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament. He was a theologian, writer, journalist and deputy for the Carlist party, which gathered most Catholics.

She was born in Rome in 1473 and was raised and educated by her grandmother and later her aunts. She was given in marriage to Giacomo, with whom she had three daughters. Their union was happy, but she was widowed young, at 32.
From then on she devoted herself entirely to a life of piety: she became a Franciscan tertiary and divided her time between caring for the poor and the sick and a life of prayer and penance.

She stood out for her generosity, joined to the desire to stay hidden and not seek human praise. This open-handedness, which led her to feed everyone, brought serious family conflicts, since she spent her fortune until she was left poor; the family granted her a pension, which she divided between her few needs and the care of the poor.

In her last years God rewarded her with a foretaste of His peace and let her enjoy extraordinary ecstasies. She died in 1533, venerated by her fellow citizens, and her tomb became a place of devotion and miracles.
Her cult was confirmed in 1671 by Clement X, and a tomb was built in the church of San Francesco a Ripa with a statue by Bernini showing her in ecstasy. Her relics are still there.

Born in 1591 into a noble family, she lost her mother and received an extraordinary education with the Dominican Sisters; she was extremely pious and exemplary. Her father died, and since she was not admitted as a religious because of her fragile health, she married Monsieur Le Gras. She was a model Christian wife. With her kindness and gentleness she softened her husband’s difficult character, and they shared everything in an exemplary way, even prayer.

Widowed at 34, she decided to give herself entirely to God and to good works. Her director was Francis de Sales, who sent her to Vincent de Paul. He had already begun his works of mercy. Louise would give them a maternal and feminine touch. She traveled through the villages, revived the confraternities, visited the sick, and everything was renewed.

Many young women joined Louise to care for so many in need. After a period of novitiate they took their vows. They spread to Flanders and Poland, and later throughout the world. War zones, poorhouses and institutions for the mentally ill: there was no ailment they had no remedy for. In early 1655 the Congregation of the Daughters of Charity was established, and it remains faithful to its charism.
Louise’s activity was superhuman. Exhausted, she gave up her life on March 15, 1660.

Daughter of Amadeus IX, Duke of Savoy, also beatified, and granddaughter of Charles VII of France, from an early age she showed extraordinary spiritual qualities. At 18 she married Hugh of Chalon, lord of Nozeroy, a man as good as he was rich and powerful.

In complete agreement, they established a fully Christian life in their home, with a high standard of moral and material life for all who lived on their lands and depended on them in any way. In contrast with the palaces of the nobility, the house of Chalon looked like a monastery. Louise kept a box for the poor, into which everyone who lived in or visited her house was obliged to put money.
After nine years of married happiness her husband died, and since there were no children, Louise sought admission to the convent of the Poor Clares in the town of Orbe, founded by Hugh’s mother.
Luisa was born in Moduça, Mozambique, in 1943. At 17 she married Adolfo, and in 1977 they took together the first catechist training course of the Mangonha Mission.

Luisa was humble, simple and full of apostolic zeal. She taught good habits and the faith. She was a catechist devoted to laypeople and families in her parish community of Kofi. Strong in prayer, she faithfully stood by her community in its times of greatest suffering.

She cared especially for the poor and the sick, and the power of her prayer seemed to grant her the grace of healing. For a sick child in danger of death she prayed and had a vision that he “belonged to the Lord.” He was saved and later entered religious life.

Before she left for a catechist training course, the community held a farewell gathering. Luisa told them she had dreamed she would not come home. She said she still felt urged to go and asked everyone to pray. On the night of the attack on the Guiúa Catechetical Center, March 22, 1992, she was kidnapped and killed with a bayonet, together with a son and a grandson.

At 30 Lucchese, a merchant, got rid of the riches he had accumulated and chose charity. His wife doubted his sanity but then followed him. Having lost their young children, they devoted themselves to God and neighbor.

He had known Saint Francis since childhood through business with Francis’s father. Francis passed through the countryside and told them: “You are married and will have to go on living together. I will give you an ascetic Rule of life to practice your vows.” He dressed them in the ash-colored tunic and girded them with the knotted cord. The first Rule of the Secular Franciscan Order was approved in 1223 by Pope Honorius III.

In 1227 they sold their house and gave the proceeds to the hospital; they kept only a humble place near a small field that Lucchese farmed with his own hands, using the produce to feed the poor. He often took in the sick; when a young man saw him, he told him: “I am carrying the suffering Christ.”

On April 28, 1260, Lucchese and Buonadonna were called home together, hours apart. There were many miracles, and every year on that day in Poggibonsi (Siena) there is a popular feast with a procession. In 1274 Gregory X authorized their cult.

Her family is believed to have been converted to Christianity by the great Saint Gregory the Wonderworker, apostle of Neocaesarea. Macrina married Basil, a devout Christian, very young. They were devout and charitable to the poor.

Under the emperor Diocletian they fled to the hills of Pontus by the Black Sea, where they lived in absolute poverty after all their property was confiscated. Seven years later they returned home, where they were received with joy and regarded as confessors of the faith.

Their son Basil “the Theologian,” later a bishop, was born during the persecution, and Macrina was his example of steadfast faith. He married Emmelia and they had 10 children, in whose formation Macrina had a notable influence.
Their grandchildren were Saint Macrina the Younger, Saint Basil the Great, Saint Gregory of Nyssa and Saint Peter of Sebaste.
Saint Macrina outlived her husband and died in the year 340.
Maisam was born in 1934 in Houaphanh province, Laos. He and many men and women of his ethnic group, the Khmu, were converted by missionaries around 1959.

After the communist guerrilla attack in 1960 he was recruited into the Royal Lao Army with the rank of captain, but as a man of peace he left as soon as he could. He married, and he and his wife were baptized in the village where they had found refuge.

Because of his education he was soon chosen as head of the small local Christian community. In the absence of the missionary and the village’s regular catechist, he led the prayer meetings and taught the children.

In 1970 Maisam was helping the catechist Blessed Luke Sy on his monthly retreat, but on March 7 they were ambushed. He was beatified in 2016 together with 16 priests, diocesan and missionary, and laypeople killed in Laos and Vietnam between 1954 and 1970, led by Fr. Joseph Thao Tiên.
Manuel was born in 1904; he was the pharmacist of the town of Xàtiva and a member of Catholic Action. Adela was a Lady-in-Waiting of the Virgin of La Seo (the local patroness).

They married in 1924, after making a few things clear with great affection but also with complete clarity and frankness: “Manolo, if you can’t share going to Mass and the rosary with me, I’ll have to leave you”... “Adela, with you always,” said the groom.
Besides their 9 children, they took two orphaned nephews into their home.

In addition to Catholic Action, both took part in Nocturnal Adoration, the Forty Hours, Caritas and the Saint Vincent de Paul Conferences. They quietly helped the needy of the city and nearby towns with medicines in the postwar years, when there was no Social Security coverage.
Adela died in 1988, and the diocese opened the couple’s cause for beatification in 2009.

A Christian through and through, a faithful husband, a loving father to his children, a conscientious worker, a layman committed to the apostolate of his parish, with an intense spiritual life nourished by the Eucharist.

He was a member of the Catholic Action of Mexican Youth and president of the National League for the Defense of Religious Freedom, an association that sought by peaceful means the repeal of the impious laws.

On August 15, 1926, at the height of the Masonic government’s restrictions on the free practice of the faith, he mobilized to demand his parish priest’s release. The troops showed up and began beating him. He was taken out of the city with the priest, and when he heard the priest ask that his life be spared for the sake of his family, full of courage and faith he told him: “Father, I die, but God does not die. He will take care of my wife and my children.” Then he stood tall and exclaimed: “Long live Christ the King and the Virgin of Guadalupe!” And the witness of his life was signed with his blood as a Cristero martyr.

Manuel Perrín was born in 1925 in Saldungaray, Buenos Aires. He had been an engineer in the Navy, with several expeditions to Antarctica. While they were dating, she did everything to bring him closer to the faith, which he finally embraced, with periods of uncertainty.

He came to know the spirituality of the Focolare Movement in 1967 and was one of its first members in Punta Alta. His house became the center of the work in the region. He was a leader of the volunteers’ branch, made the movement known to others and was a great formator. He stood by every family, especially those in material or spiritual hardship. He was in charge of dialogue with other religions and with people of good will.

Strong-willed and quick to decide, but also great fun, he felt called to be an apostle of unity and to live like the first Christians, transforming his life and that of his brothers and sisters. He did not consider himself worthy enough, but he kept saying: “We have to be locomotives, not caboose cars!”
He died on November 22, 2000. His daughter Cecilia is also a Servant of God.

Manuel was born in 1905 in Suchitoto, El Salvador; he married Eleuteria Antonia Guillén, with whom he had 10 children. He was transferred for work to Aguilares, where he worked in the buying and selling of seed and livestock.
He was very active in parish life, especially in the apostolate. With Father Rutilio Grande he began the evangelization of the local parish.

The priest was aware of the risks of his apostolate, since he had received death threats a few days earlier; even so, he kept bearing witness to the faith, without compromising with power and avoiding flashy or provocative tones.
The laypeople knew the situation but stayed by his side. On March 12, 1977, in an ambush, Manuel was struck by several bullets and died at 72.
In 2020 Pope Francis authorized the promulgation of the decree of martyrdom of Father Grande and his 2 lay companions: Manuel Solórzano and Nelson Rutilio Lemus.

The Swiss Anna Maria and the Italian Marcello, both musicians, first met at the Messina Conservatory; they met again in the poor neighborhoods of Catania serving those in need, and this time they understood they were made for each other, except that... he was Catholic and she a Waldensian Protestant; even so, study, prayer and special grace opened her eyes, and Anna Maria fell in love with the Eucharist.
They married in 1968, with God present at the reception too: 30 people with disabilities were served by the couple in her wedding dress and his tailcoat.

Later, during concert intermissions, Marcello would cover his suit and slip out to care for sick people who lived near the theater. They enlarged their house to shelter people with disabilities and homeless drug addicts.
They met Fr. Antonio Fallico and Miss Dina and founded the “Church-World Mission,” becoming the first leaders of its married couples’ branch.
Margaret was 16 when they married, and some time later, in 1553, Bartholomew was elected mayor of Dublin.
Living a comfortable life with several servants, she organized classes at home for Catholic children and young people, who began coming from all over the country.
Their eldest son took up a political career, adopting the “new Anglican religion,” which set him against his mother; in her grief she never lost hope of converting him.

As a widow she sheltered in her home several priests persecuted by Queen Elizabeth, for which her son denounced her. Jailed and tortured, she died at 70 after 3 years in a cold, dark dungeon, without giving in and renouncing her faith.
Margaret was born in 1473 in England. Henry VII arranged her marriage to Sir Richard, a knight who had rendered the king great services in military campaigns.

By 1505 Margaret was a widow, and Henry VIII, who considered her the holiest woman in England, restored her brother’s estates to her; he made her Countess of Salisbury and governess of the heiress Mary Tudor. But when she later openly disapproved of his marriage to Anne Boleyn, she lost the king’s favor and her place at court. Her fourth son, Cardinal Reginald Pole, reversed Henry’s religious reform together with Mary Tudor. The king was so enraged that he wanted to eliminate Margaret’s whole family, also because of their claims to the throne, a permanent danger to the royal family.

When a certain Sir Neville took up arms in the north, the king had her interrogated to implicate her in the conspiracy; despite her skillful defense, Margaret was nonetheless imprisoned in the Tower of London. Since there was no evidence to convict her in a lawful trial, the king had Parliament declare her guilty of high treason.
On May 28, 1541, Margaret was beheaded at 70. She refused to kneel and lay down her head because she did not consider herself guilty of any such treason.

Margaret was the granddaughter of King René of Sicily. She married René, Duke of Alençon, in Lorraine. Her life was not easy, since the duchy of Alençon was taking part in the Hundred Years’ War and her husband had to devote himself to those affairs.

René died in 1492, and she was left a widow at 32 with young children. She looked after the duchy for 22 years, until her children were grown, after which she divided her inheritance into thirds: for the poor, for the Church and for her own support.

She turned the castle of Alençon into a kind of convent where life followed the rule of Saint Clare, and she devoted herself to dressing the sores of the sick in a dispensary she opened in Mortagne. She led her religious life with such self-denial and sacrifice that the bishop himself told her to give up excessive penance.

Finally she entered the monastery founded under her patronage in Argentan, wishing to share the life of the daughters of Saint Clare. After 2 years of austere Franciscan life she fell ill and died in 1521 at 58 as a Poor Clare.

The noble blood of Europe’s leading royal houses ran in Margaret’s veins: her father was Amadeus of Savoy and her mother was the sister of Clement VII, who claimed to be Pope in Avignon during the “Great Schism.”

In 1403 she married Theodore Palaiologos, Marquis of Montferrat, a widower with 3 children, a brave warrior and a good Christian. They had no children, but Margaret cared for her stepchildren with true devotion, the same she showed to all the people of the marquisate, above all during the plague and famine in Genoa.

The marquis died in 1418, and she withdrew to live on her estates in Piedmont, vowing to remain a widow and to devote herself to good works. Since she had met Saint Vincent Ferrer in her youth, she later took the habit of the Dominican Third Order and with other ladies formed a small community in Alba.

Her secluded life of prayer, study and works of charity lasted 25 years. She had many ecstasies and worked many miracles. In a vision Christ offered her three arrows with inscriptions: Illness, Slander and Persecution. Margaret suffered all three. She died in 1464, comforted by a vision of Saint Catherine of Siena, which other sisters also witnessed. Her cult was confirmed in 1669.
Her parents, humble farmers, gave her a Christian upbringing.

At 15, while she was tending a flock, Jesus appeared to her as a poor pilgrim asking for food, and Margaret offered him the only bread she had in her bag; when she got home, her mother was astonished to find the bag so full of bread that it supplied the needs of the family and the neighbors.

So as not to go against her parents’ wishes, Margaret agreed to marry a young man of the town and had a daughter, whom she raised on Christian principles. When she was widowed, she decided to devote her life to serving the poor, to prayer and to penance.

To recall the Passion of Christ she imposed penances on herself and walked barefoot through the streets (hence the name “Margaret the Barefooted”). She bore a long and painful illness with great faith and resignation.

Margaret was born in 1788 in Asti to peasant parents of Christian sentiment. From an early age she was a hard worker with a great love of prayer, and her duties gave her no chance to study. In 1812 she married Francesco Bosco, a widower with a son and a sick mother. In 1817 he died of pneumonia.

At 29 Margaret was left managing the family at a time of great famine, while also caring for her mother-in-law. A woman of great faith, God was always in her thoughts and on her lips. An intelligent educator, she knew how to combine gentleness and firmness, raising her children with selfless, patient and demanding love.
Hearing 9-year-old Johnny’s dream, she told him: “Who knows, maybe you’ll become a priest.” When he was ordained, her words sank into Don Bosco’s heart for life.

When Don Bosco fell gravely ill in 1846, she went to help him and discovered what he was doing for abandoned boys. Her presence turned the work into a family. For 10 years their lives were one: she became the maternal gene of the Salesian system. She died in Turin at 68, and many boys accompanied her and wept for her as for a mother. Generations of Salesians would call her “Mamma Margherita.”

Marguerite was born in 1737 and at 20 married Jean, from the village of Agizoux. Their son Augustin was ordained a priest and exiled to Switzerland, since in Haute-Loire 50% of the martyrs of the Revolution were clergy, compared with 10% in the rest of France. In 1794 he returned and hid at his parents’ house, said Mass and thought he was safe, but they were soon denounced as suspects.

The National Guard surrounded the house to arrest him, and he had time to hide, but they saw the bed was still warm. Because they sensed the priest’s presence, his mother, then in her sixties, and 2 sisters were later arrested.

On hearing her sentence before the Criminal Court, she told the judges: “A dog may feed her pups, and you kill a mother for taking in her son!” Three hours later the patriots were amusing themselves watching her head being cut off.

Fr. Augustin became superior of the Major Seminary and a canon of the cathedral of Le Puy. It is said that on that day in 1794 a sister dressed him in women’s clothes and that, as the cart taking his mother to the scaffold passed by, he blessed her.

Born in 1701 in Quebec. At 7 she lost her father, and her family went through great poverty. She studied for 2 years with the Ursulines of Quebec. When she returned she helped her mother in the house and with her siblings’ education.

In Montreal she met François, and they married in 1722. He took no interest in the family and was often away trading alcohol with the Indigenous peoples. When he suddenly fell ill, she nursed him tenderly until he died in 1730. She saw to the education of her 2 surviving sons until they became priests in 1737.

Marguerite undertook many works for the needs of others. Then, with 3 friends, she consecrated herself to God and, without seeking it, became the foundress of the institute that would become the “Grey Nuns” (Sisters of Charity of Montreal).

By putting herself at the service of the poor, Marguerite overturned the customs of her time and was the target of gossip and slander. Despite her delicate health, she persevered and took over the management and rebuilding of the Charon Brothers’ Hospital as a refuge for the destitute. After a fire she had to rebuild it once more. She died in 1771, and since 1990 she has been the first Canadian-born saint.

A native of Govone (Italy), after her marriage to Carlo Gallo, Maria moved to Asti and there devoted her life to raising her 3 children and to evangelizing the young, both as a catechist and in caring for the elderly, the sick and the poor.
In February 1945 a building was bombed and 25 people lost their lives; a witness saw Maria digging through the rubble until she rescued a pregnant woman, who gave birth shortly afterward.

These were the hard postwar years, when many families had nothing to eat and many children and elderly people were malnourished; Maria often went without her own food to give it to those most in need and, defying the checkpoints, rode her bicycle to other towns to bring back at least flour and milk for them.

She came from Punta Alta (Buenos Aires province), from a family that practiced the Catholic faith. Her parents, Angelita and Manolo Perrín (today also a Servant of God), were among the first to join the Focolare Movement in that city.

At 26 she married Luis and soon became pregnant. A tongue cancer was soon detected, and she was advised to have an abortion to treat her illness. She flatly refused, with firm Christian conviction, aware that she was risking her life.

When she had to tell her students about her health, she confided: “We have often talked about God being Love. Now I can tell you it is the deepest experience I am living. [...] You don’t know what it is to abandon yourself to Him and tell Him, ‘You act. This is your will, show yourself as You wish.’ He covers everything. His love truly makes itself felt. It’s as if the heart bursts.”
She died on March 1, 1985, weeks after giving birth to her daughter Agustina. Her remains rest in the Focolare Mariapolis, “a joyful place,” as she wished.

Concetta was born in Minnito in 1894 and as a girl suffered greatly from her father’s harsh treatment; he took her with him to Brazil, where he went looking for work. There she married a young railway worker, Vito, who died in the First World War.

After many hardships, in 1930, with her only daughter, who later became a Poor Clare, she moved to Benevento. She had to wear a monastic habit in the Passionist style and live in a house for the education of little children. From then on everyone called her Sister Concetta, though she was never a nun.

The Lord poured out many gifts on her: prophecy, miracles, visions, ecstasies, stigmata and the pains of the Passion. In the humble little room where she lived, on Via Monteoliveto, on February 17, 1947, for 3 hours blood gushed as from a spring from an image of Jesus of the Holy Shroud and stayed boiling. The phenomenon was repeated on February 28 and March 4. From that day on, miraculous events followed one another.
She died on Good Friday, March 27, 1953, at 59. The miraculous events of her life have been officially recognized by the diocesan bishop.
She had served as a catechist and youth leader in her parish and met Carlo. In 1991 they married and moved to Carpanè, Vicenza (Italy).

In 1994, during her third pregnancy, a tumor that had struck her at 18 reappeared. She made the difficult decision to give priority to the baby’s life. The letter she wrote from the hospital to her son, a few months old, sensing the outcome, tells the story: “Dear Riccardo, you must know that you are not here by chance. The Lord wanted you to be born in spite of everything... when we learned you existed, we loved you and wanted you with all our strength. To face the fear, we were given a boundless willpower to have you. I strongly refused to give you up. You are a gift to us. When you moved for the first time you seemed to say, ‘Thank you, Mom, for loving me!’ I can only thank God for the great gift our children are.”
Cristina died on October 22, 1995, at only 26. On August 30, 2021, Pope Francis recognized her heroic virtues.

Marie Guyart was born in 1599 in Tours into a humble family. In 1617 she was given in marriage to the merchant Claude, who died 2 years later, leaving her with a son. For a time she worked as manager of her brother-in-law’s business.

She had remarkable visions of the Trinity and of the Incarnate Word, and in 1631 she entered the Ursulines as Marie of the Incarnation. In 1639, with the young Marie de Saint-Joseph, she went to Quebec to found the missions of New France. These were years of the highest mystical life, reflected in her thousands of letters.

Amid wars and uprisings, uncertainty, martyrdom and missionary challenge, Marie became the heart of the newborn Church. To support the missionary work she learned the native languages, Iroquois, Algonquin and Huron, even compiling dictionaries and catechisms. Joining prayer and penance to her fiery words, she won converts by the grace of God.
She died in 1672 with a great reputation for holiness. Her son Claude, a Benedictine, wrote her biography in 1677. She was beatified in 1980 as a mother of the Church in Canada.

Born in 1866 into a well-off family of eight children. As a teenager she was a fervent catechist. At 20 she married Ángel, a 35-year-old widower and tax collector. She won over and changed her husband’s heart; it was the first of the miracles of her life. In 1891 she was widowed with her eldest son, aged 3, and fell into a deep depression. During a spiritual retreat she experienced a profound renewal.

She joined the Franciscan Third Order and became novice mistress because of her gifts and religious zeal. She carried out an intense apostolate for the neediest and for families in economic crisis; she visited prisoners, the sick and the dying. She treated her employees as family and prayed the rosary with them every day.

She founded the Apostolate of Eucharistic Jesus and a Blessed Sacrament school, with her daughter as academic director. The Holy See granted canonical erection and joined it to the Order of Mercy in 1925; they then became known as the Mercedarian Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament. She was superior general for 27 years. The Cristero persecution scattered the sisters, and so seminaries and schools were founded across the Americas and Europe.

On Holy Monday 1906, in the Granada village of Chauchina, Our Lady of the Hawthorn appeared to Rosario. She healed the sores Rosario suffered from, which gave off a foul smell and forced her to live alone, away from people.

Rosario’s reputation for holiness also came from the forgiveness she granted the murderer of her son, who was stabbed to death. She said she forgave “as the Virgin forgave the executioners of her Son.”
Rosario’s remains lie in a small crypt beside the shrine of the Virgin of the Hawthorn.
Mary was born in China in 1849 and was a fervent Christian.
Married and a mother, she had the joy of seeing one of her sons become a priest and of watching him celebrate Holy Mass.

During the xenophobic fanaticism of the Boxer persecution she first fled, but then returned home and was identified as a Christian by the persecutors, who demanded that she renounce her faith; she refused with complete fortitude and was then beheaded. It was June 28, 1900.
She was canonized on October 1, 2000.

At 12, in Caracas, the Virgin appeared to María Esperanza and gave her her mission: “Help me save this world that is being lost.” At that moment she acquired the ability to read hearts, to sense when visitors would arrive and to know about friends who were sick or had had something happen to them.
Later the Virgin revealed to her that she was not to be a nun but a mother, and through a prophecy of Don Bosco she learned where and when she would meet her husband.
Don Geo was her most faithful companion, at her side at every moment, identified with her mission and with raising their large family.

On the feast of the Annunciation in 1976 the Virgin appeared on their farm “Betania”; 80 people saw various luminous phenomena and the sun spinning. This was repeated in later years, and some 2,000 people were able to see her. Betania became the fourth apparition approved by the Church in the twentieth century.

Maria was a noblewoman of Lleida (Catalonia). She married Joan Llonc, regent of the Chancery of the Kingdom of Aragon, and later suffered a poisoning attempt at the hands of a servant, which left her hands and feet paralyzed.

In 1506 she moved, following Joan, who had been appointed regent of the Viceroyalty of Naples. Three years later, a widow with 3 children, she went on pilgrimage to Loreto, where she felt miraculously healed, and she changed her name to Maria Lorenza.

She began to devote herself to charity among the Neapolitans, building the hospital of Santa Maria del Popolo (“the Incurables”). She founded the monastery of Santa Maria di Gerusalemme and the Order of Capuchin Poor Clares (Franciscan tertiaries) under the guidance of Saint Cajetan.

After giving up the office of abbess, she died in 1539. She had received every papal guarantee that the monastery would follow strict poverty and enclosure in the spirit of Clare and Colette. Despite her reputation for holiness, her beatification process did not begin until the nineteenth century. In 2020 Pope Francis approved the miracle for her beatification.

María Luisa Josefa de la Peña Navarro was born on June 21, 1866, in the town of Atotonilco el Alto, Jalisco (Mexico). She married the doctor Pascual Rojas in 1882. She and her husband went to daily Mass, had an intense prayer life and were always open to helping others. Every day she prayed with the people who helped them on the hacienda, looked after their material needs and assisted her husband as a nurse. Pascual died in 1896, a painful event that shaped her for her next mission in life.

Concluding that the Lord was calling her to be a Discalced Carmelite, in 1904, at 36, she entered the monastery in Guadalajara, taking the name María de los Dolores of the Blessed Sacrament. That year she founded the Congregation of the Carmelites of the Sacred Heart.

During the severe religious persecution in Mexico that left thousands of “Cristero” Catholics dead, Mother Luisita, as she was known, fled to the United States. In 1927, with two other sisters, she founded 12 Carmels and a novitiate in California.
After about 10 years she returned to Guadalajara, where she continued her work helping the poorest. She died on February 11, 1937. In 2000 John Paul II declared her Venerable.
Born in 1771 in Florence into a very Christian family. At 19 she married Marquis Capponi, a very religious aristocrat. They lost 3 daughters in childhood.

Napoleon’s troops occupied Florence in 1796, and Pietro went into exile with the court, accompanying Duke Ferdinand III. Maddalena had to face alone the invasion of French soldiers, who made Palazzo Capponi their barracks. Then she too went into exile.

The city was left in misery, and she became a volunteer at the hospital for incurables. She discovered that ignorance is a disease that leads to impoverishment and loss of dignity. A great educator, in 1812 she founded the first “Retreat” house to take in young women who wanted to leave prostitution. She presented her project to Pope Pius VII, who approved it and encouraged her.

In 1815 four former prostitutes began a new community life. Later the small community of sisters was received into the Passionist Family. In 1825 Maddalena was widowed. She died in 1839 after a life given for the weakest.

The Mancini family was among the most distinguished in Pisa, at a time of great political turmoil in the cities of Italy. Catherine (her birth name) had a mystical experience at 5: an ecstasy or vision in which she witnessed the torture of Pietro Gambacorta. Then the Virgin appeared and told her that God’s goodness would sustain her in danger.

Catherine married at 12 and had two children, but her first husband, Baccio, died when she was 16. Yielding to family pressure, she married again, to Guglielmo. In 8 years she had 5 children, and she nursed her husband through his final illness.

Catherine’s family tried to marry her off a third time, but she firmly refused and gave herself to works of piety and charity. She turned her house into a hospital. Renamed Mary, she entered the Dominican Third Order, which probably put her in touch with Catherine of Siena; a letter that saint wrote to her has been preserved.

She entered the lax Dominican convent of Santa Croce to restore strict observance there. Then she left to found another community that became a model of religious life throughout Italy. She died in 1431; her cult was approved in 1855.

María Teresa, already a widow and 83 years old, was taken under arrest on October 19, 1936, to the Franciscan convent of Fons Salutis together with her four daughters, Poor Clare and Augustinian nuns. The militiamen wanted to leave the mother behind, but she refused, since she wished to accompany her daughters to encourage them in their supreme hour.
On October 25, the feast of Christ the King, they were all killed together in the town of Alzira, Valencia.
On March 11, 2001, Saint John Paul II beatified them together with the 233 Martyrs of the religious persecution in Valencia during the Spanish Civil War (1936).

She was born in 1562 into a noble family of Genoa with 9 children. At 17 she married Angelo, a man of great talents and also very devout. They respected and loved each other deeply. In 1587 Angelo died, leaving Vittoria with 5 children and one on the way.

Heartbroken, she fell into a deep depression. She asked the Virgin to care for her children and saw her reach out her arm and say: “Vittoria, I want to take not only your children but you yourself… Be calm and cheerful, and do not fear. I want you to devote yourself in everything and seek only to love God above all things.”

She began to live more simply, to do penance and to help the poor and the sick. She was a model for her children. Two daughters entered a monastery and three sons became friars. Fra Tommaso, the youngest, died as a deacon and was declared Venerable.

Vittoria could then fulfill a wish she had had since the Virgin’s intervention: to found a congregation devoted entirely to Mary. She was named its first prioress in 1604 and guided her sisters with motherly care.
When she died in 1617 her body gave off a perfume “not of this world” and remained incorrupt. In 1828 she was beatified by Pope Leo XII.
Mary was the wife of Clopas, and probably a relative of the Blessed Virgin Mary. She is considered the mother of James the Less, who later was bishop of Jerusalem.

They were part of the group that followed the Lord throughout Galilee. Saint John places her among the holy women with the Virgin and Mary Magdalene at the foot of the Cross. Mary of Clopas stayed on Calvary after the death, was present at the burial, went with the women to the tomb and bore witness to the resurrection.

According to the Palestinian historian Hegesippus, Clopas was the brother of Saint Joseph and the father of Jude Thaddeus and of Simeon, who succeeded James as bishop of Jerusalem. And this same Clopas would be one of the “disciples of Emmaus.”

Salome appears twice in the Gospel of Mark. Tradition usually identifies her as the wife of Zebedee and therefore the mother of the apostles James and John: “Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee” (Mt 27:56) and “Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, and kneeling before him, she asked him for something” (Mt 20:20).
Born into an Orthodox family, she became a Catholic at 17. They lived off her husband’s small farm until he died.
She was a religious, kind person with a rich interior life, always fostering love, solidarity and peace.
In 1943 Nazi soldiers tried to take away her son and her pregnant daughter-in-law Anna. To save Anna’s life and that of her future grandchild, Marianna offered to be executed in Anna’s place.
13 days later, together with her son and 50 inhabitants of Lipsk (Poland), she was shot in reprisal for the deaths of German soldiers. Her last wish, to pray her rosary, was granted.
Anna lived to 98, and her descendants still live in the town.
Having finished his medical studies with the most brilliant marks, he settled in Lleida, where he married Dolores and formed a Christian family, leading the Holy Rosary together every day.

He made sure his gravely ill patients received the last sacraments and never missed a chance to spread good reading. He served as mayor of Arbeca for 7 years, enthroning the Sacred Heart in the town hall.

When the civil war broke out and word spread that he would be the first to be killed, he told his family he was ready to appear before God’s judgment at any moment and that he forgave his future murderers. From that day on, before going out, he prayed the prayer for a good death before a crucifix.

Even on his last day he showed heroic Christian devotion to the sick: one of the militiamen who were to execute him was wounded when his gun went off, and Dr. Mullerat treated him on the spot with his medical instruments.

Married at 16, she was a wealthy mother admired by high society and became somewhat frivolous. Providence arranged for some writings her husband brought her to spark a radical conversion. She began to help everyone in need in a district of Paris.

Her husband was banished for political reasons and later kidnapped for ransom. Alone with 6 children, she suffered the seizure of her house, placed the children with friends or relatives and fought for justice for her husband. She suffered a bad fall from a horse and then two more that required botched surgeries, leaving her lame for life.

But she fought on, recovered her property and reunited her family. She received invisible and very painful stigmata and had ecstasies she feared were of demonic origin, so she hid them. She guided young nuns and advised religious authorities on reforming their communities. She received from Teresa of Ávila the command to bring Carmel to France, founding several cloisters. She then came into contact with Saint Francis de Sales.
Pierre died in 1613, and Marie lived in several Carmels as Mary of the Incarnation, as cook or portress, accepting the humiliations of her superiors. She died in 1618.
From a poor family, Marie received no formal education and left home at 13 to work as a domestic servant in Quebec. She spent part of her wages learning writing and arithmetic from a seminarian.

Marie felt drawn to religious life, but when her employer, Mr. Roy, was widowed, she accepted his marriage proposal. Five years later he died, and Marie was left with 5 daughters to raise. Later one died, two joined the Sisters of Charity and the 2 stepdaughters went to live with their grandmother.

Alone at 43, Marie moved into the Charity Hospice to live in silence and prayer, close to her daughters. But in 1850 she was asked to manage the city’s refuge for women released from prison. To staff it, she helped found the Sisters of the Good Shepherd and served for 3 years as their first superior, with the name Mother Mary of the Sacred Heart. She lived there for her last 29 years.
Born in 1794 in Lavaltrie (Canada). At 17 she married Jean-Marie, and they had 11 children. She was widowed in 1832, and 13 years later, free of child-rearing, she took a new path.

For five years she had been caring for several unmarried mothers in her home, something rare for the time. The bishop asked Rosalie to carry on her work of charity by founding a religious community. In 1845 she and one penitent settled in a small house given to the new community by a benefactor in Montreal.

In 1848 they made their religious profession and she became Sister Mary of the Nativity, turning down a position of authority. Behind the scenes, she took part in receiving the penitents and caring for the newborns, and visited the sick and prisoners.

In the following years she was glad to see people lose their aversion to unmarried mothers and recognize the value of her community. Finally, in 1859, she welcomed the foundation of the secondary order of the Magdalens: the sisters of this order, recruited among the penitents, could take religious vows and live in community, following particular rules devoted to contemplation.
After 5 years of illness and isolation, Rosalie died on April 5, 1864.

Marius and his wife Martha, of the Persian nobility (today Iran/Iraq), left their land and went to Rome with their sons Abachum and Audifax to visit the tombs of the martyrs and comfort the Christians suffering in prison.

With the help of the priest John they were able to give Christian burial to 260 martyrs whose beheaded bodies had been left in the open on the Via Salaria. The Roman authorities caught them and interrogated them.

The emperor Decius had ordered that those suspected of being Christian, to avoid being sentenced to death, had to show adherence to pagan worship, such as adoring the emperor’s statue or burning incense before a pagan god. Marius and his family refused and were then beheaded by the governor Marcianus.

They were buried in a field where a church was later built, the destination of countless pilgrimages during the Middle Ages. In 1590 their bodies were discovered, and since then they have been honored in churches in Rome, Cremona and Germany. The relics of Saint Marius were hidden for many years in the church of Saint Ignatius of Loyola in Santiago, Chile, until they were found by chance in June 1994.
Martha was born in Antioch at the beginning of the sixth century.
A revelation from Saint John the Baptist announced to her the birth of her son, and even the name he was to bear.

After some years her husband, John of Edessa, died, and she devoted herself zealously to the education of her son Simeon, who would become famous for his very unusual life and his ascetic practice of living permanently atop a pillar.
An angel announced to her the date of her death a year in advance, and she told Simeon, including where she wished to be buried.

Mary Grace grew up between Italy and the United States until she married her church’s master plasterer in 1903 and they left for New York. There her husband gave himself over to vice and mistreated her for many years; she bore it with fortitude, since he would not let himself be helped.

She is said to have had three apparitions of the Virgin and Our Lord, and miraculous cures. She acquired a special insight for reading people and knowing what was in their hearts. She knew who needed help most and when someone was on the way to see her for an important purpose. She prayed alone for long hours, lying face down on the floor of her bedroom in the shape of a cross, with her arms outstretched.

Through her ministry to the sick, many people were healed and brought back to the faith. She comforted many hearts and taught people to pray. Her reputation for holiness and works of mercy spread everywhere. She passed on to everyone her own living faith in the Most Holy Trinity. Her wish to build a chapel in honor of Saint Gerard Majella came true in 1922.
After her death in 1927, pilgrimages to her tomb began spontaneously, and many claimed cures through her intercession, which continues to this day.

Nicknamed Mulumba (the Strong), he was born in Kirumba, Uganda, in 1836. He was captured in a raid and sold as a slave. He was first a pagan, then a Muslim, then an Anglican, and he converted to the Catholic faith in 1882 at 45. He had practiced polygamy, but on becoming a Christian he kept only one wife.

He was the catechist of the Mityana community, a role he carried out with great zeal. A man of social standing, he devoted himself to drawing as many as he could to Christianity. Out of humility he did work reserved for slaves and women, not caring about gossip. He was a deputy judge in Mukwenda and stood out for his prudence and justice.
By order of the king he had to accompany his province’s governor to the capital, and since there were rumors of an anti-Christian persecution, he said goodbye to his household.

He could have hidden together with Saint Luke Banabakintu, the governor’s servant, but they decided to give themselves up and openly confess their faith. Their captors noticed that they were very cheerful. They were sentenced to death, and in an open field their bodies were horribly butchered. The missionaries were able to bury the body. He was 50, and his wife and children were also arrested after his death.

Mathilde Chelhot was born in Aleppo (Syria) in 1904 into a well-off family. She studied with the Armenian Sisters of the Immaculate Conception, where she developed a rich interior life. In 1922 she married Georges, a wealthy businessman, authoritarian and possessive. She needed great patience to calm him. They discovered they could not have children, and he developed diabetes. He dreamed of a technical school to train Christian workers, but in 1944 he died suddenly. She took on that great project.

At the head of the Georges Salem Foundation, the city’s poor young people became her family, and she was a true mother to them. She went to see the Rector Major in Turin, and from then on the Salesians were her home and her family. She became the “Mamma Margherita” of the young people of Aleppo, contributing to the catechesis society, the Saint Vincent de Paul Society, summer camps for the poor, Islamic charitable works and work for offenders, and she served as vice president of the Red Cross.
In 1959 she discovered she had cancer and only said, “Thank you, my God.” She gave all her property to works of charity and died with a reputation for holiness in 1961, at 56.

She was born in 895 in Enger and was entrusted to the care of her grandmother, abbess of a convent. She married Henry, and their marriage was very happy. She had a moderate but edifying influence on her husband. His reign was a constant struggle in which he often triumphed remarkably. The king and his subjects attributed his successes as much to the queen’s prayers as to his own efforts. But she went on living in the humility that marked her; she seemed more a loving mother than a queen.

In 936 King Henry died of a stroke. Matilda had a Mass offered and left the jewels she wore on the altar as a pledge that she renounced the pomp of the world. From then on she led a life of complete self-sacrifice. She founded hospitals and monasteries and was so lavish in her gifts that even her son accused her of squandering the royal treasury.

Her bitterest suffering was discovering that her son Henry was stirring up his brother against her. She bore it all with unshakable patience; it comforted her to see her sons united, even if only to persecute her. To please them she gave up her inheritance in their favor and withdrew from the world, spending her time in one or another of her foundations. Her son Otto, heir to the throne, would be crowned Holy Roman Emperor together with his wife Saint Adelaide; another son was Saint Bruno, Archbishop of Cologne. Matilda died in 968 and is buried beside her husband.

María Geralda Guerrero was born in 1885 in La Grita, which her family left for Seboruco, fleeing an epidemic of black smallpox. Full of hope but with no money, they found that people were dying of smallpox there too. Her father instilled in her a love for the poor and the sick, and at 12 she began looking after those in need.

Soon her father and a sister caught the disease, and they too died. Then she became a mother to those who wandered the streets alone, physically and emotionally, amid the rejection that grew with the plague. Her secret was prayer, the memory of her father’s teachings and an inexhaustible desire to serve those who suffer.

José, a handsome soldier, shared her madness, approving her charitable desires to the point of giving up his house “to the children.” The room that would serve as a refuge was less than 3 meters on a side. She became famous as a protector of pregnant women and as a midwife, and she never lost a single one. Later her beloved José passed away.
In her old age, the mother decided to provide funeral care and went door to door begging to buy coffins for the dead. Her house became a hospital and a funeral home. She died in 1972.
Mella was born in the mid-eighth century in the north of the province of Connacht, Ireland.

She was a devout matron and the happy mother of two sons. When her husband died, she decided to embrace religious life, and her son Tigernach built a religious house for her in the diocese of Kilmore.

Mella presided over a community of women and governed it for many years. Through her influence and authority she awakened the love and fear of God in the souls of her nuns and of her two sons, who would later be regarded as saints by the people. She did everything in a spirit of gentleness, tolerance and true charity.
She is believed to have died before the year 787.

He was born in Jalisco, Mexico, in 1888. From a young age he was interested in the Social Doctrine of the Church, inspired by Leo XIII’s encyclical “Rerum Novarum.” He founded a savings bank that grew into a cooperative for the benefit of the needy. He opposed anticlerical ideas and the attacks on the Church in government schools.

With his friend Anacleto González, in the ranks of the Catholic Youth Association, he found religious, moral and apostolic formation. In 1910 Miguel joined the National Catholic Party. For defending the needy he was jailed 59 times, threatened with death and often beaten. From 1917 he worked as a journalist with a Christian focus at “El Cruzado,” taking up workers’ causes, and he organized congresses and cooperatives.

In 1922 he married María Guadalupe, and they had 3 daughters. He studied law, presented his thesis and passed his professional exam, but was denied his law degree. In 1927, during the persecution of the Church, he joined the League for the Defense of Religious Freedom, using permitted peaceful means to resist the attacks on freedom of belief.
To defend freedom and justice, he accepted the appointment as governor of Jalisco conferred by the Catholics of the resistance. He was gunned down by the federal army in 1928.
The daughter of nobles, because of family commitments her parents gave her in marriage at 12 to Duke Malatesta. At 20 she was widowed with a son and many possessions.
When her son died in an epileptic fit, she felt nothing tied her to the world any longer, for possessions were nothing next to the son she had lost and the Heaven she could gain.
She became a Franciscan tertiary, first giving her goods to the poor; she devoted herself to begging and caring for the sick and lepers. She later founded the Confraternity of the Annunciation.
Her relatives locked her up as a madwoman, but the guards, seeing how good she was, let her escape. She went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land and preached there on the Passion, dying at 56.

Nerino was born in 1945 and started working very young: at 17 he was an employee at a company in Vigevano (Italy). In 1970 he married Graziella, and in the parish he actively gathered groups of young people, caught up by his charisma, to do good works. In 1983 he continued his missionary fundraising and began helping missionary priests in Sierra Leone and the community in Pavia for young drug addicts.

In 1984 Don Vittorione gave him the title of “Commander of Goodness and the Poor.” From 1985 to 1990 Nerino and his young people helped the Sahel, the Ogaden, Kenya, Somalia, Malawi, Sierra Leone and Angola, which he visited. He founded the Pianzola Olivelli Association to accompany those in need, including moral and spiritual need. He bought an old house and converted it to take in homeless young immigrants. In 1996 it began sheltering girls who were victims of trafficking and sexual exploitation.

In 1997 he opened the Solidarity Warehouse to put every surplus to good use, and John Paul II received him and some of his collaborators. On January 3, 1998, he died after an illness, and more than a thousand people said goodbye to him. In 2026 Pope Leo XIV declared him Venerable.

The Native American Black Elk grew up hunting buffalo on the plains with the Lakota and took part with Crazy Horse in the epic Sioux Wars; later he was part of Buffalo Bill’s show, even dancing for Queen Victoria’s Jubilee in London on a European tour.

At 9 he had a great vision with a call to save his people; he began working as a healer like his father and great-uncles, until his conversion and baptism as Nicholas in 1904; he taught himself to read the Bible in Lakota, and because of his ability to reach the people, the Jesuits made him a catechist; he became famous for memorizing Scripture, for his great oratory and for hundreds of pastoral letters in the style of Saint Paul.

He wove his faith together with Lakota spirituality, embodying an authentic relationship with God beyond the usual stereotypes and drawing more than 400 Native people to the faith; devoted to the rosary and the Sacred Heart, he is said to have lulled his grandchildren to sleep with Latin liturgical hymns.
Born in Chiclayo (Peru) in 1632, the son of one of the chiefs of the native settlement. From a very young age he showed remarkable intelligence and extreme devotion.

At 8 the Franciscan Fr. Juan de Ayllón took him under his protection; Nicolás faithfully nursed him in his final illness, took his surname and devoted himself to learning tailoring until he rose to master. At the same time he devoted himself to helping the poor and visiting the sick at the hospital of Santa Ana.

He married María Jacinta, a worldly mestiza woman whose life he changed through his charitable example. He founded the Jesús María shelter for 12 poor girls, whom he cared for with his wife. He founded the “School of Christ” in a local church.

He constantly stepped in as a mediator to prevent abuses against Indigenous people and slaves, which is why he is considered patron of the Indigenous. This feverish activity for others spread the belief that he had the gift of bilocation.

He died in Lima in 1677 in the odor of sanctity, and Lima’s high authorities attended his burial. His beatification was begun, and the Jesuit Sartolo wrote The Admirable Life and Prodigious Death of Nicolás Ayllón, calling him “Nicolás de Dios.” But the process soon foundered because of the Jesuits’ problems with the Inquisition.
Nicholas (Mykola) was born into a Greek Catholic family in Strusiv, Ternopil, Ukraine, in 1896. He chose the priestly vocation and studied at the University of Lviv, graduating in theology in 1923.
In 1924, in accordance with the traditions of his rite, he married Josefa Sartych before being ordained a priest. They had two sons and two daughters.

He carried out his work with zeal and perseverance. To him are owed the building of the church and the overcoming of many difficulties the Catholic communities had been facing, which grew worse with Russia’s victory in the Second World War, since the aim was to make the Greek Catholic Church disappear.

They tried to intimidate him, but he did not give up his priestly duties or his Catholic faith. He was arrested in 1946 and accused of anti-state activities, and had to await trial in prison. He was sentenced to 10 years of forced labor in the Javas concentration camp (Moldova). His health could not withstand the brutal conditions of the camp, and he died on May 25, 1951. He was beatified as a martyr by John Paul II in 2001 during his visit to Ukraine.

Nicholas was born in 1417 into a well-off family influential in his village. He was virtuous and pious, with a goodness of heart and gentleness that drew all his fellow citizens. He defended his canton in a battle and in the Thurgau war, with a weapon in one hand and a rosary in the other. His bravery earned a gold medal, but he showed himself merciful. He was a judge and a federal deputy in 1462, and by averting civil war he revived Swiss unity, receiving the title “Father of the Fatherland.” Later he even drafted the constitution.

He married a virtuous woman from his own region, Dorothea. He devoted himself entirely to raising his children: 2 sons became governors of the canton and a third a priest and doctor of theology. In his married life he grew still more in devotion: he went to bed at the same hour as his children and servants, but they would see him praying until morning in his room or in the nearby church.

Nearing 50, he begged his wife for the freedom to follow what God was asking of him. That heroic woman consented with resignation. In a small hut, given over to contemplation, for 20 years he was nourished only by the Eucharist. The pilgrims grew in number, and there were great conversions through his gifts of miracles and prophecy. He died at 69.

Nicholas, a Venetian aristocrat, entered the Benedictine monastery of San Niccolò del Lido in 1153. He had been there 19 years when all his brothers died in a failed attack on Constantinople. A xenophobic turn in Byzantine policy had led to the arrest of Venetian merchants, setting off an ill-fated war. There was therefore concern that the House of Giustiniani would die out, so a petition was sent to Pope Alexander III to release Nicholas from his monastic vows so he could take on the duty of sustaining his family line.

Nicholas then married Anna Michiel, daughter of the Venetian magistrate, and they had 6 sons and 3 daughters. Around 1179 they agreed that Nicholas would fulfill his original aspiration of devoting himself to God as a monk of the monastery of San Niccolò. There he led a very humble and penitent life during his last couple of years.
After securing the foundation of a new monastery near Venice, Anna too withdrew from the world and became a nun at the convent of San Biagio.
They were never formally beatified, but they are popularly recognized and celebrated on November 21.
At 19 he went on pilgrimage to Rome and returned deeply impressed. As a farmer, he studied and tried out new farming methods.

In 1778 he married Barbara and taught his children himself; they prayed as a family, and he took one or another of them to Mass in the morning. Of unshakable faith, he prayed for the Church and society, founding prayer groups spread across the canton.

Under the influence of the French Revolution, monasteries and churches were seized. He hoped to contribute in politics and was elected representative in parliament and member of the Great Council of Lucerne, but he withdrew, powerless against the prevailing anti-religious spirit. He later became mayor of Neuenkirch.

He discovered his gift for healing the sick, and at 50 he handed the farm over to his son to devote himself to this service. Out of envy, in 1815 the state and the Church forbade him to heal, but at the people’s insistence they reinstated him. In 2015 Pope Francis promulgated the decree of his heroic virtues.
Born near Essen (Germany) in 1898, at 19 he joined the Christian union at his job as a miner, becoming secretary of its youth section at 22. A year later he joined the Christian Zentrumspartei.
A growing interest in journalism led him to contribute to the newspaper of the Catholic Workers’ Movement (KAB), and he quickly stood out for his talent, becoming editor-in-chief 2 years later.
He saw the danger of Nazism taking power and, upheld by his faith, did not hesitate to report on the regime’s true consequences, thus becoming a nonviolent opponent of Adolf Hitler.
With the Nazis in power, the Christian community was persecuted. The newspaper became an obstacle; it was declared an enemy of the State and shut down in 1938.

Nikolaus kept proclaiming Christ through clandestine editions. In the end he was imprisoned and executed by hanging in 1945. In his letter to his wife and children he shows complete serenity before death and an unshakable faith in Christ.

Born in Portugal in 1360, the illegitimate son of a knight; a year later he was legitimized and received the typical education of nobles of the time. At 13 he entered the queen’s court and was soon a knight. At 16 he married the rich young widow Leonor; their two sons died young, and their daughter Beatriz married the son of King John I.

When a struggle broke out for the Portuguese crown against the king of Castile, Nuno was named commander-in-chief of the army and led it to final victory with brilliant tactics against a much larger Franco-Spanish army.

His love for the Eucharist and for the Virgin Mary were the pillars of his interior life. His personal standard bore images of Christ crucified, of Mary and of Saints James and George. He had churches and monasteries built.

When his wife died in 1387, he gave his property to his daughter and to the veterans, and in time he entered as a Carmelite monk the convent he had founded. He devoted himself to almsgiving and the daily distribution of food. He chose the humblest rank, lay brother, and died at Easter 1431; his reputation for holiness spread at once.

He was born in Niardo, in the province of Brescia, around 1150. His father was a knight and governor of Valcamonica. Obizio became a knight and had a successful military career. He married Countess Inglissenda Porro.

In 1191 he was leading an army against the Bergamasques, and Obizio and all the fighters sank into a river. While in the water he had a terrifying vision of hell, but he escaped drowning and decided to devote himself to the spiritual life. Despite his family’s resistance, his determination won them over, and even two of his children became a nun and a monk.

Obizio lived in complete poverty, penance and prayer and devoted himself to working for a Benedictine convent. In 1197 he was allowed to become an oblate, and he spent the rest of his life in the monastery, performing many acts of charity. He was buried with honor in the monastery of Santa Giulia in Brescia, and miracles were attributed to him.

In 1498 the urn holding his relics began miraculously to pour out water. They were moved to the altar, and in 1553 the phenomenon happened again. In 1527 Romanino painted the series “Story of Saint Obizio” in the basilica of San Salvatore in Brescia. In 1600 the cult of Saint Obizio was approved by the Vatican.
During his stay in Normandy he converted, was baptized and was formed by the life stories of European saints.
After many difficulties he was chosen king of Norway, managed to root out paganism, officially instituted the law of Christ in 1024 and brought in many priests and bishops.
He enacted a law of equality under which the aristocracy could be punished the same as peasants.
He fell in battle praying “God help me”; a year later his reputation for holiness had spread far and wide.
Norwegians see him as a great champion of their national independence; Norway’s coat of arms is a lion holding Saint Olaf’s battle-axe.

The Spanish spouses Francisco and Concepción had a daughter, Conchita Barrecheguren García, who from childhood was in poor health because of a very acute enterocolitis, and so her parents became her teachers.
At a very early age she felt called to religious life and wished to become a Carmelite, but she could not because of her illness, and she died in Granada on May 13, 1927, at 22.
In 1937 Francisco was widowed, and in 1945, after giving part of his property to the Congregation of the “Slaves of the Eucharist,” he created a School Foundation devoted to teaching poor children.
At 68 he became a Redemptorist priest and spent his last years at the service of the sick and the elderly.
On May 5, 2020, Pope Francis approved the decree recognizing at the same time the heroic virtues of Francisco and his daughter Conchita.

He belonged to a lineage of power and importance in Icelandic history. He was the nephew of the celebrated bishop Saint Thorlak, patron of the island. Educated at the English court and in a monastery, he was cultured, a lover of art and pious, and he cultivated poetry and writing. He had stories of Icelandic culture compiled, along with works of the Church Fathers and the Scriptures.

He married Herdís, a noblewoman of equal wealth and rank. When Thorlak died, his family decided he was the best suited to succeed him in governing the Church, and in 1195 he was consecrated bishop. His wife gave great support to the missionary work; she was the one who managed the diocese, which within a few years was well provided for, without excess or luxury, since its goods served the Church and the needy.

In 1207 Herdís and a daughter drowned. At that time his diocese had 220 churches and 290 priests. Paul died in 1211 and was buried in a stone coffin he had carved himself over the years, a task that served him as preparation for death. Iceland has venerated him as a saint ever since.

His remains disappeared, but in 1954, 700 years later, a stone coffin was found with a skeleton, a crosier and liturgical vestments: it was the bishop Saint Paul. His relics were placed in the cathedral.
Pammachius was a Roman citizen, a senator of great culture, who in 385 married Paulina, the second daughter of Saint Paula.

He was probably among those who denounced Jerome to Pope Saint Siricius for supporting heretical theories. He wrote to Jerome to tell him he found his praise of virginity and his disdain for marriage excessive. Jerome was later condemned in a synod in Rome and by the bishop Saint Ambrose of Milan.

After he was widowed he devoted the rest of his life to study and works of charity for the blind, the crippled and the poor. With Saint Fabiola he built a large hospice for pilgrims in Porto. He wrote to Numidia urging them to abandon the Donatist schism and return to orthodoxy, and received a letter of thanks from the bishop Saint Augustine.
Pammachius had a chapel in his house on the Caelian Hill. There, in the church of Saints John and Paul, are the remains of the saint’s house.

Xu lived during the Ming dynasty and was a colleague and collaborator of the Italian Jesuits Matteo Ricci and Sabatino de Ursis. He helped translate several classical Western texts into Chinese, including part of Euclid’s “Elements.” He also wrote a treatise on agriculture.
Ricci’s influence led Xu Guangqi to be baptized a Roman Catholic in 1603 under the name “Paul.” His descendants are still Christians in the twenty-first century.
He was called more than once to serve the Chinese state, where he rose to high rank and became known at the end of his career simply as “The Minister.”
He is considered one of the “Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism.”
On April 15, 2011, the Vatican announced his beatification process.

Costanza Cerioli was born in Cremona into a noble and wealthy family. Although she felt drawn to religious life, at 19 she agreed to marry Gaetano, also a noble, aged 58. But three of their children died young. She patiently bore this trial and her husband’s spiritual distance. She was always gentle and kind to him until his death in 1854, which left her heir to a great fortune.
Her last child died at 16, and she entered an existential crisis, sustained by the strength of her faith and the spiritual help of two bishops of Bergamo.

She began taking orphan girls into her home and educating them, training them to work the land. In her rich palace at Comonte the Institute of the Sisters of the Holy Family was born, and she was named its superior, taking the name Paola Elisabetta.

In 1863 she founded an orphanage for boys and the male branch, the Brothers of the Holy Family. She personally wrote the constitutions of both Institutes, which were approved by the bishop of Bergamo.
She died at 47 and was canonized by Pope John Paul II in 2004.
Paula was born in Rome in 347 into one of the wealthiest families, senatorial and Christian. At 15 she was married to Julius, a noble patrician who had converted to Christianity.

When she was 32 her husband died, and she devoted herself to caring for and educating her children. As they grew up, she returned to social life to devote herself to works of charity and prayer. Then Jerome came to Rome, called by Pope Damasus to be his secretary. That is how Paula met him, and he took charge of the spiritual care of this group of consecrated Roman ladies.

He encouraged them to put their treasures at the service of the poor and to study the Bible. Saint Jerome decided to return to Bethlehem in 386, where he devoted himself to translating the Bible into Latin (“the Vulgate”) with the valuable help of Paula and one of her unmarried daughters, Eustochium. With Paula’s wealth they built a hospital, a place to welcome pilgrims and two monasteries, one of which she and other nuns lived in, governed by a first monastic rule drawn up by the saint and Paula.
She died at 56 in 404 and was buried in a tomb in the grotto of the Nativity.

Born in Brescia (Italy) into a noble family, she was carefully educated by her parents and grew up inclined to piety and good works. At 16 she married Luigi Costa, Count of Bema, a very worldly man fond of pleasure and amusements. She let herself be drawn into a similar life, and her life of piety cooled.

But Blessed Angelo of Chivasso passed through Brescia, drawing many souls with his preaching and the example of his Franciscan life. Paola placed herself under his spiritual direction and entered the Franciscan Third Order. She helped the poor in their homes and visited hospitals, comforted the sorrowful and helped the needy.

Her husband neither understood nor shared his wife’s new feelings; he berated and mistreated her and even brought his mistress to the castle. She bore it in silence and offered her calvary to God. Paola’s example of patience and humility sank into her husband, who one day acknowledged his error, received a miraculous healing and joined Paola’s way of life, even allowing her to wear the Franciscan habit in the street. So Count Luigi’s last years passed in holy harmony. Paola then gave herself entirely to meditation and good works, leading an exemplary life that edified her whole town of Binasco, where her holy death took place in 1515.

Paulinus was born into an aristocratic family in Roman Gaul. He was elected senator and consul and then appointed governor of Campania, where he converted thanks to the devotion he saw toward Saint Felix, and there he built hospices for pilgrims.

He married the Iberian noblewoman Therasia, who helped him strengthen his conversion. They founded a monastery and corresponded with theologians: some of his poems survive, as do letters with Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine.
They had only one son, who lived just a few days. Then they gave away their wealth and took up an austere life of prayer.
Paulinus was ordained a priest in 394, and after he was widowed he was chosen bishop of Nola, serving as an exemplary pastor for 21 years. They were buried together in the church of Saint Felix.

Pier Pettinaio was born in Campi, in the province of Siena. Jocular and impulsive in his youth, he mended his ways after his conversion. He was a maker and seller of combs (“pettinaio”) and sought to become holy through his very profession.
He married but had no children, and on learning that his wife was infertile, they made a vow of chastity. He was an excellent husband, making her feel cared for down to the smallest details.

He faithfully attended sermons and religious services, showing great charity to the poor. He visited the hospital, tending the sick and kissing their sores. He sold his vineyard and then his house, keeping only enough to live modestly, and went to live in a hovel. His zeal for works of mercy earned him a reputation for holiness among his fellow citizens.

He joined the Franciscan Third Order and strove for the spirit of the highest poverty. He was inclined to contemplation and enjoyed raptures and ecstasies, sometimes in the presence of companions. After 14 years of effort he acquired the gift of speaking only when necessary. The Franciscans entrusted the novices to him, and he guided them along the path of perfection. He died on December 4, 1289, according to some at the age of... 128!
He was born in Alicante in 1904; a specialist in pediatrics and obstetrics, he often did not charge the needy, gave them their medicine and helped them with money, even baptizing them.
During the Spanish Civil War, in 1937, he was arrested and confined in Valencia, but a year later he was released at the request of the people of Alicante, mostly the humble.

He founded the confraternity of “Jesús Triunfante,” conceived by his father. At that time there was no Social Security, so he was doctor to incurable adults without financial means. He was one of the founders of a Cottolengo in Alicante and, with the Jesuits, co-founder of the Nazaret School for boys and girls of limited means.
President of the College of Physicians for more than 30 years, he is considered the “father of Pediatrics” in Alicante. He received the “Gold Medal,” and a street there bears his name.

He belonged to Nocturnal Adoration. He kept serving the destitute for free until his strength gave out. The bishop declared him a Servant of God at his funeral Mass, in response to popular acclaim. It is said that since he had no children of his own, he loved those of others all the more. After his death, events science could not explain were attributed to him.

Born in San Salvador de Jujuy around 1622. His family had received from the king lands and encomiendas stretching for leagues. As a nobleman and the only son, he was destined for leading posts in the town council. In 1644 he began his political career and was later elected senior mayor of the city.

He married Petronila; they were heirs to the fortunes of rival families, and their marriage was to seal those disputes. But after 10 years of happy marriage, a beam in their country house collapsed on his wife, killing her instantly.

The idea of the priesthood resurfaced in him. He was ordained and appointed parish priest of the vacant parishes of San Salvador and Humahuaca, and was very pious and charitable: “Don Pedro traveled all 100 leagues of his vicariate to preach missions.”

In 1647 relations between settlers and Indigenous people were turbulent. Pedro sought peace by setting out with Jesuits on a mission to Orán (Salta), despite the fate of similar expeditions. The initial welcome was very good, and a small village of some 2,000 was formed. But in 1683 the clan’s sorcerers, seeing their influence displaced, attacked the defenseless missionaries with clubs and poisoned darts. Pedro was beatified in July 2022 with the 20 Martyrs of Zenta, most of them unknown.

Práxedes was born in 1886 in Mieres (Asturias). She was a catechist and a leader of the Children of Mary. In 1914 she married Gabriel Fernández, an electrician who also worked in the coal mines. He died in a railway accident, and Práxedes began working as a domestic servant.

Years later a train struck the van her second son was driving, and he too died. Another son became a Dominican, and during his formation he received 47 letters from her, which would be decisive in her process.
