Práxedes lived through the Revolution of 1934, with the burning of churches, the desecration of sacred things and the murder of priests and religious, as well as the repression that followed. A woman of deep religiosity, she held to it bravely amid the persecution, without giving in to the desire for revenge. Her religiosity led her to care for the needy whatever their religion, in the midst of the revolutionary conflict. She moved to Oviedo, besieged by Republican troops, and lived through the Spanish Civil War there. But she suffered peritonitis and died in 1936 in the odor of sanctity.
He was born in Songdo, Korea, into a wealthy upper-class family, but his father later fell into poverty; they moved, and he had to work to earn a living.

He was good-natured and had noble feelings. At 30 he came into contact with Catholicism, but he was baptized only years later, when he became a servant in the house that would shelter a priest and other Catholics.
He married. They were good Christians and went through trials: he was in poor health and all their children died. He showed patience in these misfortunes and went on living as a good believer.

In March 1839 the persecution of Christianity began. Faith became hard for many and led to apostasies. Protase was arrested and under torture confessed the faith, but he was left very weak and, when the judge offered him freedom, he had the misfortune to give in.

But his conscience would not let him live in peace; he returned to the faith and washed away his apostasy in confession. He decided to appear before the judge again, but the guards stopped him. For several days he went to the door of the court, and when the judge came out he told him of his repentance. The new torments he suffered did not make him turn back, and he persevered until he gave his life for Christ in the prison of Seoul on May 20, 1839.

Rafaela began her married life surrounded by a social setting of leisure, with the activities of her social class combined with her duties as wife and mother. As she grew in prayer, she opened herself more and more to other needs. When her sister died leaving 5 orphans, she adopted them along with her own 5 children (2 had died young), and later she had another son, with a disability that required special care all his life.

Rafaela became more and more sensitive to the material and spiritual misery of the working-class poor in the slums of Bilbao: endemic tuberculosis and the lack of adequate housing, food, medical care and schooling.

With Rafael’s unconditional support she took vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, and in 1894, with 3 collaborators, she founded the religious congregation of the “Guardian Angels,” serving abandoned women and children in clinics, workshops, schools and residences. She built the community’s first residential school at her own expense in 1899.
José died at 76, and Rafaela lived only two more years, to 57, impoverished, having given everything to relieve the misery of her city. John Paul II beatified her in 1984.

Born in Gemona del Friuli (Italy) in 1921, he was a doctor who in his actions and works served Christ in the sick and the abandoned; with great availability and a sensitive soul he comforted and cared for them. He drove tirelessly around Catanzaro in his car to help the sick and offer hope of recovery. At a time when health care was not within everyone’s reach after the Second World War, he generously offered his work.

He founded the Catholic Physicians’ Association of Catanzaro, was diocesan president of the Union of Catholic Action Men and held senior posts for some 50 years in public and private nonprofit health care (INPS, Italian Red Cross, Pia In Charitate Christi). He was editor-in-chief of “Il Popolo di Oggi,” the official organ of the Christian Democratic Party in his province.

He was nourished by the Eucharist, Marian devotion and the Word. He lived his vocation to holiness as a faithful husband and loving father, and in the Church as a devoted son serving in the tasks entrusted to him. He died in 2004.
He was born in Toulouse, where his parents consecrated him to the service of the church of Saint-Sernin, and he was a member of the choir. He became a schoolmaster and had a very happy marriage.
When he was widowed he devoted his life to works of charity, giving himself entirely to helping the poor and all who needed help, with a true spirit of Christian charity.

He devoted part of his fortune to building two bridges over the Hers. He founded a hospital for the poor, the sick and pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela. He also created a free residence for 13 poor clerics, in memory of the Lord and the Apostles.
He later became a canon (living a consecrated religious life) and left his mark on the enlargement of the church of Saint-Sernin as director of works.
He died in Toulouse on July 3, 1118, and was buried in the residence he had founded. Many miraculous healings took place there.
He was born in Piacenza (Italy) in 1140 and as a young man went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land; afterward he worked as a cobbler, keeping up his spiritual life and teaching catechism.
He married and had 6 children (but 5 died early).

He went on pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela, and on his return devoted himself to works of charity; with the aid he was given and the help of companions he founded a hospice where he took in the poor and the sick, pilgrims, abandoned children and marginalized women.
He promoted public morality, peace between cities and good civic life; he died in the year 1200.

A Catalan aristocrat, she was related to the House of Aragon-Barcelona. She was baptized with the name of her great-grandmother, who had been an “archdeaconess” of the Cathars. They were of the dynasty that for three quarters of a century, until 1343, would rule this kingdom in the middle of the sea, with a mainland strip in the south of France.
At 20 Esclaramunda married James II of Majorca in Perpignan, becoming queen consort of the Kingdom of Majorca from 1276 to 1311.
Among her children were an heir to the crown and a Franciscan friar. She later took on the guardianship of her grandson James III of Majorca.
The chronicler Muntaner describes her as “one of the wisest and most honest of women.” She was admitted to the Mercedarian Order in 1291.
The spouses lived in Perpignan, where the palace of the kings of Majorca still stands today. Esclaramunda outlived her husband by only 5 years, dying in that city at 56.
Renée-Marie was born in 1751 in Angers (Maine-et-Loire). Married to Monsieur Dumont, she had raised ten children and was later widowed.
An admirable Christian, she rendered great services to the Church by receiving poor and non-juring priests in the name of the Christian faith.
In 1793 she was at the house of a canon of Angers cathedral who had perished in the drownings at Nantes. It was there that she was arrested and held in the castle.

On March 18 of the following year she appeared before the Revolutionary Committee, which had set itself up in the bishop’s residence. There she declared she would rather die than renounce her religion.
On March 28, 1794, she was sentenced to death and guillotined the same day. Renée-Marie was beatified in 1984.

The heir married Sophie at 23 in 1859, and they soon became King and Queen of the Two Sicilies, at a critical time because of the threat of invasion by Garibaldi with his Piedmontese army. Far from worrying about the crown’s frivolous affairs, they took responsibility for defending their realm. During the siege of their stronghold at Gaeta in 1860, showing uncommon heroism, Sophie stood with the soldiers, sharing their food, tending the wounded, embracing the dying, encouraging them and rallying them. From then on she was called “the Warrior Queen.”

They went into exile in Rome with Pope Pius IX and named a government in exile, but they did not manage to recover their kingdom. Along with the drama of having lost their realm, the couple faced a series of personal problems. He underwent surgery, and they finally conceived their only daughter, who sadly died at 3 months.
Francis devoted the rest of his life to prayer, daily Mass and charity, using the pseudonym Mr. Fabiani, between Rome, Paris and Trento, where he died at 58.
Rhoda was a Protestant until 1939 in Ohio, when a nun taught her to pray the rosary during a long hospital stay for cancer.

She converted to Catholicism and began having apparitions of Jesus and of Saint Thérèse; in this way she was inexplicably healed of the wounds from the removal of a 17-kilo intestinal tumor and of a broken ankle.

Miraculous healings took place in her house, such as that of her 19-year-old neighbor Rita Rizzo, who was healed and later entered a convent, in time becoming the famous Mother Angelica of the EWTN network.

Now free of chronic illness, Rhoda suffered the stigmata, bleeding from the crown of thorns and with marks on her hands; but she said the most astonishing miracle was getting her husband George to stop drinking, repentant after years of chronic alcoholism.
Some 14,000 people visited her coffin, and miraculous healings are attributed to her there.
Richard is believed to have been a king of Wessex (an ancient kingdom in the western region of England). His wife Wuna was the sister of Saint Boniface.

Through his prayers he obtained the recovery of his 3-year-old son Willibald, whom he laid at the foot of a large crucifix set up in a public place when the child’s life was in danger from a serious illness.

In 720 Richard renounced his possessions and went on pilgrimage with his sons to Rome to venerate the sacred relics of the holy apostles and meet Pope Saint Gregory II. But he never reached the Eternal City, for while passing through Lucca he fell ill and died. He is buried in the church of San Frediano.

His children continued on their way and became the great apostles Saint Walburga (abbess), Saint Wunibald (abbot) and Saint Willibald (first bishop of Eichstätt), which made their father all the more venerated in Lucca, where he has always been known as “Saint Richard the Pilgrim.”
Many miracles are said to have happened at his tomb.

Richard was raised a Protestant and opened a school. Shortly afterward he converted to Catholicism. Forty years after the dissolution of the monasteries, Wales kept its intense Catholicism in its faithful families. Missionaries arrived from the continent, and Queen Elizabeth set out to uproot the faith by cutting off the channels of sacramental grace and silencing its voices. She ordered Catholics to be dealt with more forcefully, especially all schoolmasters. The bishops had him arrested for “encouraging others to convert,” but he refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

The judge had him taken to a Protestant church, but Richard interrupted the preacher with the rattling of his chains. They had to pay some people to testify falsely. The judge summoned his wife with their little son and urged her not to imitate her husband. She replied: “You need only give the witnesses a little money and they will soon testify against me too.” In 4 years of prison he wrote religious poems in Welsh urging his countrymen to stay faithful to the Church and condemning the new religion. On October 15, 1584, he became the first Welsh victim of this phase of the persecution.
He was admitted to one of the professional associations of barristers of England and Wales, and later to the national Council.

In 1668 he was accused of a Popish plot and, with no judicial proceedings, confined for 8 months. He was convicted of an alleged conspiracy against the king, but was offered freedom if he would confess to being part of a plot and reveal the properties of the Jesuits he had advised. Richard denied any conspiracy and was then taken to the scaffold.
Dorothy, despite being a militant Protestant who had even offered reports against Catholics, stood by her husband to the end, and she is believed to have converted.

Rictrude was born in Gascony (France) in 612 into a family as rich as it was devout. Another French noble, Saint Adalbard, used to visit that house; he won the favor of King Clovis II and, despite the opposition of the Gascon aristocrats, obtained Rictrude as his wife. They went to live in the region of Flanders and led a “devout and charming” life, as her biographer says. All their children were venerated as saints: Adalsind, Clotsind, Mauront and Eusebia.

However, in 652 Adalbard was murdered by Gascons, presumably still hostile to his marriage to Rictrude. He thus earned mention as a martyr, although his commemoration is in fact no longer in the Roman Martyrology.

Because of her husband’s tragic death, Rictrude expressed the wish to become a nun, but her confessor Amand advised her to wait, at least until her son was old enough to enter life at court. Clovis II intended to give her as a wife to one of his protégés, but Amand managed to persuade him, and she was able to go happily to Marchiennes, where she founded a monastery for men and one for women. She was abbess for many years, and her two eldest daughters were also nuns in that monastery, one of them succeeding her as abbess when she died in 678.
She was born in 1381 in Cascia, in Umbria near Assisi, to devout parents who were called the “Peacemakers of Jesus Christ” because they used to settle quarrels between neighbors.

Though unable to read or write, they taught Rita everything about the faith. She wanted to be a nun, but her parents chose Paolo as her husband. Rita obeyed, and so God wished to offer her as an example of an admirable wife in the harshest circumstances. He was a drinker, a womanizer and abusive, but Rita was faithful to him, finding her strength in Christ, in prayer and in silence.

After 20 years Paolo asked forgiveness and promised to change his ways. Rita forgave him, and so they shared the ways of God. But in the eyes of his old friends and enemies he had not changed, and so one night he was found murdered. Her grief grew when her sons swore to avenge his death. Rita’s pleas could not dissuade them, and she understood that it is better to save the soul than to live a long time. She begged the Lord to take their lives before they were lost for eternity. They fell mortally ill, and during their illness she spoke to them of love and forgiveness. So, before dying, they were able to forgive the murderers.
Rita spent the rest of her days as a nun and received the grace of great mystical experiences, suffering for many years the stigma of a thorn in her forehead.

In 1938 he married Neonila, and in 1941 he was ordained a priest (married men may later be ordained in the Eastern-rite Catholic Churches). He carried out his apostolate in Lviv, and in 1944 he was named parish priest of Belzec (Poland).
In 1946 the Soviet government suppressed the Greek Catholic Church and forced its bishops, priests and faithful to join the Orthodox Church. The Lyskos took refuge in his native village.

Roman kept carrying out his pastoral ministry without causing trouble. He baptized in the yard of the house and celebrated weddings in the forest, and offered Mass in the villages, in the homes of the faithful with the windows shut, beside a table with vodka to make it look like a party among friends.
His refusal to join the Orthodox Church cost him prison, where he died in 1949 at 35, allegedly of “cardiac arrest.”

Ruth Van Kooy was born in 1957 in New Jersey. While studying at Harvard she met Michael Pakaluk. They considered themselves atheists but were searching for the truth, and together they began reading the Bible regularly. They married in 1978, by then converted Christians. They continued their search more deeply, until Ruth was baptized one Christmas Eve in 1980.

In 1983, with 3 companions, she founded a pro-life chapter, which grew so much that in 1987 she became president of her state’s pro-life group “MCFL.” She enjoyed public debates on radio, TV and at universities. Her rhetorical skill was so great that abortion advocates often refused to face her.

While pregnant with her sixth child, she developed cancer but decided to stay active, mobilizing hundreds of citizens to defeat a new curriculum designed by Planned Parenthood. She created training programs for pro-life speakers. In 1993 she conceived a seventh child, knowing the risks. She got involved in the successful campaign of the pro-life candidate for the House of Representatives and hosted her own monthly cable program. She took part in the March for Life in Washington in 1998 and died shortly afterward.

Sabina lived at the beginning of the second century. She was born into a noble family and was married to the Roman senator Valentinus. Her conversion to Christianity is attributed to the influence of her Syrian slave, a woman named Serapia.

Through Serapia, Sabina began to frequent the Christian community of Rome in the time of the emperor Hadrian. This forced her to hide in the catacombs, since the practice of Christianity had been outlawed once again.

During the persecution, around the year 126, Serapia was seized and sentenced to death for her faith. Sabina was brought before the prefect of Rome, Helpidius, who gave her the chance to save herself if she renounced Christ, which she refused to do. Because of this response, taken as an affront, Sabina was beheaded and her property confiscated.
In 430 the relics of Saint Sabina were placed in the basilica that bears her name, considered for its beauty a landmark in the history of art.

Saint Eustace of Luxeuil was traveling back from Bavaria and was lodged where the girl Salaberga lived; she was blind. The saint anointed her eyelids with blessed oil and prayed, and God restored her sight.
In time her parents married her to the noble knight Blandin. They had 5 children, of whom Baudin and Anstrude became saints.

Salaberga had endowed a convent at Poulangey, and after several years of happy marriage she and her husband decided by mutual agreement to withdraw from the world. Blandin became a hermit and is venerated as a saint in the diocese of Meaux.

Salaberga founded a new monastery in Laon around the year 650 and was its abbess. During the last 2 years of her life she suffered great pain continually, which she bore with courage and patience. After her death her daughter Saint Anstrude took over the government of the community.
Mary was the wife of Clopas, and probably a relative of the Blessed Virgin Mary. She is considered the mother of James the Less, who later was bishop of Jerusalem.

They were part of the group that followed the Lord throughout Galilee. Saint John places her among the holy women with the Virgin and Mary Magdalene at the foot of the Cross. Mary of Clopas stayed on Calvary after the death, was present at the burial, went with the women to the tomb and bore witness to the resurrection.

According to the Palestinian historian Hegesippus, Clopas was the brother of Saint Joseph and the father of Jude Thaddeus and of Simeon, who succeeded James as bishop of Jerusalem. And this same Clopas would be one of the “disciples of Emmaus.”

Salome appears twice in the Gospel of Mark. Tradition usually identifies her as the wife of Zebedee and therefore the mother of the apostles James and John: “Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee” (Mt 27:56) and “Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, and kneeling before him, she asked him for something” (Mt 20:20).

Born in Montevideo, he was orphaned and with help went to study in Europe intending to follow a priestly vocation, but he soon discovered his passion for Medicine. The First World War forced him to return, and he did his medical internship in a prison while serving as president of the Federation of Catholic Youth. He specialized in Medical Semiology and went to work at the Post Office and as a teacher. In 1919 he married Esther.

He was president of the Catholic Workers’ Circle, the National Catholic Union for Social Action and the Association of Catholic Professionals. He was a prolific journalist, at El Bien Público, El Debate, El Plata and La Tribuna Popular, and a driving force behind Radio Sarandí.

With the Civic Union of Uruguay he was elected to the House of Representatives in 1943 and was reelected 3 times. There he was a determined pro-life activist at a time when abortion on demand had been approved, and he succeeded in having abortion reinstated as a crime. In recognition of his struggle, Pius XI conferred on him the Order of Saint Gregory the Great.
He died prematurely while pursuing his great hobby, fishing, and received many tributes.

Sándor (Alexander) was born in Szeged, Hungary, in 1904. He lost his father as a small child and was raised by his peasant mother in humble circumstances, though not cut off from the city’s museums and culture. Deeply Marian, he devoted himself to religious ethnography grounded in the Christian vision: “The Catholic faith interweaves my worldview and my science.”

At the end of the Second World War he secretly drafted a Hungarian Christian Democratic proposal seeking a moral revolution based on the teachings of Christ. For 2 years he was a member of parliament, fighting the gradual removal of Christian roots from religious education. In 1947, with the newborn socialist people’s republic, he resigned from parliament; his ideas made him persecuted and accused from both right and left. He never stopped fighting for freedoms by proposing the social doctrine of the Church, but he now concentrated on religious ethnographic research, earning his place in Hungarian and European literature. Barred from the universities by the Soviet regime, he would have had a greater professional career had he not persevered in his faith.

He paid for the schooling of poor families, even while in need himself. He suffered the annulment of his marriage, but he forgave and, on learning that his former wife had conceived a child, gave her financial and emotional support, cared for her in her illness and adopted the child as his own. He died in a traffic accident in 1980.

In the year 304 in Abitina (in present-day Tunisia), during the persecution of the emperor Diocletian, the priest Saturninus was celebrating the sacred mysteries one Sunday when the magistrates and their guards seized them for having gathered against the orders of the authorities.

The 49 men and women were taken to Carthage and interrogated by the proconsul Anulinus. Despite the torments they confessed their Christian faith and that they could not give up celebrating the sacrifice of the Lord.

Saturninus was brought with his wife Mary and their children. Little Hilarion, who was barely 4 years old, said: “I am a Christian; I went to the assemblies because I wanted to, no one forced me.” The governor told him, “I will cut off your nose and ears,” but Hilarion answered: “You can do that, but I am a Christian all the same.”
All of them died in prison, either from their long confinement or from the torments they suffered. They are venerated as “Saturninus and companions, martyrs of Abitina.”
Padre Pio met this remarkable Italian couple in 1924, when Licia was just 17 and Settimio was a 38-year-old secondary school teacher.

Settimio and Licia married in 1926 and settled in Rome. They became Franciscan tertiaries and joined themselves spiritually to the future Saint Pio of Pietrelcina, who foretold that they would have at least 20 children.

Despite living through the hard years of the war and the postwar period, they always saw their children as gifts from God. One of them, Father Stefano Manelli, is co-founder of the Franciscan Friars of the Immaculate, now with 1,000 members around the world.
Known as Boethius, he lost his parents very young and was left in the care of Aurelius Symmachus, of whom he became a close friend, marrying his daughter Rusticiana.

Before he was 30 he was already famous for his learning. He undertook the translation into Latin of the works of Plato and Aristotle, and thanks to his translations Italians also came to know the musician Pythagoras, the astronomer Ptolemy, the mathematician Nicomachus, the geometer Euclid and the physicist Archimedes. With his many talents and interests he contributed to logic, mathematics, geometry and music, and he was asked to build water clocks and sundials for the king of Burgundy.
Boethius was also a theologian. His works had great influence in the Middle Ages and were long the basis for the study of Greek philosophy.

He entered public life and became consul in 510. He lived “the most brilliant moment of his life” when his 2 sons were named consuls. But he was accused of conspiracy, imprisoned and charged with treason and “sacrilege.” During his 9 months in prison he wrote his famous “Consolation of Philosophy.” He was brutally tortured and killed, and the people regarded him as a martyr.

He was born in Mai-Vinh, Vietnam, into a pagan family; after his father died, a Christian family adopted him, and he was baptized at 12, taking the name Simon. He became a doctor, married Yem and rose to be head of his village, Nhu-Ly.
He took his 12 children to Mass and to confession and read religious books to his family. He was charitable to the poor, working for the Paris Foreign Missions Society.

During the persecution of Christians he was arrested while looking for a hiding place for Father Delamotte. He suffered every kind of torment. His family and missionaries went to visit him and bring him Communion, but fearing for his family’s safety he asked them not to come again. He told his good wife: “Be brave and do not be sad about my fate. My death glorifies God. Encourage our children to obey God’s will. As for my students, treat them as your own children.”

After cruel tortures and insistence that he save himself by stepping on a crucifix, he asked them to stop insisting, since it was useless: he would never turn away from the faith. He was then beheaded. In 1988 Pope John Paul II canonized him.

He spent part of the Second World War as a doctor for the German paramilitary Organisation Todt, which employed forced laborers from the conquered countries. It allowed him to avoid the horrors of the occupation in his native Kraków.

After the end of hostilities he entered the Theological Seminary of Kraków, where he probably met Karol Wojtyła, with whom he would have close contact in the future. He decided to remain a layman, married and had five children.

For years head of infectious diseases at the Nowa Huta Hospital, he was one of the first to let parents stay with their children to help them recover. A very devout man, he had to deal with both Nazi and communist totalitarianism: for a speech on the role of the Catholic doctor he was arrested by the Security Office and from then on monitored by the communist police.

He combined his work with a deep faith, professed in the Marian Sodality. He treated his profession as a mission to help the weakest, from birth to the end of their lives, and was a pioneer of the hospice movement in Poland. He died in 1995 at 80, in the odor of sanctity.

He was born in Ustrobna into an aristocratic family. He joined the Marian Sodality, and in 1914 he had to give up his law studies because of the First World War. He fought in the Austrian army and later in the Polish one. In 1918 he was promoted to captain and was twice decorated for bravery against the Bolsheviks in 1920, but he fell gravely ill in combat.

In 1921 he married Maria Szeptycka. He devoted his life to supporting the Church through works of charity and to preaching the Gospel. In 1934 he organized the diocesan Eucharistic Congress, and Pope Pius XI named him his chamberlain. He was vice president of Catholic Action.

During the Second World War he made his house a refuge for fugitives, until he was arrested for his Catholic activism and ended up in the Dachau camp. Among the prisoners he always shared the Word of God and offered help to anyone in need. For this he was harshly persecuted and his health was gravely damaged. He died on April 13, 1941, the night between Holy Saturday and Easter. Stanisław was beatified by John Paul II in 1999 in Warsaw, together with 107 blessed Polish martyrs of the war.
Born in 1896 in Łódź, Poland. She qualified as a midwife and at 20 married Bronisław.
She was captured by the SS, as were three of her children, and later her husband was killed. She was sent to the Auschwitz camp with her daughter, where she offered her experience as a midwife.

There, babies were drowned at birth or used by Dr. Mengele for experiments. He ordered her to euthanize the newborns, but Stanisława answered: “No, not now and not ever.” She assisted some 3,000 women in childbirth in barracks with inhuman conditions: cold, lice, rats and typhus. Because of the love she showed them, they nicknamed her “Mother.”

When the camp was liberated she was reunited with her 4 children and worked as a midwife until she retired. She published “A Midwife’s Report” telling her experience, which became a play. In 1970, 25 years after the liberation of the camp, she attended a commemoration and met former prisoners and some 30 adult children born in Auschwitz whom she had delivered and baptized.
Considered among the 4 great Christian women of Polish history, her cause was opened in 1992.

She became a mother at 13, when her mother died suddenly and she had to raise her 4 siblings, leaving school; she devoured the books inherited from her mother, mostly religious, and those given to her by an uncle who was a priest, and this contributed to her strong spirituality.

She managed the family fortune, taking care to give much to the poor, and thought of becoming a nun, but her father pressured her to choose a husband of her station. So at 21 she married Giuseppe, and they began a quiet life, though with several misfortunes: financial problems brought on by her father-in-law, a son born dying, smallpox in a daughter, the death of a son and then of her husband.

With the ravages of war on her properties and the family’s financial difficulties, she still helped others with food and medicine. Imbued with Franciscan spirituality, she filled her last days with prayer and penance that little by little withdrew her from the world.

Teresa was born in Valladolid around 1450. She was raised by her grandmother in a Franciscan monastery. She was a cousin of King Ferdinand the Catholic and aunt of Saint Francis Borgia and Saint Juan de Ribera. Her husband was a prominent figure at the court of the Catholic Monarchs and became one of the richest men in Castile. Together they built the chapel of the Virgen de la Antigua in Toledo, where the family portrait with their children appears.

She worked as a nurse alongside Isabella the Catholic in the reconquest of Granada, at the Hospital de la Sangre in Santa Fe. When she was widowed in 1503 she gave everything to works of charity and abandoned all luxury, living as a poor woman. She never left anyone without help; she herself cared for the needy every day, offering them food, alms, work or land. She founded two hospitals, convents, the Brotherhood of the Blessed Sacrament of Torrijos and the Confraternities of the Blessed Sacrament, which spread across Europe and the Americas.

Because of her great devotion, Pope Julius II nicknamed her “the Madwoman of the Sacrament.” Her incorrupt body rests in the Convent of the Franciscan Conception, which she had built. In Torrijos (Toledo) a street and a school bear her name. She has been Venerable since 2023.
Born in 1850 in Sant Hipòlit, Barcelona. She lost her father at 10 and worked as a shepherdess, at a loom and then as a servant to a priest, who instilled in her a life of piety.

She married the bricklayer Manuel, and at 32 she was widowed with two little ones; she begged door to door. In Barcelona she could not find work, and she prayed at the shrine of Montserrat. When she returned, a doctor offered to teach her obstetrics, and she trained as a midwife. She soon saw that life was not always respected, ending in abortion or abandonment. Advised by her confessor, she founded houses to provide Christian midwives for women.

She raised funds for a Way of the Cross at the shrine of Our Lady of Núria. One day there she heard an inner voice: “It is my will that this work be done, through which so many souls are to be saved.” In 1886 the bishop approved her Asylum of the Visitation, which took in pregnant women, and she taught them catechism and educated them. The city saw “sinners” receiving help without punishment.

By 1904 the asylum of the Servants of the Passion in Barcelona had cared for 2,500 women, with spiritual formation and emergency baptisms. The congregation was approved in 1926 and today is also in Cameroon and Mexico. She died in 1907 and has been Venerable since 1996.

Teresa was born in the province of Alessandria (Italy) in 1855. She met her future husband, the cultured and brilliant infantry captain Giovanni Battista. They married in 1877 and moved to the various cities to which her husband was transferred. In Naples, in 1891, Captain Michel was struck down by sudden sunstroke during a military parade. Teresa sank into a deep anguish bordering on despair.

Her later recovery, owing partly to reading the life of Venerable Cottolengo and to the help of her cousin, a priest, led to her decision to embrace the cause of the poor and needy. Teresa threw open the doors of her own stately home to poor children and to people who were abandoned and in need of help. Around 1893 she sold the large Michel house, acquired an old building and bought small neighboring houses: the “Little Home of Divine Providence” was born.

In 1899, taking the religious habit in the little chapel of the Little Home, Teresa and 8 collaborators gave life to the Little Sisters of Divine Providence. In 1942 apostolic approval was granted to the congregation, which had 25 houses in Italy, 19 in Brazil and 7 in Argentina. Teresa died in Alessandria in 1944 at 89.
Thomas, the 7th Earl of Northumberland (on the English border with Scotland), lost his father, Sir Thomas Percy, at 8, when he was executed for his prominent part in the “Pilgrimage of Grace.”

In 1558 he married Anne Somerset, also of noble lineage. Of their 6 children, Mary Percy became a nun and founded the Benedictines of Brussels, from whom almost all the Benedictine nuns in England descend.

His loyalty to the Catholic Church was well known, but at first he managed to keep the favor of Queen Elizabeth I, while anti-Catholic measures were passed in Parliament. Then a systematic persecution of Catholics broke out.

He then took part in a failed Rising of the North that tried to free the Catholic Mary and restore her as queen. He had to flee to Scotland, where he was captured, and 3 years later he was sold to England for... just 2,000 pounds.
He refused the offer to save himself by renouncing Catholicism, and so he was beheaded for treason in 1572. Leo XIII beatified him as a martyr in 1895.

Tom was born in 1938 in South Dakota (USA). A man of solid faith and later a member of Opus Dei, he flew for the Navy and was a commercial pilot and flight instructor. He was known in the community for his work, his quiet generosity and his readiness to help without charge.

The family prayed the rosary every night; he received Communion and made a holy hour daily, usually between two and three in the morning. Their youngest son, Joseph, was born with Down syndrome; they had been advised not to have him. They loved him with special tenderness and supported him in everything.

On September 8, 2008, Joseph, then 20, fell into a septic tank at their home in Virginia. Without hesitating, Thomas jumped in to hold his son’s head up and keep him from drowning. “You pull and I’ll push,” he shouted to the rescuer who pulled Joseph out, but by then he had suffered irreversible harm from inhaling the liquid. He was 60. His cause was opened in 2012.
He was a simple man of faith and commitment who supported people however he could, always smiling and in good spirits to work for the parish.

After the murder of Father José María Gran in 1980, the threats grew stronger for everyone who held a position in the Church. Tomás always looked after the convent and the church and was in charge of distributing Caritas food to the needy. This greatly annoyed the army, but Tomás was faithful to his tasks and knew that looking after the church was his duty. After each threat he told Rosa what they were saying to him and, with deep sorrow, told her he would never stop caring for the church, even if it cost him his life.

On September 6, 1980, soldiers burst into the church, went to where Tomás was praying, seized him violently and shot him in the back. He died doing his duty, without giving in to fear and threats. Six other laypeople were executed there out of hatred for the faith, along with 3 Spanish missionary priests, in a civil war that lasted until 1996. The Pope beatified them on April 23, 2021.

Born in Modena in 1926, at only 17 Uberto saved 107 Jewish children, who thanks to his warning were able to hide from the Germans in a seminary and in private homes. He married Gilda in 1952. His family would be a source of deep joys and sufferings, always consecrated by him to the Virgin.

In 1959 he graduated in Mechanical Engineering in Bologna with top marks and became a professor of Chemistry and Technology of Ceramic Products. In 1967 he opened a company making roller kilns for ceramics. He bought a NASA patent used in the space shuttles, and with this innovation cut a process of hours or days to under 60 minutes.

Success did not blind him; instead it deepened his Christian commitment: he supported the Ghirlandina Village project in Africa, created the radio station Antenna 1 in 1980 to spread the Word and the messages of Medjugorje, and founded the Association of Hospital Volunteers. Highly respected as a Catholic businessman by peers and employees, he died in 1989 and was declared Venerable in 2014.

Both were born in 1893 in southern Italy and settled in Rome, where they met and married on September 29, 1930. Ulisse, balanced, attentive and gentle, worked at the Ministry of the Interior. They discovered that they shared a deep, convinced faith and the desire to form a Christian family. The newlyweds were challenged by living with his parents and with Ulisse’s scheming sister, her husband and son; Lelia handled it gently but with a leader’s spirit.

With their children they took up their role as educators. They lived a simple but very solid faith, imbued with the Carmelite spirit; Ulisse joined the Third Order, living its spirituality intensely; 2 of their children would follow priestly and religious vocations. During the war they took refuge in the Abruzzi and went hungry. The Fascists watched him for his loyalty to the Pope, and to protect him he was taken in as librarian at the seminary.

In 1951 Lelia developed cancer, which took her within a couple of years, as she entrusted herself to the Virgin amid terrible suffering. Ulisse endured loneliness and several strokes with a faith of granite; he died in 1969. The diocesan phase of the beatification process ended in 2011.

Born in Manises (Valencia) in 1889, the youngest of 8 siblings, he grew up in a Christian home. He graduated as an industrial engineer from the higher school in Barcelona, and in those years stood out for his apostolate. He married Isabel in 1922, and both gave themselves to the apostolate in Manises. He was a catechist and a member of Eucharistic associations.

When his father died he took over the ceramics company, where he set an example in social matters and sought peace in disputes. He stood out for the respect, courtesy and charity with which he treated the workers. He was repaid with the affection of all his people, who saw in him the perfect image of the Catholic employer. He founded a ceramics school to keep them up to date so they could compete internationally.
With the persecution of the Church from 1931, Vicente helped the priests with teaching and other parish organizations through the founding of the Social Action Board.

In 1936, when the Spanish Civil War broke out, he was dismissed as secretary and teacher of the ceramics school for being Catholic. On February 14, 1937, before a tribunal, he reaffirmed that being Catholic was the greatest title he had. He was killed immediately, while forgiving everyone. Pope John Paul II beatified him in 1995.

She belonged to one of the most powerful families of this African country. She received an excellent moral education in schools of the Society of Jesus and the Sisters of Saint Joseph of Cluny. Catholic teaching and the example of priests and nuns led her to convert and be baptized in 1863, at 14.

During the persecutions against the Catholic mission her parents wanted her to deny her faith, but she did not give in. The missionaries supported her becoming a nun, but she was forced to marry her cousin, the son of the prime minister. Since he was a violent alcoholic, Victoria went through a true martyrdom. Even so she remained faithful, against the advice of her parents and of the queen herself.

Her exemplary Christian life won her the esteem of the court and the people. She became the mainstay of the Church in the country when the missionaries were expelled, defending it publicly before the authorities. When the missionaries returned in 1886, they found a vigorous, flourishing community, mainly thanks to Victoria’s merit and initiative.
Her husband died in 1888, repentant and asking to be baptized. Victoria lived six more years, caring for the poor, the sick and the imprisoned.
He was born in 1925 in Palencia (Spain) into a poor Catholic family. He prayed the rosary daily with his parents and helped in the fields without neglecting his studies.

In 1948 he married Asunción, aged 22, and they had 10 children. Seeking to be a complete Christian, he joined the Oratories of Saint Philip Neri to better care for the sick, and there he became director. He knew how to treat them with love and delicacy and to bring them joy and peace; he gave the little he had without reserve to anyone in need.

As an employee at the Pepsi factory in Madrid, he swapped shifts with workers to help them attend Cursillos de Cristiandad. For health reasons he returned to the Palencia area; there he used to visit the tabernacle at night when there was no Mass.

He handed out envelopes of money to people in need, saying that his children ate every day but others could not. When a neighbor’s house burned down, he lent them his own for a time and moved his family to another one where they kept the hens.
After a life of total lay self-giving, he died in the odor of sanctity in 2012.

Her parents emigrated from Genoa to Buenos Aires, and Victorina was born there in 1867. She wanted to enter a convent, but Providence led her to marry Rafael at 20. She led a simple life as an exemplary, austere and generous mother.
They moved to Curuzú Cuatiá, where Rafael hoped to get ahead financially. When she was 26 they returned, and later Rafael died, leaving them well provided for.

Educated by the Salesian Sisters, Victorina traveled with her daughter to Rome for the canonization of Saint John Bosco in 1934. On the way back they traveled with the holy priest Don Orione (who founded the Cottolengo of Itatí, Corrientes) and began a holy friendship. Her desire to work for the poor and for children grew, and she became a Salesian cooperator. She returned to Corrientes with her daughter for the rest of her life.

In Curuzú Cuatiá she founded the San Rafael school in honor of her husband, devoted to educating boys, and another for girls, and donated them to the Salesians. She built a church dedicated to Saint John Bosco. At 90 she died a holy death, in 1957.

She was born in Florence in 1322 and had a serene, religious adolescence, but her marriage to Rosso brought her into contact with the lavish and frivolous Florentine world, which seemed to have made her forget God.
A portentous vision of the Devil, as she was getting ready before the mirror to attend a worldly party, was the beginning of her conversion.
Moved by repentance, she went to the Dominican friars, and then sought through a humble, penitent life to make amends for her past.
She took the habit of the Penance of Saint Dominic and devoted herself to studying Scripture and contemplating Christ Crucified.
Her austere life influenced other women in her circle, and many decided to imitate her. She gave her goods to the poor and begged for them in the streets of Florence.
Rich in merits, she died at only 29 on January 29, 1361.

Virginia was born in 1587 in Genoa, the daughter of Giorgio Centurione, Doge of the Republic. By her father’s decision she married Gaspare in 1602, a rich young heir of an illustrious family but given to a disordered life and the vice of gambling.

Gaspare did not give up his way of life, to the point of endangering his own life. Virginia, with silent patience, prayer and kind attention, tried to persuade him to adopt more moderate conduct. But he fell ill and finally died a Christian death in 1607 in Alessandria, with his wife at his side.
Widowed at only 20, she took a vow of chastity, refusing the second marriage her father proposed in the hope of becoming Doge.

Once her daughters were married, she devoted herself fully to caring for abandoned young people, the elderly and the sick. In the postwar famine she went through the city seeking out those most in need or in danger of being corrupted. So the Hundred Ladies of Mercy, Protectors of the Poor of Jesus Christ, were born. With the plague of 1629 she rented a convent where she began the work of Our Lady of Refuge, which gathered nuns with and without vows. Later, stripped of the authority to govern her work, she took the last place among the sisters. Blessed with ecstasies, visions and other mystical gifts, she died at 64.
Although Christianity was winning many followers, Vladimir remained a pagan in Kievan Rus (today Ukraine), keeping many wives and concubines and erecting pagan statues and temples.

Finally Vladimir converted to Christianity after his envoys came back amazed by the liturgical celebrations and feasts of the Church in Constantinople. He was baptized, and his wedding in 988 was the first between a Greek princess (the sister of the Byzantine emperor) and a barbarian.
His baptism and his marriage to Anna brought very positive changes in Vladimir’s character and morals. He showed this publicly by tearing down the pagan monuments and building many churches.
The spouses then brought Christianity to the Slavic peoples: Ukraine, Russia and Poland. Vladimir was later considered one of the founders of the Orthodox Christian Church.
A member of the Ukrainian Catholic Church, he was a husband and father and also choir director of the parish of Stradch.
Captured by communist agents as he was returning from visiting a sick person with his parish priest, Father Mykola Konrad, they were tortured and killed in a forest outside Stradch on June 26, 1941.

Saint Volusian was bishop of Tours, in what is now central France, from 488 until his death in 496, at the time of the conversion of the Merovingian king Clovis, who gave a great boost to Christianity in Gaul.
Volusian had been attacked by the Goths, who finally managed to remove him from his see, forcing him into exile in Spain.

It was the time of married Latin bishops, and Volusian was married too: he had a cross-eyed wife with a very bad temper who “terrorized” everyone who knew her, and he devoted all his patience to her. Proof of his wife’s reputation is the answer Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, gave him when Volusian wrote to him about his fears of the Goths: “He who already bears the enemy at home need not fear foreign enemies.”

Walfrid, a noble of the Gherardesca family, which later ruled Pisa in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, became a prosperous and esteemed citizen. He married a young woman with whom he was deeply in love, and they raised their children as Christians.

After many years of marriage, in agreement with his wife, he withdrew to Monteverdi in the province of Pisa with two companions: Forte, a noble from Corsica, and Gundualdus of Lucca, his relative. Together they led a hermit’s life, drawing other disciples with their reputation for austerity. They built the monastery of San Pietro in Palazzuolo, placing it under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Walfrid was the first abbot, and his 4 sons followed him as monks. They founded another monastery, not far from Palazzuolo, for their wives, who also wished for the monastic life.

His son Gimfrid, already a priest, had a spiritual crisis and left the monastery, taking documents and horses. While a fugitive he somehow lost a finger joint and returned to the monastery converted; he succeeded his father as abbot when Walfrid died.
The miracles and wonders at his tomb and the example of his virtue soon spread his cult throughout the region. It was confirmed in 1861 by Pope Pius IX.

Wenceslao was born in San Luis (Argentina) and was not a religious man, but one day, going with Coca to a novena, he was struck by the Gospel. Later they became catechists of the Diocesan Rural Movement in La Rioja. They formed a cooperative, gathered goods for the needy and brought families together in their home to read the Bible.

In July 1976, in a time of great internal unrest, someone knocked at their door. Coca, frightened, asked him not to answer, but Wenceslao replied that it might be someone needing a favor. When he opened, four hooded men emptied their weapons into him in front of his wife and daughters.
In 2018 he was beatified by Pope Francis, who set his memorial on July 17, making him the first Argentine Blessed who was a father of a family.

Wilhelm was born in 1875. In 1926 he was named deputy consul in Kleve for the Netherlands. There he founded the local branch of the Catholic Commercial Association. In 1938 Queen Wilhelmina made him a Knight for his 40 years of service.

As vice-consul and a practicing believer, many refugees eager to leave the country turned to him. He came into conflict with Nazi policy, and the Gestapo began following him. Even so he took part in processions and kept in contact with the clergy and with German Jews. The Nazis took him for a Catholic fanatic and a friend of the Jews.

In 1941 he was jailed and interrogated about his help to refugees and his refusal, for religious reasons, to join the National Socialist Party. He was taken to the Sachsenhausen camp, and on March 13, 1942, he froze to death when they doused him with icy water while he hung from a wall. The official notice said “death from pneumonia due to a weak heart.” The Diocese of Münster opened his beatification process in 2020. In Kleve a street, a sports facility and a school bear his name today.

William became Viscount Stafford in 1637 after his marriage to the heiress. King Charles I made him and his wife barons. In the civil war that soon broke out they supported the royalist side and so lost almost all their lands, which were only restored to them in 1660 with the accession of Charles II.

William did not feel sufficiently rewarded for his loyalty to the Crown and harbored resentment toward the new king. In 1678 he quarreled publicly with an earl in the House of Lords, making many enemies. He was denounced on suspicion of complicity in Titus Oates’s “Popish Plot,” which supposedly planned to assassinate Charles II. William could hardly have been an accomplice at his mature, advanced age. But in the atmosphere of suspicion and fear, his mere membership in the Catholic Church was enough to incriminate him.

Imprisoned in the Tower of London, he was tried by his peers, and even some relatives voted against him. William’s impressive serenity stood out; he “spoke very little and behaved very humbly, as was his custom,” but he was found guilty and beheaded on December 29, 1680. He was beatified in 1929.

A princess of Poland, sister of the queen Saint Kinga and niece of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, she was born in 1235, the daughter of King Béla IV of Hungary (a descendant of the kings Saint Stephen and Saint Ladislaus).

She and Boleslaus had three daughters: two married, and when she was widowed she withdrew with the third, who aspired to religious life, to the Poor Clares, where her sister the foundress, the widowed queen Kinga, was already living.

Though she was the superior, she acted as if she were beneath everyone: she intensely practiced the Christian and religious virtues, especially humility, prayer and meditation on the Passion of Christ. It is even said that she had revelations and apparitions of Jesus Crucified. Her solitude did not keep her from caring for the poor, to whom she joyfully gave food and generous gifts.
In 1298 she fell gravely ill and foretold the hour of her death. She spoke to the sisters of the magnificent reward awaiting her in Heaven.

Born in 1591 in Ker Anna (Sainte-Anne), France. A man of values, deeply humble, a hardworking farmer, devoted to the rosary and to Saint Anne, his “good mistress.” He spoke only Breton and had no schooling, but he was very capable.

On July 25, 1624, the eve of Saint Anne’s feast, a White Lady appeared to him with a torch in her hand. He went to pray in his barn and on the way heard a crowd marching... but there was no one there. She appeared to him surrounded by light, saying: “I am Anne, mother of Mary and grandmother of Jesus. God wishes the chapel dedicated to my name to be rebuilt, like the one that was destroyed 924 years and 6 months ago.”

In March 1625 Saint Anne appeared again and told him, with his brother-in-law and neighbors: “Follow this torch and you will find the image.” She led them to dig up an old wooden statue with traces of white and blue. The first Mass was celebrated there by decision of the bishop on July 26. Yvon became a builder, directing the work and the cutting of timber and paying the contractors. He and his wife had been married 10 years without children, their greatest sorrow. But when the chapel was finished 3 years later, their first son was born, who became a priest, and then 3 more. The village became “Sainte-Anne-d’Auray,” the third most visited pilgrimage site in France. In 1996 John Paul II went to pray there with 150,000 pilgrims. His beatification cause of 1937 was reconsidered and presented again in 2000.
Zdislava was born into a very religious noble family of Bohemia (today the Czech Republic); as a girl she ran away to a forest to become a hermit but was brought back home.

At just over 15 she was married to Havel, a noble of the allied Lemberk family. The marriage was difficult at first, since her works for the poor were extremely generous and a cause of conflict with her husband. She used to take homeless people into her castle and personally cared for the sick. When the Mongols invaded, many sought refuge with Zdislava, who took them all in.

When her exasperated husband wanted to throw a sick beggar out of the house, he found Jesus crucified lying in the bed instead; he was so struck that he changed his mind about his wife’s works, to the point of allowing her to enter the Dominican Third Order. She had her husband found two convents. She received the Eucharist every day, an unusual custom for the time, and had ecstasies and visions.

Zdislava was struck down by a fatal illness while still young, in 1252. Shortly afterward Havel had a vision of her in glory, which encouraged him in his desire for conversion. Her incorrupt body rests in the Dominican shrine church of Jablonné. She was canonized in 1995 by John Paul II during his visit to the Czech Republic.

Born into a family of German immigrants with 13 siblings. At 21 she married the carpenter Aloysio Neumann. She graduated as a pediatrician specializing in public health and sanitation and began practicing at the Children’s Hospital of Curitiba.

She later became founder and international coordinator of the Pastoral of the Child, the social action body of the National Conference of Bishops of Brazil (CNBB). One of the largest programs in the world, it cut child mortality by more than half in 31,000 communities, helping more than 1.5 million children. It reached 72% of Brazil’s territory and 20 countries in Latin America, Asia and Africa. In 2004 she launched the Pastoral for the Elderly, providing medical care to more than 100,000 older people.

In 2002 she received the “Public Health Heroine of the Americas” award from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), and in 2006 she was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize; she held honorary doctorates from 6 universities. She died during a humanitarian mission in the 2010 Haiti earthquake. Her body was carried through Curitiba, applauded by a crowd. In 2015 the Church opened her beatification process.

The name Zechariah means “God remembered me”. Elizabeth means “Consecrated to God”. The story of these two holy spouses is told by St. Luke in the first chapter of his Gospel: “In the days of King Herod there was a priest named Zechariah, married to Elizabeth, a woman descended from Moses' brother, the high priest Aaron.”

St. Luke says: “Zechariah and Elizabeth had no children, because she was barren, and both were advanced in years. One day, when it was Zechariah's turn to go up to the altar (behind the veil) to offer incense, the whole crowd was praying outside. The Angel of the Lord appeared to him, and when Zechariah saw him he was filled with fear and great terror seized him.” The angel said to him: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall name him John. He will be your joy and delight, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord; he will drink no strong drink; he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, he will turn many to God, and he will have the spirit of the prophet Elijah, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.”

Zechariah said to the angel: “How can I know that what you tell me is true? For I am very old and my wife Elizabeth is barren.” The angel answered: “I am Gabriel, one of those who stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to bring you this good news. But because you did not believe my words, you will be mute and unable to speak until the day these things happen, which will all be fulfilled in their time.”

The people were waiting for Zechariah to come out and wondered why he was taking so long. When he came out he could not speak to them, and they realized he had seen a vision. He made signs to them and remained mute. Afterwards Elizabeth conceived a son and kept herself hidden for five months (without telling the neighbors she was going to have a child). And she said: “God has taken away my humiliation and has remembered me.”

On the day of the Annunciation, the angel Gabriel told the Blessed Virgin Mary that Elizabeth was going to have a child. Mary hurried to Elizabeth's house and stayed there three months, keeping her company and helping her in everything, until the child John was born, a birth that was a true event.
They embody the era of Christian resistance for religious freedom against the Moors in Spain.
At first they hid their faith, and some pretended to be Muslims, but later they resolved to bear witness to their Christian faith, whatever the consequences.
The enthusiasm of Aurelius and Natalia inspired their friends Felix and Liliosa to give public witness, even knowing they were risking their lives.

Forewarned by two angels, the friends, together with the monk George, took up a regime of discipline and prayer to prepare for martyrdom, which finally came when they publicly professed their faith in a town square.
